'''Raúl González Blanco ''' (born 27 June 1977 in [[Madrid]], [[Spain]]), usually known simply as Raúl,  is a [[Spanish people|Spanish]] [[Association football|football]] [[Forward (association football)|forward]] who plays for Spanish club [[Real Madrid]] for whom he is the all-time leading goalscorer. He is a three-time winner of the [[UEFA Champions League]] and has long been the competition's all-time leading goal scorer. He has also scored more goals (44) for the Spanish national team than any player in history.

== Real Madrid ==
[[File:Raúl González 2009.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Raúl González]]
Raúl has spent his entire club career with Madrid, with whom he has won six Spanish league titles. Although he started out with cross-town rivals [[Atlético Madrid]], he began the 1994-95 season in Madrid's [[Real Madrid C|C-team]], but was promoted to first team status by coach [[Jorge Valdano]] after impressing with sixteen goals in nine games. He became the youngest player (seventeen years and four months) ever to play for the senior side, scoring in his second senior game against derby rivals Atlético Madrid. In all, Raúl registered nine goals in 28 appearances to help Real Madrid win the [[La Liga 1994-95|1994-95 league]] championship in his first season. Over the next eight seasons, he won several honours, including another three La Liga titles and three Champions Leagues. For most of this time, Raúl struck up a prolific scoring partnership with [[Fernando Morientes]] (and later, [[Ronaldo]]). Raúl took over the captaincy of Real Madrid when [[Fernando Hierro]] retired in 2003, a responsibility he holds to this day.  Unusually for such a successful and long-serving player, and despite appearing in two finals, 2002 (in which he scored) and 2004, Raúl has never won the [[Copa del Rey]] (Spanish Cup).

[[File:Raúl González 11dic2008.jpg|thumb|200fx|left|Raúl González]]
He became the first player to score fifty Champions League goals when he netted in a 2-1 group stage win over [[Olympiacos FC|Olympiacos]] on 28 September 2005<ref>http://www.hindu.com/2005/09/30/stories/2005093007521800.htm</ref>, and continues to be the all-time leader in both Champions League goals (66) and appearances (128).<ref>{{cite web| title = Defeat mars Raúl record | url = http://www.uefa.com/competitions/UCL/news/Kind=1/newsId=396659.html | publisher = UEFA.com | date =2007-02-22 | accessdate =2007-12-13}}</ref> He was also the first player to score in two Champions League finals, netting in the finals of both 2000 vs. [[Valencia C.F.|Valencia]] in [[Paris]], and 2002 vs. [[Bayer Leverkusen]] in [[Glasgow]]. [[Samuel Eto'o]] later accomplished this feat, scoring in the 2006 final against Arsenal and in 2009 against Manchester United.

Raúl holds the distinction of having never received a [[Penalty card|red card]] throughout his 15 years at the professional level.<ref>{{cite web| title = The captain hasn't been booked in two and a half years (Raúl, a gentleman of fair play)| url = http://www.realmadrid.com/articulo/rma39016.htm | publisher = Realmadrid.com | date =2007-04-24 | accessdate =2007-12-15}}</ref> On 11 November 2008, Raúl scored his 300th goal for Real Madrid with a hat-trick against [[Real Unión]], with Real winning the game 4-3 but being eliminated on [[away goals]] after drawing 6-6 on aggregate.<ref>[http://www.realmadrid.com/cs/Satellite/es/1202754820540/noticia/Noticia/Raul_alcanza_los_300_goles.htm Raúl alcanza los 300 goles]</ref> He has scored 321 career goals for Real Madrid, breaking the long-standing club record of [[Alfredo di Stéfano]] with a volleyed goal vs. [[Sporting Gijon]] on 15 February 2009. He is also the top active La Liga goalscorer with 226 of his 321 goals scored in La Liga matches,<ref>[http://archivo.marca.com/edicion/marca/futbol/1a_division/real_madrid/es/desarrollo/1197432.html]</ref> and is presently 4th on the all-time list, which is headed by [[Telmo Zarra]] with 251 goals.<ref>
[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Liga#All-time_top_scorers]</ref> Raúl holds the record of all-time top La Liga scorer for Real Madrid with 226, a record previously held by Alfredo di Stéfano who scored 1 out of an overall La Liga tally of 227 in a Real Madrid shirt, for whom he played between 1953 and 1964.

Raúl and fellow long-serving teammate [[Iker Casillas]] were both awarded a 'contract for life' in 2008 - the terms of which stipulate that it will be renewed annually for as long as they play 30 games per season.<ref>[http://www.fifa.com/worldfootball/clubfootball/news/newsid=691686.html Raul and Casillas commit to Real]</ref>

{{nihongo|'''Keisuke Honda'''|本田 圭佑|Honda Keisuke|born 13 June 1986}} is a [[Japanese people|Japanese]] [[Association football|footballer]] who currently plays for [[Eredivisie]] side [[VVV-Venlo]]. He is a midfielder and can also play as a left full back.

==Club career==
===Early career===
Born in [[Settsu, Osaka|Settsu]], [[Osaka Prefecture]], Honda started playing football with a local club called Settsu Club when he was a second-grader at primary school. He joined [[Gamba Osaka]]'s junior youth team but the club did not promote him to their youth team. He entered Seiryō High School in [[Ishikawa Prefecture]] and started playing for the school club. He was one of the key players when Seiryō advanced to the semi-final stage of the national high school championship for the first time as a representative of Ishikawa Prefecture. He was chosen as one of the Designated Players for Development by [[J. League]] and [[Japan Football Association|JFA]] in 2004. 

===Nagoya Grampus Eight===
Because of this status, Honda was able to register as a [[Nagoya Grampus|Nagoya Grampus Eight]] player while he was still eligible to play for his high school club. He played one [[J. League Cup]] match for Nagoya while he was still a student.

After the graduation, he officially joined Nagoya in 2005. He started the first match of the season and recorded an assist. In 2006, he became a regular in the club.

[[File:Keisuke Honda Eredivisie 2.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Honda with VVV]]
===VVV-Venlo===
On January 16, 2008, he signed a two and half year deal with [[Eredivisie]] side [[VVV-Venlo]]. Since then he has become a vital player for VVV-Venlo. Despite VVV-Venlo being relegated in his first season, they stormed back to the Eredivisie with Honda the fulcrum of their attacking play, contributing 21 goals in 52 appearances. At the start of the 2009-2010 season Honda was in imperious form, netting twice against [[ADO Den Haag]] to earn his side a draw, and claiming another goal and a backheeled assist against [[PSV Eindhoven]] to help his team to a 3-3 draw. 
On 16 August Honda scored perhaps the best goal of his career against [[FC Utrecht]] with a 30 yard piledriver in the final minutes of the game to gain another draw for his team. Honda had earlier provided an assist with a purposeful run and through ball. 

Honda's success at VVV-Venlo has gained him a cult following with the Venlo fans and admiration from an adoring Dutch public prompting his nickname, 'Keizer Keisuke', which is Dutch for Emperor Keisuke. Honda's prowess from freekicks and other set pieces is one of the reasons for his adoration.

Standing at 1.82 meters tall, Honda primarily plays as a midfielder but can also fill in as a left full back. This designation allowed him to register with Nagoya Grampus Eight while still playing for his high school club. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

During his tenure at Nagoya, he made 90 appearances and scored 11 goals across all competitions. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

Despite the club being relegated in his first season, Honda's performances were instrumental in their return to the Eredivisie. His prowess from free kicks and set pieces further endeared him to the Dutch public. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

'''Levi "Levy" Thorpe''' (18 November 1889 – 1935) was an [[England|English]] professional [[association football]] player who played as a wing half. He made 98 appearances for  [[Blackpool F.C.|Blackpool]], all of which were in consecutive games. 92 of these were in the [[The Football League|Football League]]; the other six were in the [[FA Cup]].

==Blackpool==
Thorpe made his debut for  [[Blackpool F.C.|Blackpool]] late in the [[Blackpool F.C. season 1910–11|1910–11]] campaign, in a 2–0 victory against [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester Fosse]] at [[Bloomfield Road]] on 29 March 1911. He went on to appear in their six remaining League games, beginning a long run of consecutive appearances for the club.<ref>''[[Blackpool: A Complete Record 1887–1992]]'', Breedon Books Sport (1992), pp.196–197</ref>

The following season, [[Blackpool F.C. season 1911–12|1911–12]], he was an ever-present, appearing in the number-4 jersey in all of Blackpool's 42 League and [[FA Cup]] games. He also scored his first and only goal for the club. It came in a 2–0 victory over [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]] at Bloomfield Road on 23 March 1912.<ref>''Blackpool: A Complete Record 1887–1992'', Breedon Books Sport (1992), pp.198–199</ref>

The ever-present record was preserved the following [[Blackpool F.C. season 1912–13|1912–13]] season, at the end of which he had made 89 consecutive appearances for ''the Tangerines''.<ref> ''Blackpool: A Complete Record 1887–1992'', Breedon Books Sport (1992), pp.200–201</ref>

In [[Blackpool F.C. season 1913–14|1913–14]], Thorpe appeared in the first nine League games, continuing his appearance streak to 98 games, before being sold to [[Lancashire]] rivals [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]].<ref>''Blackpool: A Complete Record 1887–1992'', Breedon Books Sport (1992), pp.202–203</ref>

## 2008 FIFA World Player of the Year Awards

The 2008 FIFA World Player of the Year awards ceremony took place on January 12, 2009, at the Zurich Opera House in Zürich, Switzerland. This event recognized the best male and female players in football for the previous year. Cristiano Ronaldo, who played for Manchester United and Portugal, won the men's award, while Marta, representing Brazil and Umeå IK (now Los Angeles Sol), secured her third consecutive women's award.

### Men's Award

Cristiano Ronaldo topped the rankings with 935 points, followed closely by Lionel Messi from Argentina, who scored 678 points. Fernando Torres from Spain came in third with 203 points. Other notable players in the top ten included Kaká from Brazil with 183 points and Xavi from Spain with 155 points. Steven Gerrard, Samuel Eto'o, Iker Casillas, Andrés Iniesta, and David Villa rounded out the top ten positions.

### Women's Award

Marta led the women's category with an impressive 1002 points. Birgit Prinz from Germany followed with 328 points, and Cristiane from Brazil secured third place with 275 points. Nadine Angerer from Germany and Kelly Smith from England completed the top five with 198 and 150 points respectively.

### Additional Awards

Several other awards were also presented during the ceremony:
- **FIFA Development Award**: This honor went to the Palestinian Football Federation for maintaining its organization and national team despite challenging circumstances. The refurbishment of the Al-Husseini Stadium brought it up to international standards, marking a significant achievement.
- **FIFA Presidential Award**: Women's football received this prestigious award, with the US women's national team being recognized for their accomplishments. Heather O'Reilly accepted the award on behalf of the team.
- **FIFA Fair Play Award**: This award was given to the representatives of the Turkish and Armenian national teams. The handshake between the presidents of the two federations, Mahmut Özgener and Ruben Hayrapetyan, symbolized a significant step towards peace between the two historically hostile nations.

### Shortlisting Process

The shortlisting process for these awards began on October 29, 2008, with initial lists of 23 men and 10 women. These were then narrowed down to five nominees each by December 12, 2008. The final nominees for the men's award were Kaká, Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Fernando Torres, and Xavi. For the women's award, the nominees were Nadine Angerer, Cristiane, Marta, Birgit Prinz, and Kelly Smith.

This comprehensive recognition of outstanding performances in football highlighted the achievements of both individual players and organizations, celebrating excellence and sportsmanship across the globe.

# Commonwealth of Independent States Cup Overview

The Commonwealth of Independent States Cup (CIS Cup) is a football tournament established following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Initially, it was designed for national champions from the former Soviet republics, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Russia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan. Additionally, the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania also participate. Over time, the tournament expanded to include teams from Serbia and Finland, marking a shift towards broader Eastern European participation.

## Historical Context and Evolution

### Early Years (1993-1995)

The CIS Cup began in 1993 as an open tournament for champions from the USSR successor states. Notably, Ukraine initially boycotted the first two competitions but joined in 1995. During these early years, the tournament featured prominent teams like Spartak Moscow from Russia and Dynamo Kyiv from Ukraine, which won the cup multiple times. These teams brought significant prestige and popularity to the event within the former Soviet territories.

### Mid-Period Challenges (1995-2006)

From 1995 to 2006, the Russian national under-21 team participated as the 16th team. However, starting in 2007, Serbia replaced this role, becoming the first non-former Soviet Union nation to join the tournament. Unlike other participants, Serbia consistently sent OFK Beograd to compete. This period also saw a decline in the tournament's popularity, particularly among Russian and Ukrainian teams, who often sent reserve players or runners-up due to concerns about playing on artificial turf at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow. This trend significantly reduced the event's appeal and international standing.

### Recent Developments (2006-Present)

In 2006, the Channel One Cup emerged, further diminishing the CIS Cup's attractiveness for Russian and Ukrainian teams. A notable incident occurred in 2006 when the Armenian champion, FC Pyunik, refused to play against the Azerbaijani team PFC Neftchi, citing political tensions. This led to a series of controversial decisions, ultimately resulting in PFC Neftchi advancing to the final and winning the tournament.

Efforts to reform the tournament and merge it with the Channel One Cup were discussed in 2007, but these plans did not materialize. In 2009, the Uzbek team Bunyodkor, coached by Luis Felipe Scolari, announced it would not participate in the 2010 tournament, preferring to focus on the Asian Champions League.

## Final Matches Summary

Below is a summary of the final matches from recent years:

- **2009**: FC Sheriff Tiraspol (Moldova) defeated FC Aktobe (Kazakhstan) via a penalty shootout (5-4) at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow.
- **2008**: Khazar Lenkoran (Azerbaijan) defeated Pakhtakor Tashkent (Uzbekistan) 4-3 at SCC Peterburgsky in Saint Petersburg.
- **2007**: Pakhtakor Tashkent (Uzbekistan) defeated FK Ventspils (Latvia) via a penalty shootout (9-8) at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow.
- **2006**: Neftchi Baku (Azerbaijan) defeated FBK Kaunas (Lithuania) 4-2 at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow.
- **2005**: Lokomotiv Moscow (Russia) defeated Neftchi Baku (Azerbaijan) 2-1 at Dynamo Stadium in Moscow.
- **2004**: Dinamo Tbilisi (Georgia) defeated Skonto Riga (Latvia) 3-1 at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow.
- **2003**: Sheriff Tiraspol (Moldova) defeated Skonto Riga (Latvia) 2-1 at the Olympic Stadium in Moscow.

These results highlight the diverse range of winners over the years, with Moldovan and Azerbaijani teams emerging as frequent champions. Despite challenges and controversies, the CIS Cup continues to serve as a unique platform for football clubs across Eastern Europe.

He is also the first choice goalkeeper for the [[Uruguay national football team|Uruguayan national team]]. ==Club career== ===Uruguay=== Muslera started his professional football career with [[Montevideo Wanderers F.C.|Montevideo Wanderers]] in 2004, having come through the club's youth system. After impressive performances for Wanderers, giants [[Club Nacional de Football|Nacional]] opted to take him on loan in [[2006]]. Despite only playing at Nacional for a short time, Muslera's performances saw him linked with some of Europe's biggest clubs such as [[S.L. Benfica|Benfica]], [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]], [[S.S. Lazio|Lazio]] and [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]]. ===Lazio=== Muslera joined [[S.S. Lazio|Lazio]] at the close of the 2007 summer transfer window for €3 million as a replacement for the retired [[Angelo Peruzzi]] and after plans to sign [[Juan Pablo Carrizo]] were delayed due to the non-EU status of the Argentine. Muslera was signed by the Roman side to become the new first choice goalkeeper ahead of veteran [[Marco Ballotta]]. Muslera made his debut for Lazio in a 3-1 home win against [[Cagliari Calcio|Cagliari]] on [[16 September]] [[2007]], and made four more consecutive starts, the last which was a disastrous performance in Lazio's 1-5 home loss to [[A.C. Milan|Milan]] on 7 October, a match in which he was at fault on four of the five goals Lazio conceded. That result saw him benched in favour of 44-year-old [[Marco Ballotta]]. Muslera remained as the second choice for the remainder of the season, making only four more league appearances and none in the [[UEFA Champions League]]. He did however play all of Lazio's remaining [[Coppa Italia]] matches, putting in good performances. Muslera started as second-choice keeper for the [[Serie A 2008-09|2008-09]] season behind new signing [[Juan Pablo Carrizo]] but regained the starting spot in January 2009 following a run of poor form by Carrizo, coupled with conflicts with team management. Muslera's first starting appearance in the league this season saw him make several saves in a 3-1 loss to [[U.C. Sampdoria|Sampdoria]], including blocking an [[Antonio Cassano]] penalty. Further impressive performances in away wins over [[S.S.C. Napoli|Napoli]] and [[Genoa C.F.C.|Genoa]], as well as that in in first ever [[Derby della Capitale]], saw Muslera regain a considerable amount of faith he had lost the previous season. Known to the Lazio fans as ''castorino'', or the "little beaver", Muslera was also an integral part of the club's successful [[Coppa Italia 2008-09|Coppa Italia]] campaign, making decisive saves against [[A.C. Milan|Milan]] and [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]] as Lazio reached the final for the first time in five seasons. In the final on [[May 13]], [[2009]], Muslera saved two [[Penalty kick|penalties]] as Lazio emerged victorious 6-5 in the shootout after the match ended 1-1 in extra time.[http://uk.eurosport.yahoo.com/13052009/3/muslera-hero-lazio-win-italian-cup-penalties.html Muslera the hero as Lazio win Italian Cup on penalties] - Yahoo! Muslera played in goal as Lazio opened the season with a 2-1 win over [[F.C. **Néstor Fernando Muslera Micol**, commonly known as Fernando Muslera, is a Uruguayan footballer born on June 16, 1986, in Montevideo, Uruguay. He currently plays as a goalkeeper for S.S. Lazio in the Italian Serie A and is the first-choice goalkeeper for the Uruguayan national team. Muslera began his professional career with Montevideo Wanderers in 2004, where he came through the club's youth system. His performances caught the attention of larger clubs, leading to a loan spell with Club Nacional de Football in 2006. During this period, he was linked with several European clubs, including Benfica, Juventus, Lazio, and Arsenal.

# Club Career

## Lazio

In August 2007, Muslera transferred to S.S. Lazio for €3 million, replacing the retired Angelo Peruzzi. Initially, he struggled to establish himself as the first-choice goalkeeper, making his debut in a 3-1 win against Cagliari on September 16, 2007. However, a poor performance in a 1-5 loss to AC Milan on October 7, 2007, led to him being benched in favor of Marco Ballotta. Despite this setback, Muslera regained his place as the first-choice goalkeeper during the 2008-09 season after Juan Pablo Carrizo's poor form and conflicts with the coaching staff. Muslera's performances, particularly in the Coppa Italia, were crucial in Lazio's success, culminating in a victory in the 2008-09 Coppa Italia final against Juventus, where he saved two penalties in the shootout.

## Achievements

Muslera has been instrumental in Lazio's recent successes, helping the team win the Coppa Italia in the 2008-09 season and the Supercoppa Italiana in 2009. His consistent performances have solidified his position as the club's first-choice goalkeeper, even with the arrival of Albano Bizzarri in the 2009-10 season.

# International Career

Muslera's international career began in October 2009 when he earned his first cap for the Uruguayan national team in a 2-1 away win over Ecuador. This match was part of Uruguay's qualification campaign for the 2010 FIFA World Cup. Since then, Muslera has been a key figure in the Uruguayan national team, contributing significantly to its defensive solidity.

Fernando Muslera has established himself as one of the top goalkeepers in Italian football and a reliable presence for the Uruguayan national team. His journey from Montevideo Wanderers to becoming a pivotal player for S.S. Lazio and the Uruguayan national team is marked by resilience and consistent performances. As a full back, Russell was a key player for the Wales national football team. He earned over 20 caps, showcasing his consistent performance and reliability on the international stage. His ability to defend effectively and contribute to the team's overall strategy made him a valuable asset to both his club and country [Data: Wikipedia (GTJ18236)].

During the First World War, Russell served with the Royal Army Service Corps. This period marked a temporary hiatus in his football career but did not diminish his passion or skill for the game. After the war, he returned to Plymouth Argyle, continuing his contributions to the club and the sport [Data: Wikipedia (GTJ18236)].

### Legacy

Moses Russell's career exemplifies the dedication and skill required to succeed in professional football during the early 20th century. His journey from a miner to a respected international player and his significant contributions to various clubs, particularly Plymouth Argyle, have left a lasting impact on Welsh football history. '''Weymouth F.C.''' also known as "The Terras", are a [[England|English]] [[Association football|football]] club based in the town of [[Weymouth, Dorset|Weymouth]], who currently play in the [[Conference South]]. The Terras spent many years in the top level of [[non-League football]] (initially the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]], then later in the [[Football Conference]]). The club suffered severe financial difficulty during the 2008–09 season, and were relegated from the [[Conference National]] on 21 April 2009.

==Club background==
In the 2005–06 season, the club briefly reached national attention after holding former [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] winners [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]] to a 1–1 draw in the [[FA Cup]]. Forest won the replay 2–0, in front of 6,500 fans at the Wessex Stadium and a live [[British Sky Broadcasting|Sky TV]] audience.

The location of the club's [[The Wessex Stadium|Wessex Stadium]] on the south coast of [[England]] is such that they rarely have home matches frozen off even when other non-league grounds in south-west England are unplayable, though their home fixture against [[York City F.C.|York City]] was frozen/snowed off twice in the unusually cold weather of early 2009. The club has a great rivalry with its more famous neighbours [[Yeovil Town F.C.|Yeovil Town]], although it has been many years since the two clubs last met competitively, with the sides moving in different directions.

==History==
{{neutral}}
Weymouth Football Club were founded in 1890 and played their first game on 24 September of that year. Nicknamed 'The Terras' almost immediately, due to their terracotta strip, the team won the Dorset Junior Cup for the first three seasons, becoming a senior club as the team rose in stature. Founder members of the Dorset League, Weymouth joined the [[Western Football League|Western League]] in 1907–08. The club embraced full-time professionalism in 1923 after winning the [[Western Football League|Western League]], joining the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]] in the process. By 1928–29, with debts mounting, the club withdrew from the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]] to become amateur once again. They climbed back up the table and reached the Premier League and then folded for five years and reformed.

The [[Second World War]] saw an end to football in Weymouth as the Recreation Ground was requisitioned for the War effort in 1939. The club reformed in 1947 on a semi-professional basis, and soon achieved promotion back into the Southern League. In successive seasons 1964–65 and 1965–66, The Terras were Southern League champions, and they share with [[Telford United F.C.|Telford United]] and Yeovil the distinction of playing all twenty seasons in the Premier Division prior to the re-organisation of the league structure at that time.

Weymouth have enjoyed considerable [[FA Cup]] success since first entering in 1893–94. They first reached the national stages in 1905–06 when they were thrashed 12–1 by [[Gainsborough Trinity F.C.|Gainsborough Trinity]]. In 1949 they lost 4–0 at [[Old Trafford (football ground)|Old Trafford]] to [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] in the Third Round, then in 1962 they reached the Fourth Round where they lost 2–0 at [[Deepdale]] to [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]]. In 2005, the team held former European Champions [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]] to a 1–1 draw at the [[City Ground]], before losing 2–0 in the replay. In the 2006–07 [[FA Cup]], Weymouth held [[Bury F.C.|Bury]] to a 2–2 draw at home, in front of [[BBC]] cameras in what would be the first ever match to be broadcast live on free to air television at Weymouth.

A move from the club's town centre ground to the new Wessex Stadium in 1987 brought initial success, but the club entered somewhat of a slump after relegation from the [[Conference National|Conference]], see-sawing between the Premier and Southern Divisions of the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]].{{ref|popular}}

Journalist and author Ian Ridley took control of the club in 2003–04 and his appointment of former [[Millwall F.C.|Millwall]], [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester]] and [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham]] striker [[Steve Claridge]] as manager brought a new optimism. Within a season they had turned the club around from relegation fodder to just missing out on promotion to the [[Conference National|Conference]]. Gates also increased from around 500 to 1,200. The arrival on the board of Martyn Harrison and his decision to put the club in the hands of his company Hollybush Hotels as well as interference in playing matters prompted Ridley to leave in September 2004. Harrison sacked Claridge within a month. 

Harrison was to appoint Steve Johnson - the brother of [[Gary Johnson (footballer)|Gary Johnson]] - as manager in November 2004 prompting a huge-turnover in playing staff including the departure of star striker [[Lee Phillips]] on a free transfer to [[Exeter City F.C.|Exeter]]. When the team dropped down the league Johnson was sacked by Harrison in March 2005 with [[Garry Hill]] taking over. The club won automatic promotion to the [[Conference National|Conference]] in May 2006 but at a heavy price with large loans from Harrison to meet soaring wage bills of around £20,000 a week and a full-time regime. 

At the club's 2005 AGM, Harrison confirmed plans, pending local authority approval, to re-develop the Wessex Stadium, a scheme funded by selling the current ground to the [[Asda]] supermarket chain. This now looks very unlikely with local planners opposed to such a deal. Harrison is now looking at moving to another site and developing leisure facilities on the current land. Coincidentally, Asda's current base in Weymouth is on the site of the old Recreation Ground which Weymouth left to move to the Wessex Stadium in 1987, at a time when 32 years had gone by since a [[Football League]] club had built a new stadium.

In January 2007, Harrison announced that in order to guarantee the long-term financial future of the club, the entire first team had been transfer listed, and the management team of Hill and [[Kevin Hales]] had left the club by mutual consent. Days later, it was announced that Tindall had been appointed player-manager, with [[Roy O'Brien]] appointed player-coach, and the squad had been taken off the transfer list.

Weymouth Football Club, affectionately known as "The Terras," is an English football club based in the coastal town of Weymouth, Dorset. Founded in 1891, the club has a rich history and has spent many years competing at the highest levels of non-League football. Currently, Weymouth competes in the Conference South division, having previously played in the Conference National. The club's home ground is the Wessex Stadium, which is located on the south coast of England, providing a unique advantage in terms of weather conditions compared to other non-League grounds in the region.

### Club Background and Notable Moments

In the 2005–06 season, Weymouth gained national attention when they managed to hold Nottingham Forest, former UEFA Champions League winners, to a 1–1 draw in the FA Cup. Although Forest eventually won the replay 2–0, the match drew a significant crowd of 6,500 fans and was broadcast live on Sky TV. This achievement highlighted the club's ability to compete against higher-ranked teams and showcased their resilience and determination.

### Historical Highlights

#### Early Years and Success

Weymouth Football Club was founded in 1890 and played their first game on 24 September of that year. The club quickly became known as "The Terras" due to their terracotta-colored strip. In the early years, Weymouth dominated local competitions, winning the Dorset Junior Cup for the first three seasons. They joined the Western League in 1907–08 and embraced full-time professionalism in 1923 after winning the Western League. However, financial difficulties forced them to withdraw from the Southern League in 1928–29 and return to amateur status.

#### Post-War Reformation and Success

During World War II, the club's Recreation Ground was requisitioned for the war effort, leading to a temporary hiatus. After reforming in 1947, Weymouth quickly returned to the Southern League and achieved significant success, becoming Southern League champions in 1964–65 and 1965–66. They maintained a consistent presence in the Premier Division for twenty consecutive seasons, sharing this distinction with Telford United and Yeovil Town.

Despite these setbacks, the club continues to strive for stability and success under the leadership of current chairman George Rolls and manager Ian Hutchinson.

Weymouth Football Club has a storied history marked by resilience, determination, and notable achievements in both league and cup competitions. ## Overview of Fulham Football Club

Fulham Football Club, commonly referred to as "The Cottagers," "The Whites," or "The Lilywhites," is an English professional football club based in Fulham, London. Established in 1879, Fulham is the oldest professional football team in London, celebrating its 125th anniversary in 2004. The club competes in the top tier of English football, the Premier League, and plays its home matches at the historic Craven Cottage, which has been their home since 1896. The club's crest, introduced in 2000, symbolizes their rich history and identity.

### Key Figures and Leadership

As of the 2009–10 season, the club was chaired by Mohamed Al-Fayed, an Egyptian businessman who significantly influenced the club's financial and strategic direction. Under his leadership, Fulham achieved notable success, including qualifying for European competitions. The manager during this period was Roy Hodgson, who led the team to their highest-ever Premier League finish, securing 7th place in the 2008–09 season.

### Historical Milestones

#### Early Days (1879–1898)

Fulham began as Fulham St Andrew's Church Sunday School F.C., founded by worshippers at the Church of England on Star Road, West Kensington. The club won the West London Amateur Cup in 1887 and the West London League in 1893. They adopted their current name in 1888 and moved to Craven Cottage in 1896, marking the beginning of their professional journey.

#### Southern League Era (1898–1907)

In 1898, Fulham gained professional status and joined the Southern Football League's 2nd division. They wore a kit similar to modern Arsenal colors during the 1900-01 season. By 1902-03, they had won promotion to the Southern League 1st Division and adopted their iconic all-white shirt and black shorts combination. Fulham won the Southern League twice, in 1905-06 and 1906-07.

#### Entry into the Football League (1907–1949)

Following their second Southern League triumph, Fulham joined the national Football League in 1907. Their first league game ended in a 1-0 loss to Hull City, but they quickly found their footing, finishing 4th in their debut season. Despite occasional struggles, Fulham remained in the 2nd Division until 1928 when they were relegated to the 3rd Division South. They returned to the 2nd Division in 1932 and stayed there until 1949.

### Modern Successes and Achievements

In recent years, Fulham has made significant strides, including qualifying for the UEFA Cup in 2002 by winning the Intertoto Cup. They reached the quarter-finals of the competition, defeating teams like Bologna and Hertha Berlin. Additionally, Fulham has produced numerous British football legends such as Johnny Haynes, George Cohen, Bobby Robson, Rodney Marsh, and Alan Mullery.

### Current Status and Facilities

Today, Fulham continues to compete in the Premier League, with a strong focus on youth development through their Academy at Motspur Park. The club also maintains a partnership with the Boston Red Sox, further expanding their global reach and influence.

This summary encapsulates the rich history and ongoing achievements of Fulham Football Club, highlighting key milestones and figures that have shaped the club's legacy. [Data: Infobox Football club (1)]

}} '''Robert Walls''' (born 21 July 1950) is a former [[Australian rules football]]er and coach who now works primarily as a television commentator and newspaper columnist on the sport. On 22 June 2006 he was inducted into the [[Australian Football Hall of Fame]]. == Playing career== === Carlton === Walls attended [[Coburg High School]] and was used in a variety of roles. He was recruited from Coburg Amateurs by the [[Carlton Football Club]] and made his senior VFL debut with them as a tall, skinny 16-year-old on 22 April 1967 against [[Hawthorn Football Club|Hawthorn]] at [[MC Labour Park|Princes Park]]. He gave a sign of things to come when he scored a goal with his first kick. Walls would go on to play in three premierships with Carlton - in 1968, 1970 and 1972. He was judged Man of the Match in the [[1972 VFL Grand Final]] when he kicked six goals against arch-rivals [[Richmond Football Club|Richmond]] in a masterful display. He played 218 games and scored 367 goals for Carlton before obtaining a clearance to [[Fitzroy Football Club|Fitzroy]] midway through the 1978 season. === Fitzroy === {{Expand-section|date=May 2008}} 41 games, 77 goals == Coaching career == === Fitzroy === After he retired as a player, Walls immediately took over as coach of Fitzroy. With a major clean-out of older players who were clearly "past it" in the club's disappointing 1980 season, Walls lifted the Lions to their best era since winning a premiership in 1944. They improved from last in 1980 to fifth at the end of the home-and-away season in 1981, securing their finals berth with an upset win over [[Collingwood Football Club|Collingwood]] and then beating [[Essendon Football Club|Essendon]] in the Elimination Final before failing by the narrowest of margins in the First Semi against the Magpies. 1982 was relatively disappointing due to a poor start, but with players like [[Gary Pert]] and [[Paul Roos]] from the club's [[recruiting zones]] and South Australian recruit [[Matt Rendell]] growing into stars, the Lions were back as a force at the end of the season. 1983 saw the Lions emerge after five rounds as favourites for the premiership and maintain that favouritism with a sensational win in a top-of-the-table clash with [[North Melbourne Football Club|North]] by 150 points with Rendell kicking eight goals besides destroying [[Gary Dempsey]] in the ruck. However, inevitable overconfidence saw the Lions lose form and finish fourth after losing two hard-fought finals. 1984, with injuries plaguing the club and its lack of depth apparent, was initially disappointing but a remarkable recovery saw them enter the five after the final round only to be crushed by Collingwood. In 1985, the Lions' financial crisis emerged to threaten their future and this, along with more injuries, caused them to drop to ninth with only seven wins and two losses to wooden spooners St. Kilda. After this, Walls moved to his former club Carlton in a swap with Parkin. === Carlton === Walls joined Carlton from [[Fitzroy Football Club|Fitzroy]] at the start of the 1986 season in a direct swap with [[David Parkin]]. Thanks in part to an influx of interstate recruits including [[Stephen Kernahan]], [[Craig Bradley]] and [[Peter Motley]], he had immediate success, taking the side to a Grand Final in 1986 and a premiership in 1987. The Blues made the finals again in 1988 but by mid-1989 they were struggling and Walls was sacked after the team lost a home match to the lowly [[Brisbane Bears]]. === Brisbane Bears === Walls coached the [[Brisbane Bears]] from 1991-1995. It was revealed in the video "Passion To Play" that in Walls first year as Bears coach in 1991, as disciplinary action Walls authorised his players to don boxing gloves and beat 21 year old teammate [[Shane Strempel]] repetitively in the headhttp://www.abc.net.au/lateline/stories/s280733.htm until he was severely bashed and bloodied after which Strempel quit playing football. Walls' coaching style was criticized about the incident by [[Kevin Sheedy (Australian footballer)|Kevin Sheedy]] who has several times questioned his credibility as a football coach.http://www.news.com.au/heraldsun/sport/afl/story/0,,21359741-19764,00.html In his last season, 1995, he had been told after Round 15 that with 4 wins and 11 losses for the season, he would not be re-appointed for 1996. But a major turning point in the season for the Bears soon came. In Round 16, against [[Hawthorn Football Club|Hawthorn]], Brisbane trailed by 45 points at 3-quarter time and ended up winning by 7, which remains a [[VFL/AFL]] record for the biggest 3-quarter time deficit turned into a win. From there, the Bears continued their run and won 6 of their next 7 games. They found themselves in eighth position, and [[McIntyre Finals System|qualifying]] for the [[AFL Finals Series|finals]], after being second-last just 7 weeks earlier. They faced Carlton, the top ranked side in week one of the finals, and went down by just 13 points, a monumental achievement considering Carlton won the next two weeks by more than 10 goals to claim the [[List of VFL/AFL premiers|premiership]]. Despite this turnaround, a change of heart was not considered, and Walls moved to [[Richmond Football Club|Richmond]] the following year to coach. === Richmond === The Richmond Football Club appointed Walls as senior coach for the 1996 season. He was sacked after a 137 point defeat by the [[Adelaide Crows]] in Round 17, 1997. ==Post-football career== ===Media=== At the end of his coaching career, Walls was immediately in demand as a football commentator. He became a columnist for ''[[The Age]]'' in Melbourne (a role he continues to fill), and joined the [[Seven Network]] providing special comments during [[Australian Football League|AFL]] matches. Later he replaced [[Malcolm Blight]] on the football discussion show ''[[Talking Footy]]''. When Seven lost the broadcast rights for AFL matches at the end of 2001, Walls was recruited by both [[Network Ten]] and the now defunct AFL-dedicated [[Fox Footy]] pay television channel. He continues to work for the Ten network, providing special comments during match broadcasts, and with [[Steven Quartermain]] co-hosting the new football discussion show [[One Week at a Time]]. He is also is a radio commentator on [[3AW]]. Walls has been involved in a feud with [[Sydney Swans]] coach [[Paul Roos (Australian rules footballer)|Paul Roos]], after Walls stated that "the Swans can't possibly win the [[AFL Premiership]] with Paul Roos' style of coaching". In 2005 the Sydney Swans went on to win the flag and Roos refused to accept Walls apology. ==Honours== In 2006, Walls was inducted into the [[Australian Football Hall of Fame]]. His wife Erin, suffering from cancer, attended the dinner in one of her last public appearances before passing away on 9 July 2006. == References == ==External links== *[http://www.blueseum.org/tiki-index.php?page=Robert+Walls Profile at Blueseum] *[http://ten.com.au/ten

Over his career with Carlton, he played 218 games and scored 367 goals, contributing significantly to the team's success. Walls was instrumental in helping Carlton win three premierships in 1968, 1970, and 1972. One of his standout performances was in the 1972 VFL Grand Final, where he was named Man of the Match after kicking six goals against **Richmond** [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Playing career (Carlton)].

Midway through the 1978 season, Walls obtained a clearance to join **Fitzroy Football Club**, where he played 41 games and scored 77 goals before retiring as a player [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Playing career (Fitzroy)].

#### Coaching Career

After retiring as a player, Walls immediately took over as coach of **Fitzroy**. Under his leadership, the Lions experienced a significant improvement, moving from last place in 1980 to fifth in 1981. This period marked one of the best eras for Fitzroy since their 1944 premiership. Walls coached Fitzroy from 1981 to 1985, achieving notable successes such as reaching the finals and competing strongly in the early stages of the season [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Coaching career (Fitzroy)].

In 1986, Walls moved to **Carlton** in a direct swap with David Parkin. He led the Blues to a Grand Final in 1986 and secured a premiership in 1987. However, his tenure at Carlton ended in 1989 after the team struggled and lost a home match to the lowly **Brisbane Bears** [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Coaching career (Carlton)].

Walls then coached the **Brisbane Bears** from 1991 to 1995. During this period, he faced controversy over his coaching methods, particularly an incident involving the use of boxing gloves to discipline a player, which was widely criticized [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Coaching career (Brisbane Bears)]. Despite these challenges, Walls led the Bears to a remarkable turnaround in 1995, qualifying for the finals and nearly upsetting the top-ranked team, **Carlton** [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Coaching career (Brisbane Bears)].

He is also a radio commentator on **3AW** [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Post-football career].

Despite his successful media career, Walls has faced some controversies, notably a feud with **Paul Roos**, the coach of the **Sydney Swans**, over comments he made regarding Roos' coaching style [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Post-football career].

### Honours

In recognition of his contributions to Australian rules football, Robert Walls was inducted into the **Australian Football Hall of Fame** in 2006. This honor was shared with his wife, Erin, who passed away shortly after the induction ceremony [Data: Infobox afl player (1); Honours].

[[Association football]] is the prominent sport in [[Brazil]]. The [[Brazilian national football team|National Team]] has won the [[FIFA World Cup]] tournament a record five times, in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002 <ref>[http://www.fifa.com/en/mens/awards/alltimeawards/0,4638,FWC-7,00.html ]{{dead link|date=July 2009}}</ref> and is the only team to succeed in qualifying for every World Cup competition ever held, and to be among the favorites to win the trophy every time the competition is scheduled. [[Pelé]], one of the most recognized footballers in history, led Brazil to three of those championships and is the top scorer of all time in the sport. After Brazil won its third World Cup, they kept the [[Jules Rimet Trophy]] permanently. All of the contemporary talents in the national team prominent in the football world include [[Robinho]], [[Marta Vieira da Silva|Marta]], [[Ronaldinho]], [[Kaká]]. Some of these players can be considered super-stars, achieving celebrity status internationally and signing sports contracts, as well as advertisement and endorsement contracts, in the value of millions of [[euro]]s.

The governing body of football in Brazil is the [[Brazilian Football Confederation]].

==History==
In the 1870s an expatriate named John Miller worked on the railway construction project in São Paulo together with some 3000 other immigrant families from the British Isles in the last decades of the 19th century. In 1884 Miller sent his ten year old son [[Charles William Miller]] to Bannisters school in Southampton, England to be educated. Charles was a skilled athlete who quickly picked up the game of football at the time when [[the Football Association]] was still being formed, and as an accomplished winger and striker Charles held school honours that gained him entry into the Southampton Club team and later into the County team of Hampshire.

In 1888, the first sports club was founded in the city, [[São Paulo Athletic Club]].

In 1892 while still in England, Charles was invited to play a game for [[Corinthian F.C.|the Corinthians]], a team formed of players invited from public schools and universities.

On his return to Brazil Charles brought some football equipment and a rules book with him. He then developed the new rules of the game amongst the community in São Paulo. São Paulo Athletic Club won the first three years championships. Miller's skills were far above his colleagues at this stage. He was given the honour of contributing his name to a move involving a deft flick of the ball with the heel "Chaleiro".

Charles Miller kept a strong bond with English football throughout his life. Teams from [[Southampton F.C.|Southampton]] and Corinthians Club travelled to Brazil to play against São Paulo Athletic Club and other teams in São Paulo.  After a tour of Corinthians to Brazil in 1910 a new team in Brazil took on the name of Corinthians after a suggestion from Miller.

The [[Brazilian Football Confederation]] was founded in 1914, and the current format for the [[Campeonato Brasileiro Série A|Campeonato Brasileiro]] was established in 1971.

In 1988 São Paulo Athletic Club celebrated its centenary playing the English side Corinthians at Morumbi Stadium. English Corinthian finish its tour by going against the local professional Corinthians Paulista team,  who counted the likes of [[Sócrates]] and [[Rivelino]] amongst its roster, at Pacaembu Stadium in São Paulo and true to Corinthian principles of good clean football the score was 1 to 0 in favour of the locals when as agreed Socrates changed shirts to play alongside the English amateurs. This did not affect the score unfortunately although a largely packed stadium was cheering on for a drawn result.

It was announced that on [[September 29]], [[2007]] that the CBF will launch a [[women's football|women's]] league and cup competition in October 2007 following pressure from [[FIFA]] president [[Sepp Blatter]] during the [[2007 FIFA Women's World Cup]] in China.<ref name="peoples">{{Cite web|url=http://english.people.com.cn/90001/90779/6274126.html|title=Brazil to set up women's soccer league|accessdate=2007-09-30|publisher=[[People's Daily]]|work=Sports|date=2007-09-29}}</ref><ref name="peoples2">{{Cite web|url=http://english.people.com.cn/90001/90779/6274148.html|title=Brazil will create women soccer cup|accessdate=2007-09-30|publisher=[[People's Daily]]|work=Sports|date=2007-09-29}}</ref>

==Football style==
Brazilian football is known for its trickery, fast flowing, attacking style of play and considered a reflection of the country's [[multiracial]] society. Brazil's unique style is characterised by much [[creativity]], [[swing]] and is infused with various [[rhythm]]s and [[Choreography|choreographie]]s. The combination of those elements is called ''[[ginga]]''.

The great foot ability could be traced to the physical coordination and rhythm associated with the [[capoeira]] and [[samba]] which are characterized by footsteps to dance or to play under the rhythm of African drums.<ref>[http://www.thesportjournal.org/2004Journal/Vol7-No1/AntoniooMullerSoccerCultureinBrazil.asp ]{{dead link|date=July 2009}}</ref>  It is believed that this unique style was developed in the low income areas largely populated by people of [[Africa]]n descent.

==Football culture==
[[Image:Ronaldinho and Lula.jpg|thumb|300px|Brazilian President [[Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva|Lula]] with [[Ronaldinho]] at [[Wembley Stadium]]]]
Football quickly became a passion for Brazilians, who often refer to their country as "o país do futebol" ("the country of football"). Over 10,000 Brazilians play professionally all over the world.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.natal-brazil.com/communities/football-brazil.html |title=Natal Brazil |publisher=Natal Brazil |date=2006-09-29 |accessdate=2009-07-23}}</ref>

Football has a major effect on [[Culture of Brazil|Brazilian culture]]. It is the favorite pastime of youngsters playing football on streets. The World Cup draws Brazilians together, with people skipping work to view the national team play, or employers setting up apparatus for employees to watch. The [[Elections in Brazil|general elections]] are usually held in the same year as the World Cup, and critics argue that political parties try to take advantage of the nationalistic surge created by football and bring it into politics. Former footballers are often elected to legislative positions.

One unique aspect of football in Brazil is the importance of the [[Brazilian Football State Championship|Brazilian state championship]]s.  For much of the early development of the game in Brazil, the nation's size and the lack of rapid [[transport]] made national competitions infeasible, so the competition centered on state tournaments and such inter-state competitions as the [[Torneio Rio-São Paulo]].  Even today, despite the existence of a national tournament, the state tournaments continue to be hotly contested and the intrastate rivalries remain intense.

==Women's football==
[[Women's association football|Women's football]] is not as popular in Brazil as men's football, although increased in popularity in the 2000s.

Due to a strong and recurring [[social stigma]], Brazilian society refuses to support woman playing football. There is a [[sexist]] concept that football is not a sport for women. # History and Development of Football in Brazil

Football, or *futebol* as it is known in Brazil, is deeply ingrained in the cultural fabric of the country. The sport's history in Brazil dates back to the late 19th century, when expatriates like John Miller and his son Charles William Miller introduced the game to São Paulo. Charles Miller played a pivotal role in establishing the first football club, São Paulo Athletic Club, in 1888. His contributions extended beyond founding the club; he also brought football equipment and rules from England, helping to develop the game among the local community. This early introduction laid the foundation for what would become a passionate and widespread love for football across Brazil.

## Early Development and Growth

The establishment of the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) in 1914 marked a significant milestone in organizing the sport nationally. However, due to the vast size of Brazil and the limitations in transportation at the time, the focus remained on state-level competitions. These state championships became highly competitive and fostered intense rivalries between clubs within each state. The Torneio Rio-São Paulo, an inter-state competition, further fueled the growth of football by bringing together teams from different regions.

## International Success and Cultural Impact

Brazil's international success in football began with its first World Cup victory in 1958. Since then, the Brazilian national team has won the FIFA World Cup five times, making it the most successful team in World Cup history. This success has not only brought immense pride to the nation but also cemented football's place as a unifying force in Brazilian society. The World Cup draws Brazilians together, with people often skipping work to watch matches and celebrate victories. The influence of football extends beyond the pitch, with former players frequently elected to legislative positions, reflecting the sport's deep-rooted cultural significance.

# Women's Football in Brazil

Despite the overwhelming popularity of men's football, women's football in Brazil faces significant challenges. Historically, there has been a strong social stigma against women participating in the sport, rooted in sexist beliefs that football is not suitable for women. This attitude has hindered the development of women's football, leading to a lack of structured leagues and limited financial support. The Campeonato Brasileiro de Futebol Feminino, a national league for women, was established but was short-lived due to these issues.

## Current Status and Future Prospects

In recent years, there have been efforts to improve the situation for women's football in Brazil. The announcement in 2007 by the CBF to launch a women's league and cup competition marked a step towards addressing the disparities. Despite these initiatives, the sport remains less popular compared to men's football. However, the rise of talented players like Marta and Cristiane has helped to raise the profile of women's football and challenge traditional stereotypes. As awareness grows and more resources are allocated, there is hope for a brighter future for women's football in Brazil.

# Conclusion

Football continues to be a defining element of Brazilian culture, with its rich history and international success contributing to its enduring popularity. While men's football enjoys widespread support and recognition, efforts are underway to address the challenges faced by women's football and promote greater equality in the sport. The ongoing development of both aspects of the game reflects the dynamic and evolving nature of football in Brazil.

'''FC Lorient Bretagne Sud''' is a [[France|French]] [[football (soccer)|football]] club based in [[Lorient]], [[Brittany]]. In 2005-06, it played in [[Ligue 2]]. It returned to the top flight for the 2006-07 season.<ref>[http://aolsearch.aol.co.uk/image_browse?query=Stade%20du%20Moustoir&first=&last=&imgurl=http://stadiony.net/pictures/fra/stade_yves_allainmat/stade_yves_allainmat01m.jpg&refurl=http%3A%2F%2Fstadiony.net%2Fstadium.php%3Fs%3D518&width=200&height=150&requestId=5f21f05a559332ec&clickedItemRank=8&encquery=Stade%20du%20Moustoir&page= AOL Web Search<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==History==
Lorient were formed as an amateur club on 2 April 1926 and known as Football Club Lorientais.<ref>{{cite web | title=De la Marée sportive au Football Club Lorientais.| work=FC Lorient official website | url=http://www.fclweb.fr/histoire/| accessdate=8 April 2007}}</ref>  They first played in the regional third division, but progressed to join the Division d'Honneur in 1929.

The club turned professional in 1995, although the club has had two earlier periods as a professional club, between 1967-1977 and 1988-1991. 

The club won the French Cup in 2002 and were finalists in the [[Coupe de la Ligue]] the same year. In the 2005-06 season, the club finished third in [[Ligue 2]], earning promotion to [[Ligue 1]].

==Honours==
* Winners of the [[Coupe de France de football|Coupe de France]] : 2002

The '''1990 FIFA World Cup''', the 14th staging of the World Cup, was held in [[Italy]] from 8 June to 8 July. Italy was chosen as the [[FIFA World Cup hosts#1990 FIFA World Cup|hosts]] by [[FIFA]] on 19 May 1984, making it the second country to host the event twice. [[USSR]] was the rival of [[Italy]]'s candidacy to host the event. It was won by [[Germany national football team|West Germany]], who beat [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]] 1–0 in the final to win the World Cup for the third time.

==Qualification==
{{main|1990 FIFA World Cup qualification}}
[[Image:1990 world cup.png|thumb|left|350px|Qualifying countries]]
Three teams qualified for the first time: [[Costa Rica national football team|Costa Rica]], the [[Republic of Ireland national football team|Republic of Ireland]] and the [[United Arab Emirates national football team|United Arab Emirates]]. The [[United States men's national soccer team|United States]] also made it back to the World Cup after a 40-year absence. The draw for the finals took place on 9 December 1989 in [[Rome]]. Tenor [[Luciano Pavarotti]] performed at the event.

====Disqualifications====
*[[Mexico national football team|Mexico]] was disqualified after the [[Federación Mexicana de Fútbol Asociación]] fielded an overage player in a prior youth tournament.

==Summary==
===First round===
[[Image:World Cup 1990 Football.jpg|thumb|right|150px|The ball ''Etrusco Unico'' used in the tournament]]
The format of the 1990 competition remained the same as in [[1986 FIFA World Cup|1986]]: 24 qualified teams were divided into six groups of four. The top two teams and four best third place finishers from the six groups advanced to the knockout stage.

The 1990 World Cup finals got off to a surprising start. In the first match, [[Cameroon national football team|Cameroon]] soaked up pressure from [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]] for most of the first half. After a quarter of an hour's play in the second half, Cameroon's [[Andre Kana]] was sent off, and it seemed certain that the world champions would now take control. But six minutes later, the ten men took the lead. [[François Omam Biyik]] scored when he placed a perfect downward header past Argentine goalkeeper [[Nery Pumpido]]. Argentina pressed hard for an equaliser, and Cameroon were reduced to nine men when [[Benjamin Massing]] got the red card in the 89th minute – but the African team still held out for a shock 1–0 win. Then, when Cameroon faced [[Romania national football team|Romania]] in their second game, [[Roger Milla]] took centre stage. His inclusion in Cameroon's squad had been controversial. He had been a favourite in the Cameroon team for years, but he was now 38 years old. He was only in Italy because of political intervention: [[Paul Biya]], Cameroon's President, had insisted that Milla be included in the squad.

Against Argentina, Milla only appeared for the last ten minutes. But in the match with Romania, Cameroon coach [[Valeri Nepomniachi]] sent him on in the 58th minute, with the score still 0–0. It proved to be an inspired move. Milla scored with 15 minutes left, then added another with five minutes remaining, thus getting two opportunities to demonstrate his trademark hip-shaking goal celebration dance. Gavrila Balint scored for Romania, but it was too little too late. Cameroon held on to win 2–1. Surprisingly, they were beaten 4–0 in their last group game by a [[USSR national football team|Soviet Union]] side desperately, and unsuccessfully, striving to stay in the tournament on goal difference. Despite the heavy defeat, Cameroon were through to the second round as group winners. Romania came second in Group B, and Argentina just scraped into the second round as one of the best third-placed teams.

Another surprise team emerged from Group C. [[Costa Rica national football team|Costa Rica]] beat [[Scotland national football team|Scotland]] 1–0 in their first match, held [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]] to another 1–0 scoreline in their second, then saw off [[Sweden national football team|Sweden]] 2–1 to claim a place in the second round. Brazil bore little resemblance to the free-flowing, free scoring Brazilian sides of earlier years, but they still took maximum points from the group. They began with a 2–1 win over Sweden, then beat both Costa Rica and Scotland 1–0. Scotland's 2–1 win over Sweden was not enough to save them from an early return home as one of the two lowest-ranked third-placed teams.

In the six Group F games, featuring the [[Netherlands national football team|Netherlands]], [[England national football team|England]], the [[Republic of Ireland national football team|Republic of Ireland]] and [[Egypt national football team|Egypt]], no team managed to score more than once in a match. England beat Egypt 1–0, thanks to a 64th minute goal from [[Mark Wright]] – and that was enough to win the group.

There were more goals in Group D, but a lot of them were due to the defensive inadequacies of a [[United Arab Emirates national football team|United Arab Emirates]] team that lost 2–0 to [[Colombia national football team|Colombia]], 5–1 to [[Germany national football team|West Germany]] and 4–1 to [[Yugoslavia national football team|Yugoslavia]]. All three of the UAE's first round opponents reached the last 16, with West Germany topping the group after an impressive 4–1 win over group runners-up Yugoslavia.

[[Italy national football team|Italy]] won Group A with a 100 per cent record achieved via cautious football. The club were initially given the use of two fields — John Harper's Field and Windmill Field — both off Lower Villiers Street in [[Blakenhall]]. David Vaughan Icke, born on April 29, 1952, in Leicester, England, is a British writer and public speaker known for his controversial theories and beliefs. His parents, Beric Vaughan Icke and Barbara J. Icke (née Cooke), were married in Leicester in 1951. Beric Icke, David’s father, had a notable military career, serving in the Royal Air Force and earning a British Empire Medal for gallantry in 1943. This medal was awarded after he helped save the crew of a crashed aircraft, demonstrating remarkable bravery and selflessness. [Data: Infobox Person (1)]

### Career Transition and Public Controversy

Icke began his career as a well-respected figure in the media, working as a BBC television sports presenter and spokesperson for the British Green Party. However, his life took a dramatic turn at the age of 38 when he encountered a psychic who claimed he was a healer with a specific purpose on Earth. This encounter led him to develop a series of unconventional theories about the control of the world by a secret group of reptilian humanoids. [Data: Infobox Person (1)]

In April 1991, Icke appeared on Terry Wogan's BBC show, where he made statements suggesting he was the son of God and predicted global disasters. These comments transformed him from a respected household name into a figure of public ridicule almost overnight. Despite this setback, Icke continued to develop and promote his theories through various publications and lectures. [Data: Infobox Person (1)]

### Theoretical Framework and Publications

At the core of Icke's theories is the belief that the world is controlled by a secret group of reptilian humanoids known as the Babylonian Brotherhood. He claims that many prominent individuals, such as George W. Bush, Queen Elizabeth II, Kris Kristofferson, and Boxcar Willie, are actually reptilians. Icke has authored several books detailing these theories, including "The Robots' Rebellion" (1994), "And the Truth Shall Set You Free" (1995), "The Biggest Secret" (1999), and "Children of the Matrix" (2001). His work has been translated into eight languages and has garnered a significant following worldwide. [Data: Infobox Person (1)]

### Criticism and Controversies

Despite his growing audience, Icke has faced considerable criticism and controversy. One of the most contentious aspects of his work involves his connection to "The Protocols of the Elders of Zion," a notorious anti-Semitic forgery. Icke argues that the "Protocols" were written by the "Global Elite," a group he believes controls the world. Although he denies any anti-Semitic intent, his theories have attracted the attention of far-right groups and raised concerns among Jewish organizations. [Data: Infobox Person (1)]

In 1999, Icke was detained by Canadian immigration officials when attempting to enter the country for a speaking tour. After convincing them that his references to lizards were literal, he was allowed to proceed, though his books were subsequently removed from Indigo Books due to protests from the Canadian Jewish Congress. This incident highlighted the sensitivity surrounding his theories and their potential to incite prejudice. [Data: Infobox Person (1)]

### Personal Life

Icke currently resides in Ryde, Isle of Wight, England. He has been married twice, to Linda Atherton and Pamela Leigh Richards, and has three children named Gareth, Kerry, and Jamie. '''Michael Kojo Essien''' (also referred to as '''Mickaël Essien''') (born 3 December 1982) is a [[Ghana]]ian [[Association football|footballer]] who currently plays for [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] in the [[Premier League]]. He is an all-round midfielder who can play multiple midfield roles (defensively and offensively). He has often been touted as a [[Midfielder#"Box-to-box" midfielder|box-to-box midfielder]] for his ability to exert boundless energy in supporting offensive and defensive play. At Chelsea, his versatility as a player has been put to effective use in various roles. He has often been deployed as a [[defensive midfielder]], but has also played as a [[centre midfielder]], a right-sided lateral defender or a right-sided midfielder, even as a [[Defender|Right Back]], and a [[Defender|Center Back]]. For the [[Ghana national football team]], Essien has played primarily in a central midfield role, with combined opportunities to go forward or support defensive play. He also has a good eye for goal and has on occasion scored important, sometimes breath-taking goals for both club and country. One of his trademark abilities is to hit a shot from distance. Between the summer of 2007 and the summer of 2009, Essien was the most expensive [[Africa]]n footballer on account of his £24.4 million move from French club Olympique Lyonnais to Chelsea FC.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/worldservice/specials/1351_afr_foot_vote/page4.shtml |title=Michael Essien |accessdate=2009-05-24 |date=2007 |work=BBC Sport:African Football |publisher=BBC}}</ref> This achievement is now surpassed by Togolese player Emmanuel Adebayor, who moved from Arsenal to Manchester City for £25 million in the summer of 2009. Essien is often referred to as '''"the Bison"''' for his tough tackling style, boundless energy and physical presence on the pitch.<ref>http://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/bison-essien-tramples-betis-underfoot-511728.html</ref>

==Background==
Born in [[Accra]] to [[Ghana]]ian parents, Aba Gyandoh and James Essien, Essien began his football career after graduating from St. Augustine's College in [[Cape Coast]], playing in a local club in his native Ghana, called [[Liberty Professionals F.C.|Liberty Professionals]]. He broke through when he played in the [[1999 FIFA U-17 World Championship]] in New Zealand.<ref name="fifa 1999">{{cite web |url=http://www.fifa.com/en/comp/PrevSquad/0,4355,GHA-U17-1999-3611-19,00.html |title=New Zealand 1999 - Team:Ghana |accessdate=2007-04-05 |Official Website |publisher=FIFA}}</ref> This led to considerable attention from European scouts, and he even had a trial at [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] in April 2000, playing in the club's youth team's defeat by [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]].

==Club career==

===Bastia===
In July 2000, Essien was signed by French club [[SC Bastia|Bastia]]. He did not immediately command a consistent place in the team, being deployed in various positions in the [[Defender (association football)|back four]]; however, because of an injury to one of his team-mates, he was given a temporary opportunity to play in central midfield, and flourished in this new role; he was even compared to Frenchman [[Patrick Vieira]] because of his ability to go from box to box.{{Fact|date=April 2009}} In the 2002–03 season, he helped Bastia to qualify for the [[UEFA Cup]], scoring six goals that season. Soon, [[Paris Saint-Germain F.C.|Paris Saint-Germain]], [[Olympique Lyonnais|Lyon]] and [[Olympique de Marseille|Marseille]] made offers for him.

===Olympique Lyonnais===
Paris Saint-Germain made Bastia the best offer and it was accepted,<ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/africa/3032604.stm |title=Ghana's Essien joins PSG |accessdate=2007-04-05 |date=30 June 2003 |work=BBC Sport:African Football |publisher=BBC}}</ref> but Essien rejected PSG's contract offer, and instead agreed terms with Lyon, who paid Bastia [[Euro|€]]7.8 million for the transfer.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/africa/3038262.stm |title=Essien turns down PSG |accessdate=2007-04-05 |date=2 July 2003 |work=BBC Sport:African Football |publisher=BBC}}</ref> At Lyon, Essien played more of a defensive midfield role, featuring regularly in the Lyon team that won the third and fourth of their ongoing string of consecutive [[Ligue 1]] titles. He was also voted the 2005 Player of the Year by France's National Union of Professional Footballers (UNFP).<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/africa/4572787.stm |title=Essien wins French award |accessdate=2007-04-05 |date=23 May 2005 |work=BBC Sport:African Football |publisher=BBC}}</ref> He was also nominated for the [[2005 FIFA World Player of the Year]] Award. He placed 22nd in [[2005 FIFA World Player of the Year|2005]].

===Chelsea===

[[File:Essien.jpg|thumb|200px|right]]
On August 14, 2005, Lyon and Chelsea agreed a [[Pound sterling|£]]24.4 million fee for the Ghanaian, finally ending one of the longest-running transfer sagas.<ref>{{cite news |title=Essien saga nears completion |publisher=www.news.bbc.co.uk |date=15 August 2005 |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/c/chelsea/4152512.stm |accessdate=24 May 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title= Cheslea finally seal deal for Essien |publisher=www.dailymail.co.uk |date= 19 August 2005 |url=http://www.dailymail.co.uk/sport/football/article-359784/Chelsea-finally-seal-deal-Essien.html |accessdate=25 May 2009 }}</ref> At the time, the fee made Essien Chelsea's most expensive signing of all time, beating the £24 million they paid for [[Didier Drogba]] the previous summer. The transfer went through on August 19.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/c/chelsea/4165004.stm |title=Chelsea delight at Essien signing |accessdate=5 April 2007 |date=19 August 2005 |work=BBC Sport |publisher=BBC }}</ref> The transfer came under scrutiny in the [[2006 allegations of corruption in English football#Stevens report|Stevens inquiry]] report, which expressed concerns because of the lack of co-operation from agents [[Pinhas Zahavi]] and [[Barry Silkman]].<ref>{{cite news |title=What Stevens said about each club |publisher=www.telegraph.co.uk |date=16 June 2007 |url=http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/main.jhtml?view=DETAILS&grid=A1YourView&xml=/sport/2007/06/16/sfnste116.xml |accessdate=17 June 2007 }}</ref>

He made his debut as a second half substitute against [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] on August 21, 2005, wearing the number 5 on his shirt. The game ended with a 1-0 victory to Chelsea.<ref>{{cite news |title=Chelsea 1-0 Arsenal|publisher=www.news.bbc.co.uk |date=21 August 2005 |u

Toronto FC is owned by [[Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment]], who operate the [[National Hockey League|NHL]]'s [[Toronto Maple Leafs]], the [[American Hockey League|AHL]]'s [[Toronto Marlies]], and the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]]'s [[Toronto Raptors]]. TFC plays its home games at [[BMO Field]], located in [[Exhibition Place]] along the Toronto lake shore. Toronto FC's title sponsor, which can be found on the front of their uniforms and on most team merchandise, is the [[Bank of Montreal]] (BMO). TFC is known for their distinct red home colours, giving them the nickname "The Reds". [[Toronto FC fans|TFC fans]] have helped make the club one of the MLS' most successful franchises, having been profitable since its first year with regular sellouts and sold-out seasons tickets. The club is the reigning Canadian Champions as 2009 Nutrilite Canadian Championship winners, beating the Montreal Impact by the 4 goals needed on the last day of the Championship to win the title. The announcement followed an online consultation in which the public was invited to vote on the name during a limited period. The voting options were "Toronto Northmen," "Inter Toronto FC," "Toronto Reds," and "Toronto FC." MLSE's strategy in choosing "Toronto FC" following this process was based on two reasons. Firstly, over 40 percent of the online vote supported the simplified Toronto FC name during the consultation; secondly, MLSE hoped that the fairly generic name would help the new club earn a more organic nickname from the Toronto fans rather than having one imposed upon the club.{{cite web |url=http://web.mlsnet.com/t280/about/ |title=Toronto FC - our brief history and bright future|publisher=mlsnet.com |accessdate=2009-03-08}} The team has been called "TFC" and "the Reds" by the media and the club.{{cite web |url=http://seattlepi.nwsource.com/scorecard/othernews.asp?articleID=238513 |title=Toronto FC acquires Ruiz from Galaxy |publisher=seattlepi.nwsource.com |accessdate=2009-02-22}}{{cite web |url=http://www.goal.com/en/Articolo.aspx?ContenutoId=830202 |title=MLS Preview: Toronto FC - New England Revolution |publisher=goal.com |accessdate=2009-02-22}} The official team colours are red (jerseys, shorts and socks) with white trim, and light grey jerseys and socks with black shorts and dark grey trim. ===MLS Expansion in Canada=== While Toronto FC was the first team to join the previously all-American [[Major League Soccer|MLS]], it will not be the last. Due to Toronto's popular success, MLS has avidly sought out other cities in Canada for expansion, most recently awarding a franchise to [[Vancouver|Vancouver]], [[British Colombia|B.C.]] that will join the league in 2011{{cite news | title=MLS awards Vancouver team for 2011 | url=http://toronto.fc.mlsnet.com/news/mls_news.jsp?ymd=20090318&content_id=227084&vkey=news_mls&fext=.jsp | publisher=MLSnet.com | date=2009-03-18}}. [[Ottawa]] and [[Montreal]] have also been cited as key players in future MLS expansion, with both cities having made the final round of nominees for 2011 expansion that saw Vancouver earn a club (see [[MLS Expansion|MLS expansion]]). Montreal is a heavy favourite in the expansion race and if the city were to win a club it would complete the Canadian professional soccer triumvirate alongside Toronto and Vancouver, who currently compete for the national title in the [[Canadian Championship|Canadian Championship]] that sends the winning club to represent the country in the [[CONCACAF Champions League|CONCACAF Champions League]]. ==Toronto FC supporters== {{main|Toronto FC fans}} [[Image:TFC invades Columbus.jpg|right|thumb|250px|Toronto FC's traveling fans in [[Columbus Crew Stadium]] during the first game of the 2008 season.]] Before the start of the 2007 season, [[Richard Peddie]], the CEO of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment Ltd., stated that he and the ownership would be content with between 13,000–15,000 fans per game at Toronto FC home games. However, this range has been exceeded. The club sold out season tickets its first three years, capping season tickets at 16,000 for the 2009 season. There are currently more than 14,000 people on the waiting list for season tickets.{{cite web |url=http://www.thestar.com/Sports/article/603933 |title=MLSE spies big BMO Field expansion |publisher=thestar.com |accessdate=2009-03-18}}. However, this has been surpassed in 2009 with addition of Seattle Sounders FC who claim more than 25,000 season tickets holders and a 9,000 person waiting list. The fans have been called enthusiastic and their passion unsurpassed in MLS{{cite web |url=http://soccernet.espn.go.com/columns/story?id=531102&root=mls&&cc=5901 |title=Toronto fan passion unsurpassed in MLS |publisher=soccernet.espn.go.com |accessdate=2009-02-22}}.
