# **Introduction to Toronto FC**
Toronto FC, commonly abbreviated as TFC, is a professional soccer club based in Toronto, Ontario. Founded in 2006, it became the first Canadian and non-American team to join Major League Soccer (MLS), making its debut in the 2007 season. The club is owned by Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment (MLSE), which also operates other prominent sports teams in Toronto, including the NHL’s Toronto Maple Leafs, the AHL’s Toronto Marlies, and the NBA’s Toronto Raptors.

# **Club Identity and History**
## **Naming Process**
The name "Toronto FC" was officially announced on May 11, 2006, following an online consultation where the public voted on several options, including "Toronto Northmen," "Inter Toronto FC," "Toronto Reds," and "Toronto FC." Over 40% of the votes supported the straightforward "Toronto FC" name, leading MLSE to choose it. This decision was also influenced by the desire to let the nickname develop organically among fans, rather than being imposed. The team is now widely known as "TFC" and "The Reds."

## **Home Ground and Uniforms**
Toronto FC plays its home games at BMO Field, located in Exhibition Place along the Toronto lake shore. The club's home colors are red, earning them the nickname "The Reds." Their uniform consists of red jerseys, shorts, and socks with white trim, while their away kit features light grey jerseys and socks with black shorts and dark grey trim.

# **MLS Expansion in Canada**
Toronto FC's success has paved the way for further expansion of MLS into Canada. Following Toronto's lead, Vancouver, British Columbia, was awarded a franchise that joined the league in 2011. Other Canadian cities like Ottawa and Montreal have also been considered for future expansion. Montreal, in particular, is seen as a strong contender for a future MLS team, which would complete a trio of Canadian professional soccer clubs competing in the Canadian Championship.

# **Supporters and Fan Culture**
## **Season Ticket Sales**
Before the 2007 season, Richard Peddie, the CEO of MLSE, set a target of 13,000–15,000 fans per game. However, the club has consistently exceeded these expectations, selling out season tickets for its first three years and capping them at 16,000 for the 2009 season. As of 2009, there were over 14,000 people on the waiting list for season tickets, demonstrating the strong demand and passionate fan base.

## **Fan Behavior and Travel Support**
Toronto FC fans are renowned for their enthusiasm and passion, often described as unsurpassed in MLS. This passion has sometimes led to incidents such as throwing seat cushions onto the field after scoring goals, prompting the club to remind fans to refrain from such behavior. Additionally, TFC fans are known for their traveling support, particularly in the Trillium Cup matches against Columbus Crew, where large contingents of fans have traveled to support their team.

# **Competitions**
Toronto FC competes in MLS but is ineligible for the U.S. Open Cup. Instead, they participate in the annual Canadian Championship to determine the Voyageurs Cup winner, representing Canada in the CONCACAF Champions League. In 2009, Toronto FC won the Canadian Championship, defeating the Montreal Impact, an achievement celebrated as "The Miracle in Montreal."

This summary provides an overview of Toronto FC's establishment, identity, fan culture, and competitive landscape within Canadian and North American soccer. [Data: Infobox Football club (1); History (1, 2, 3); Toronto FC supporters (1, 2, 3)]

Founded in 1946, the club had rapid and continual success in the mid 2000s but after falling into severe financial difficulties, the club was eventually dissolved in 2008. Despite being based in [[Scotland]], the club participated in amateur and semi-professional leagues in [[Football in England|English football]] from 1947 until they were elected to the [[Scottish Football League]] at the third attempt in 2002. Relying heavily on substantial financial support from businessman [[Brooks Mileson]], the club were [[promotion and relegation|promoted]] through the Scottish leagues from the [[Scottish Football League Division Three|Third Division]] to the [[Scottish Premier League]] in less than five years. However, the team [[Scottish Premier League 2007-08|struggled badly in the SPL]] and the club were placed in [[Administration (insolvency)|administration]] after Mileson withdrew his support due to illness.{{cite web|url=http://www.guardian.co.uk/football/2008/mar/23/newsstory.sport1|title=End of a romantic dream for the Roman Abramovich of Gretna|author=Neil Drysdale|date=23 March 2008}} At the end of the season, all of the club's staff were made redundant and the club were initially relegated to the [[Scottish Football League Third Division|Third Division]] due to their inability to guarantee fulfilment of their [[2008–09 in Scottish football|forthcoming fixtures]]. After this demotion, the one remaining offer to buy the club was withdrawn.[http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/scotland/south_of_scotland/7430745.stm Gretna no longer in existence], [[BBC News]], 2 June 2008. The club resigned their place in the [[Scottish Football League]] on 3 June[http://sport.setanta.com/en/Sport/News/Football/2008/06/03/Gretna-resign-from-SFL/ Death knell for crisis club], [[Setanta Sports]], 3 June 2008. and were formally liquidated on 8 August.{{cite news | url=http://www.cumberland-news.co.uk/1.218555 | title=Liquidation signals the final nail in Gretna coffin | work=The Cumberland News | date=2008-08-08 }} The club's [[supporters' trust]] then decided to establish a new club, [[Gretna F.C. 2008|Gretna 2008]], who were accepted into the [[East of Scotland Football League]] on 11 July 2008. Whilst sharing the same fanbase and a similar name, the new club has no legal connection with the original Gretna F.C.{{cite news | url=http://edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/Gretna-given-place-in-the.4279463.jp | title=Gretna given place in the East of Scotland League | work=The Scotsman | date=2008-07-11 | quote='We are obviously a new club carrying on the traditions of the old club and there is no connection with the old club other than the similarity in name,' said Hodge. }} ==History== ===Beginnings=== An amateur team called Gretna Green had existed in the town in the 19th century, but were bankrupt by the 1920s. This left the area without a team until Gretna Football Club was founded in 1946 by servicemen returning from the [[World War II|Second World War]].[http://sport.scotsman.com/football/Last-Post-sounds-for-Gretna.4143774.jp Last Post sounds for Gretna, set up by war heroes to give village hope], [[The Scotsman]], 3 June 2008 The club initially played in the Dumfries and District Junior League. ===Period in English football=== The following year, the club moved to the Carlisle and District League, which is run by the English [[The Football Association|Football Association]]. This was despite the club being based in [[Scotland]], although [[Gretna]] is very close to the [[Anglo–Scottish border]]. They remained in this league for all but one season until 1982, when the club moved to the newly-created Second Division of the [[Northern League (football)|Northern League]]. The club won this league and were promoted immediately, before back-to-back championship wins in the First Division, in 1990–91 and 1991–92, resulted in their promotion to the first division of the [[Northern Premier League]]. During this period, the club featured in the [[FA Cup]], becoming the first club based in Scotland to appear in the competition proper since [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] had done so in 1887. They managed to take [[Rochdale A.F.C.|Rochdale]] to a [[replay]] in [[FA Cup 1991–92|1991]] and gave [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]] a scare in [[FA Cup 1993–94|1993]] before being beaten.[http://sport.scotsman.com/scottishcupfinal/Gretna-grit-forged-in-FA.2775170.jp Gretna grit forged in FA Cup battle with Bolton], ''[[The Scotsman]]'', 13 May 2006 The club saw its future in [[Scottish football]] and applied twice to join the [[Scottish Football League|Scottish League]] in 1993 and 1999. To help boost their later application, they played a [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] XI in a game to raise money for victims of the [[Lockerbie air disaster]]. Gretna won 2–1 against a strong team.{{Fact|date=June 2007}} ===Period back in Scottish football=== ====Rapid rise through the leagues==== [[Image:CRW 1545.jpg|Pressley's penalty|right|thumb|250px|[[Steven Pressley]] scores past Gretna [[goalkeeper (football)|goalkeeper]] [[Alan Main]] in the [[2006 Scottish Cup Final]] [[penalty shootout (football)|penalty shootout]].]] In 2002, Gretna were elected to the [[Scottish Football League]] at the third attempt, taking the place of [[Airdrieonians F.C.|Airdrieonians]]. The club was soon taken over by [[Brooks Mileson]] and with his financial input Gretna's on-field fortunes rapidly improved. Gretna won the [[Scottish Football League Third Division|Division Three]], [[Scottish Football League Second Division|Division Two]] and [[Scottish Football League First Division|Division One]] titles in successive seasons from 2005 to 2007. During their seasons of successive promotions they scored 297 goals, 130 in the [[2004–05 in Scottish football|2004–05]] season alone. This was one short of the British league record of goals scored in a season. Gretna were also runners-up in the [[Scottish Cup 2005-06|2006 Scottish Cup]]. Gretna's 3–0 win in the semi-final against [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]]{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_cups/4860972.stm|publisher=BBC Sport website|title=Gretna 3–0 Dundee|date=1 April 2006}} made them the first team from the third tier of Scottish league football to reach the final. Gretna lost to [[Heart of Midlothian F.C.|Heart of Midlothian]] in [[2006 Scottish Cup Final|the final]] on [[penalty shootout|penalties]] after a 1–1 draw.{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_cups/4764967.stm|publisher

# History of Gretna Football Club

## Beginnings

Gretna Football Club was founded in 1946 by servicemen returning from the Second World War. Initially, the club played in the Dumfries and District Junior League. This marked the beginning of a long journey for the club, which would eventually lead them to the highest levels of Scottish football.

## Period in English Football

In 1947, Gretna moved to the Carlisle and District League, which was run by the English Football Association, despite the club being based in Scotland. The club remained in this league until 1982, except for one season. In 1982, Gretna joined the Northern League, where they achieved significant success, winning the Second Division and subsequently the First Division in consecutive years (1990–91 and 1991–92). These achievements led to their promotion to the Northern Premier League.

During this period, Gretna participated in the FA Cup, becoming the first club based in Scotland to appear in the competition since Rangers in 1887. Notable performances included taking Rochdale to a replay in 1991 and giving Bolton Wanderers a scare in 1993.

## Period Back in Scottish Football

### Rapid Rise Through the Leagues

In 2002, Gretna was finally admitted to the Scottish Football League, replacing Airdrieonians. The club was soon taken over by Brooks Mileson, whose financial support dramatically improved Gretna's performance. Over the next few years, Gretna won the Scottish Football League Third Division, Second Division, and First Division titles consecutively from 2005 to 2007. During these seasons, Gretna scored an impressive 297 goals, with 130 goals in the 2004–05 season alone, just one short of the British league record.

### Scottish Cup Success

In addition to their league successes, Gretna reached the 2006 Scottish Cup final, defeating Dundee 3–0 in the semi-final. This achievement made Gretna the first team from the third tier of Scottish league football to reach the final. However, they ultimately lost to Heart of Midlothian in the final on penalties after a 1–1 draw.

## Financial Difficulties and Dissolution

Despite their rapid rise and success, Gretna faced severe financial difficulties. When Brooks Mileson withdrew his financial support due to illness, the club was placed in administration. The club struggled in the Scottish Premier League and was eventually relegated to the Third Division. Unable to fulfill their fixtures, Gretna resigned from the Scottish Football League on June 3, 2008, and were formally liquidated on August 8, 2008.

## Legacy

After the dissolution of the original Gretna Football Club, a new club, Gretna 2008, was established by the supporters' trust. This new club shares the same fanbase and a similar name but has no legal connection with the original Gretna F.C.

This summary provides a comprehensive overview of Gretna Football Club's history, from its founding in 1946 to its dissolution in 2008, highlighting key achievements and challenges along the way.

The **WAFU Under-20 Championship** (also known as the **Ibori Cup**) took place in **Delta State, Nigeria**, from **November 30 to December 14, 2008**. This tournament was organized by the **West Africa Football Union (WAFU)** and featured 14 teams from various countries in the West African region. The championship aimed to provide young football talents with a platform to showcase their skills and compete at a high level.

### Eligible Participants

- Benin

- Mali
- Mauritania
- Niger
- Nigeria
- Senegal
- Sierra Leone
- Togo

### Group Stages

#### Group A

In Group A, **Nigeria** emerged as the top team with 6 points after winning both of their matches. They defeated Togo 2-0 and Benin 1-0. Both Togo and Benin finished with 1 point each, drawing their match 1-1.

'''Marcus Stephan Hahnemann''' (born June 15, 1972, in {{city-state|Seattle|Washington}}) is an American [[Association football|soccer]] player who currently plays as a [[Goalkeeper (association football)|goalkeeper]] for English [[Premier League]] side [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolverhampton Wanderers]]. 

==Club career==
===Early years===
Hahnemann grew up in the Seattle area and attended [[Kentridge High School]] where he was named the team's MVP his junior season. He transferred to [[Newport High School (Bellevue, Washington)|Newport High School]] in [[Bellevue, Washington]] for his senior season. That year, he kept eleven clean sheets en route to being named the All-King County goalkeeper.

He played college soccer for the [[Seattle Pacific University]] Falcons. A Division II powerhouse, Hahnemann led SPU to the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] [[NCAA Men's Soccer Championship#Division II|Division II National Championship]] in 1993. Over his four seasons at SPU, Hahnemann had a 64-9-5 record as a starter, with forty-six career clean sheets.

===Seattle Sounders===
Hahnemann's professional career started when he signed the [[Seattle Sounders (USL)|Seattle Sounders]] of the [[A-League (American)|A-League]] on 1 May 1994.<ref>
{{cite press release
  | title = 1995 Seattle Sounders Media Guide
  | publisher = Seattle Sounders
  | date = 1995
  | url = http://goalseattle.com/gallery/1995SeattleSoundersMediaGuide/players8
  | accessdate = 2008-07-08 }}
</ref> In his first season with the Sounders, Hahnemann registered a .57 [[Goals against average|GAA]] in fourteen games to take the league's top goalkeeper honors. In 1995, he played twenty-nine games as the Sounders won the league championship. In 1996, the Sounders repeated as champions while Hahnemann kept eleven clean sheets and made 119 saves.

===Colorado Rapids===
He waited until 1997 to join [[Major League Soccer]], signing with the [[Colorado Rapids]]. In his [[1997 Major League Soccer season|first season in MLS]], the Rapids went all the way to the [[MLS Cup]] before losing 2-1 to [[D.C. United]]. During his second season, he set a club record for the most games and minutes played in a single season by a goalkeeper, playing 2,520 minutes in 28 games and compiling a 16-12 record, and was named their Defender of the Year.

===Fulham===
After two and a half seasons with the Colorado Rapids, he signed with [[Football League First Division|English First Division]] club [[Fulham F.C.|Fulham]], for £80,000 in June 1999. He failed to displace [[Maik Taylor]] in goal though, and only made four appearances in total for the London club (all during their promotion season of [[2000–01_in_English_football#Football_League_First_Division|2000/01]]). 

With [[Edwin van der Sar]] signed upon promotion by Fulham, Hahnemann slipped further down the pecking order and to gain playing time, he was loaned out to lower league sides [[Rochdale A.F.C.|Rochdale]], and then, [[Reading F.C.|Reading]] during the 2001-02 campaign. He made six appearances for the latter as part of [[2001–02_in_English_football#Nationwide_League_Division_Two|their promotion]] from the third tier.

===Reading===
Hahnemann then joined Reading permanently in Summer 2002 on a free transfer, becoming their first choice 'keeper. His first full season with the ''Royals'' saw them miss out on promotion to the Premier League in the [[Football League Championship Play-Offs#2003|play-offs]], before two successive seasons saw them narrowly fall short of further play-off finishes.

He missed just one game of the [[2005–06 in English football#Football League Championship|2005-06 season]] that saw Reading win promotion to the top flight of English football for the first time in their history, as they topped the [[Football League Championship|Championship]] with a record 106 points. He was named in that season's ''Championship Team of the Year'' by the [[Professional Footballers' Association]].<ref>{{cite news | date=2006-04-23 | url=http://www.givemefootball.com/display.cfm?article=8213&type=1 | title=The PFA Team of the Year: Coca-Cola Championship | publisher=[[Professional Footballers' Association]] | accessdate=2006-05-24}}</ref>

His first season in the Premier League saw him keep thirteen clean sheets as the club finished eighth, only one place short of European football. He made the most saves (139) in the Premier League during 2007,<ref>{{cite news | first=Rob |last=Bateman | title=Opta statistical snaps for 2007 | url=http://sport.setanta.com/en/Sport/News/Football/2007/12/31/Opta-statistics-for-2007/?facets/sport-space/football/north-america-locale/ | date=2007-12-31 | accessdate=2008-07-05 | publisher=[http://www.setanta.com Setanta Sports]}}</ref> but could not halt relegation in their second EPL campaign.

He remained with the club for one further season as they attempted an immediate return back to the top level, but Reading ultimately lost out to {{fc|Burnley}} in the play-off semi finals. Subsequently Reading announced that they would not renew Hahnemann's contract making him a free agent.<ref>{{Citation |title=Reading release four, including Hahnemann |url=http://soccernet.espn.go.com/news/story?id=646565&sec=england&campaign=rss&source=soccernet&cc=5901 |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=2009-05-15 |accessdate=2009-05-15}}</ref> 

===Wolves===
Hahnemann joined newly-promoted Premier League side [[Wolverhampton Wanderers F.C.|Wolverhampton Wanderers]] on a free transfer on June 17 2009, signing a one-year contract. On 29 November 2009 he made his debut for Wolves. It was in the match against Birmingham City as they lost 1-0.<ref>{{Citation |title=Wolves draft in keeper Hahnemann |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/w/wolverhampton_wanderers/8105049.stm |publisher=BBC Sport|date=2009-05-17}}</ref>

==International career==
Hahnemann made his international debut for the [[United States men's national soccer team|United States national team]] on November 19, 1994, in a 0-1 friendly defeat to [[Trinidad and Tobago national football team|Trinidad and Tobago]].

Martín Palermo, born on November 7, 1973, in La Plata, Argentina, is a renowned Argentine professional footballer who plays as a striker. Known affectionately as "El Loco," Palermo began his career with Estudiantes de La Plata in 1992. However, it wasn't until he joined Boca Juniors in 1997 that he gained international recognition for his exceptional goal-scoring abilities and performances in international matches. His time at Boca Juniors saw him score 81 goals in 102 appearances, cementing his status as a fan favorite and idol. [Data: Infobox football biography 2 (1)]

### International Recognition and Injury

Palermo's talent caught the attention of several European clubs, including S.S. Lazio, Real Betis, and A.C. Milan. However, his career took a significant hit on November 13, 1999, when he suffered a complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee during a match against Colón de Santa Fe. Despite the severity of the injury, he managed to score his 100th goal in the Argentine First Division before leaving the field. This injury required a six-month recovery period, but he made a triumphant return on May 24, 2000, scoring a crucial goal in the Copa Libertadores quarterfinal match against River Plate. [Data: Infobox football biography 2 (1); Club career (1)]

### Spells in Spain

In January 2001, Palermo moved to Villarreal CF in Spain for a transfer fee of €7.6 million. His time at Villarreal was marked by another significant injury. On November 29, 2001, after celebrating a goal, he stood on a small concrete wall that collapsed under the weight of fans, breaking both the tibia and fibula of his left leg. This led to two months of inactivity, and despite returning to play, he never fully regained his form. After two and a half seasons, he decided to leave Villarreal on August 20, 2003. The following day, he signed with Real Betis, but his stint there was short-lived, and he moved to Deportivo Alavés in the Segunda División in March 2004. [Data: Infobox football biography 2 (1); Spell in Spain (1)]

### Return to Boca Juniors

On July 13, 2004, after spending nearly four years in Spain with three different clubs, Palermo returned to Boca Juniors. This move proved to be a successful one, as he continued to be among the top scorers in the Argentine league. In December 2004, he scored his 100th goal for Boca Juniors in the final of the Copa Sudamericana, contributing to a 2–0 victory over Bolívar. Over the next few years, Palermo maintained his goal-scoring prowess, becoming the top scorer in the 2007 Clausura tournament. One of his most memorable moments during this period was scoring a half-pitch goal against Independiente on February 25, 2007, and achieving a hat-trick against his former team, Estudiantes, without celebrating any of the goals. [Data: Infobox football biography 2 (1); Back to Boca Juniors (1)]

### Conclusion

Throughout his career, Martín Palermo has been known for his resilience, goal-scoring ability, and dedication to Boca Juniors. Despite facing significant injuries and challenges abroad, he has remained a beloved figure in Argentine football, celebrated for his contributions both on and off the field. ### Biography and Career Overview

Thomas Kyparissis, born on March 26, 1970, in Katerini, Greece, is a retired Greek football player known for his time as a striker. Standing at 1.87 meters tall, Kyparissis had a notable career spanning several clubs across different levels of Greek football. His journey began with Pierikos, his hometown club, where he started his professional career in 1988. Over the course of his career, he played for various teams including Niki Volou, Panarkadikos, Korinthos FC, Panelefsiniakos, Skoda Xanthi, Aris Thessaloniki F.C., PAS Giannina, and Larissa FC. He also made a return to Pierikos in 2007 before retiring in 2008. [Data: BLP sources (1)]

### Notable Achievements and Playing Style

Throughout his career, Kyparissis was renowned for his goal-scoring abilities, netting over 140 goals in total. This impressive tally includes significant contributions to his clubs, particularly during his time with Larissa FC. From 2003 to 2005, he played a crucial role in helping Larissa attempt to return to the Super League Greece (the top division) after being relegated to the third division. His passion and strong mentality earned him the nickname "Psychara" (Big Soul) among Larissa's fans. [Data: BLP sources (1)]

### International Experience

In addition to his club career, Kyparissis represented the Greece national football team. He made 14 appearances for the national side between 1999 and 2000, scoring two goals during this period. His international experience added another layer to his already rich footballing history. [Data: BLP sources (1)]

### Post-Retirement Activities

After retiring from professional football in 2008, Kyparissis has remained involved in the sport. He currently serves as a sports director for Pierikos, the club where he began his professional career. This role allows him to continue contributing to the development of young talent and the growth of the club. [Data: BLP sources (1)]

Thomas Kyparissis's career is marked by his dedication, goal-scoring prowess, and strong mental fortitude. His journey through various Greek clubs, including a significant stint with Larissa FC, showcases his impact on the game. The '''2009 William & Mary Tribe football team''' represents the [[College of William & Mary]] in [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] (NCAA) [[Division I]] [[Division I#Football Championship Subdivision|Football Championship Subdivision]] (FCS) [[college football]] during the [[2009 NCAA Division I FCS football season|2009 season]]. William & Mary competes as a member of the [[Colonial Athletic Association]] (CAA) under head football coach [[Jimmye Laycock]] and play its home games at [[Zable Stadium]]. The 2009 campaign comes on the heels of a 7–4 record in 2008.

On September 5th, William & Mary opened their season against their academic rivals, the [[2009 Virginia Cavaliers football team|Virginia Cavaliers]] (UVa) in [[Charlottesville, Virginia|Charlottesville]]. UVa, an [[Division I (NCAA)#Football Bowl Subdivision|FBS]] team, was expected to win handily. However, the Tribe forced a UVa school record-tying seven turnovers and won the game 26–14. It was William & Mary's first win over Virginia since 1986 and their first over an FBS school since 1998 (a 45–38 win over [[Temple Owls football|Temple]]). Tribe [[redshirt]] freshman [[cornerback]] B.W. Webb intercepted three passes, including a 50-yard [[pick six]] late in the fourth quarter to seal the victory. Webb was named the College Football National Defensive Player of the Week by the press. This selection marked the first time since the award's inception in 2001 that any player from an [[Football Championship Subdivision|FCS]] school earned the distinction. Webb's game-sealing third interception was also chosen as [[SportsCenter]]'s #5 play of the day on its daily Top 10 Plays segment.

The October 3rd match-up pitted the #5 Tribe against the #2 Villanova Wildcats. Both teams headed into the contest with 4–0 (1–0 CAA) records. The 3:30 p.m. game was broadcasted live on the [[Versus (TV channel)|Versus]] network, making it the first-ever nationally televised CAA football game. Villanova won the game 28–17.

After defeating the #8 New Hampshire Wildcats on November 14th, the Tribe tied their program's best record through 10 games since the [[1947 William & Mary Tribe football team|1947 season]].<ref name=CAA>[http://www.caasports.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=8500&ATCLID=204833677 CAA Football Recap - November 14, 2009]. Retrieved on 14 November 2009.</ref> The victory improved William & Mary's record to 5–0 at home on the season, marking the first time since [[2004 William & Mary Tribe football team|2004]] that they had posted an undefeated regular season mark at [[Zable Stadium]].

The I-64 Trophy, given to the winner of the annual rivalry game with Richmond (dubbed the I-64 Bowl), was replaced in 2009 with the [[Capital Cup]], which honors the entire 118-game history of the rivalry (through 2008) between the two schools and the status of the two cities as the last two capitals of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Both the trophy and game's names were changed to be called the Capital Cup.<ref>[http://www.richmondspiders.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/111109aaa.html Richmond, William & Mary Rename Football Rivalry As Capital Cup]. Retrieved on [[November 11]], [[2009]].</ref>

## Overview of the 2009 William & Mary Tribe Football Team

The 2009 William & Mary Tribe football team represented the College of William & Mary in the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I Football Championship Subdivision (FCS) during the 2009 season. Under the leadership of head coach Jimmye Laycock, who was in his 30th year with the program, the Tribe competed in the Colonial Athletic Association (CAA) and played their home games at Zable Stadium. The team finished the season with an overall record of 9–2 and a conference record of 6–2, placing them sixth in both the Sports Network's FCS College Football Poll and the FCS Coaches Poll.

### Key Achievements and Notable Games

One of the standout moments of the season occurred on September 5th when the Tribe faced off against their academic rival, the Virginia Cavaliers (UVa), in Charlottesville. Despite expectations that UVa would dominate, William & Mary forced seven turnovers, tying a UVa school record, and secured a surprising 26–14 victory. This win marked William & Mary's first over Virginia since 1986 and their first over an FBS school since 1998. Redshirt freshman cornerback B.W. Webb played a crucial role in this victory, intercepting three passes, including a 50-yard pick six late in the fourth quarter. His performance earned him the College Football National Defensive Player of the Week award, making him the first player from an FCS school to receive this honor since its inception in 2001.

Another significant game took place on October 3rd, when the #5 ranked Tribe faced the #2 Villanova Wildcats. Both teams entered the contest with perfect 4–0 records (1–0 in CAA play). The game was nationally televised on the Versus network, marking the first-ever nationally televised CAA football game. Unfortunately, Villanova emerged victorious with a score of 28–17.

### Home Performance and Program Milestones

Throughout the season, the Tribe demonstrated strong home-field advantage, finishing with an undefeated 5–0 record at Zable Stadium. This marked the first time since 2004 that William & Mary had achieved such a feat. On November 14th, after defeating the New Hampshire Wildcats, the Tribe tied their program's best record through 10 games since the 1947 season. This milestone highlighted the team's consistent performance and improvement over the years.

### Rivalry Game and Trophy Changes

The annual rivalry game with Richmond, known as the I-64 Bowl, saw a change in tradition in 2009. The I-64 Trophy was replaced with the Capital Cup, honoring the entire 118-game history of the rivalry and the status of the two cities as the last two capitals of the Commonwealth of Virginia. This change aimed to elevate the significance of the game beyond just the immediate matchup.

## Season Schedule Summary

Below is a summary of the key games played by the William & Mary Tribe during the 2009 season:

- **September 5**: Defeated Virginia 26–14 in Charlottesville, VA.
- **September 12**: Defeated Central Connecticut State 33–14 at home in Williamsburg, VA.
- **September 19**: Defeated Norfolk State 27–15 in Norfolk, VA.
- **September 26**: Defeated Delaware 30–20 at home in Williamsburg, VA.
- **October 3**: Lost to Villanova 17–28 in Villanova, PA.
- **October 10**: Defeated Northeastern 34–14 in Brookline, MA.
- **October 24**: Defeated James Madison 24–3 at home in Williamsburg, VA.
- **October 31**: Defeated Rhode Island 39–14 in Kingston, RI.
- **November 7**: Defeated Towson 31–10 at home in Williamsburg, VA.

These results reflect the Tribe's strong performance throughout the season, particularly in their home games and against other CAA opponents. The team's ability to secure victories against both FBS and FCS competition showcased their competitiveness and potential for future success in the FCS division.

## Early Life and Background

Lionel Andrés Messi, born on 24 June 1987 in Rosario, Argentina, comes from a humble background. His father, Jorge Messi, worked as a factory worker, while his mother, Celia (née Cuccitini), was a part-time cleaner. This upbringing instilled in him a strong work ethic and determination, traits that would later contribute to his success in football [Data: Profile (1)].

His paternal lineage traces back to Ancona, Italy, where his ancestor, Angelo Messi, emigrated to Argentina in 1883. This Italian heritage adds another layer to Messi's identity, blending his Argentine roots with European ancestry [Data: El origen de los Messi (2); Las raíces italianas de Leo Messi (3)].

## Early Career and Move to Barcelona

Messi's talent was recognized early on. He began his football journey with Newell's Old Boys in Rosario, where he played from 1995 to 2000. However, due to his growth hormone deficiency, Barcelona offered to provide medical treatment and a platform to nurture his skills. Thus, in 2000, Messi and his family moved to Spain, marking the beginning of his professional career [Data: Profile (1)].

In 2004, Messi made his debut for Barcelona's B team, FC Barcelona Atlètic, playing five matches without scoring. Soon after, he joined the first team, breaking the La Liga record for the youngest player to both play and score in a league match. His debut season coincided with Barcelona's La Liga victory, setting the stage for his future successes [Data: Profile (1)].

## Rise to Prominence

Messi's breakthrough came during the 2006–07 season when he became a regular in the first team. He scored a hat-trick against Real Madrid in El Clásico and finished the season with 14 goals in 26 league games. However, his most prolific season was the 2008–09 campaign, where he scored 38 goals, contributing significantly to Barcelona's treble-winning season [Data: Profile (1)].

## International Career

Internationally, Messi has been a key figure for the Argentine national team. He first represented Argentina at the 2005 FIFA World Youth Championship, where he was the top scorer with six goals. He then made his senior debut in the 2006 FIFA World Cup, becoming the youngest Argentine to participate in the tournament. Over the years, he has won numerous accolades, including an Olympic gold medal with the Argentina Olympic football team in 2008 [Data: Profile (1)].

## Legacy and Comparisons

Messi's playing style and achievements have often drawn comparisons to Diego Maradona, another Argentine football legend. Maradona himself has declared Messi his "successor," highlighting the younger player's exceptional talent and impact on the sport [Data: Gardner (4); Reuters (5)].

Overall, Lionel Messi's journey from a young player in Rosario to one of the world's best footballers is marked by perseverance, skill, and a relentless pursuit of excellence. His contributions to both club and country have cemented his status as a modern-day football icon.

A '''corner kick''' is a method of restarting play in a game of [[association football]]. It was first devised in [[Sheffield]] under the [[Sheffield Rules]] 1867. It was adopted by the [[The Football Association|Football Association]] on February 17, 1872.

A corner kick is awarded to the attacking team when the ball leaves the [[football (soccer) field|field of play]] by crossing the goal line (either on the ground or in the air) without a goal having been scored, having been last touched by a defending player (including the [[goalkeeper]]).

In most cases, the [[assistant referee]] will signal that a corner should be awarded by first raising his flag, then using it to point at the corner arc on their side of the pitch; however, this is not an indication of which side the kick should be taken from. The referee then awards the corner by pointing to the relevant arc.

==Procedure==
[[Image:BarwellFC.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Player takes a corner kick]]
When taking a corner kick, the football is initially placed so that some piece of the ball touches the corner arc closest to where the ball went out of play. The corner arc is located at the intersection of the goalline and touchline and has a radius of one yard. All defending players must be at least ten yards (9.15m) from the ball until the corner kick is taken. A corner kick is taken as soon as it is kicked and moves. 

A goal may be scored directly from a corner kick, but only against the opposing side; an [[own goal]] may not be scored. A player cannot be penalised for [[offside law (football)|offside]] by playing the ball direct from a corner kick.

===Infringements===

Opposing players must retire the required distance as stated above. Failure to do so may constitute misconduct and be punished by a [[Yellow card|caution]] (yellow card). 

It is an offence for the kicker to touch the ball a second time until it has been touched by another player; this is punishable by an [[indirect free kick]] to the defending team from where the offence occurred, unless the second touch was also a more serious handling offence, in which case it is punishable by a [[direct free kick]] or [[penalty kick]], as appropriate.
[[File:Corner kick.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Corner kick at [[UEFA Europa League 2009-10]]]]

===Tactics in taking and defending a corner===
A common tactic is for several attackers to stand close in front of the goal, whereupon the corner taker [[Cross (football)|crosses]] the ball for them to [[header|head]] into the goal.

The defending team may choose to form a wall of players in an attempt to force the ball to be played to an area which is more easily defended. This is not done often, however, because defending players must remain at least 10 yards from the ball until it is in play.

The defending team also has the choice of whether to instruct a player to place himself beside one or both of the goalposts to provide protection to the goal in addition to the [[goalkeeper]] himself. Some teams will only place a player on one post, while it is unusual for a team to not have a player beside either post. The thinking behind placing a player beside a goalpost is that it means more of the goal area is protected and there is no loss in the ability to play an [[Offside_%28football%29#Offside_trap|offside trap]] because offside does not apply for the first touch from a corner.

The defending team also has to decide how many players it needs to defend a corner. It has become increasingly common for defending teams to withdraw every player into a defensive area. Some coaches argue against this strategy because it means that the attacking team can commit almost every player to attacking the goal, except the goalkeeper and perhaps one defender. Withdrawing all players into a defensive area also means that if the ball is cleared from an initial cross, it is more than likely that the attacking team will regain possession of the ball and begin a new attack.

====Short corner====
An alternative strategy for the attacking team is to take a ''short corner''. The ball is kicked to a player located within ten yards of the kicker, to create a better angle of approach toward the goal. An example of this was when [[Maniche]] scored a spectacular goal for [[Portugal national football team|Portugal]] against [[Netherlands national football team|Holland]] in [[UEFA Euro 2004|Euro 2004]].

A rarely-seen "trick" version of the short corner was famously attempted during a tense top-of-the-table [[Premier League]] clash between [[Manchester United]] and [[Chelsea FC|Chelsea]] in the [[Premier League 2008–09|2008-09 season]], causing much controversy and media discussion. The strategy involved United's [[Wayne Rooney]], standing at the corner flag, pretending to change his mind about taking the corner and signalling to fellow striker [[Ryan Giggs]] to do it instead. While leaving the arc, however, Rooney sneakily touched the ball, effectively putting it into play. With Chelsea's defense unprepared and expecting a conventional corner, Giggs took the ball, sprinted with it towards goal and crossed it for teammate [[Cristiano Ronaldo]] to score with a header. On this occasion the goal was immediately disallowed after the [[assistant referee|linesman]], not having seen Rooney's taking of the corner, raised his flag, thus prompting the referee to stop play; however the routine has been considered legal on previous occasions <ref name="ManU">[http://www.soccer-training-info.com/trick_corner_kick.asp Soccer Training Info], retrieved Feb 2009</ref><ref name="Celt">[http://www.independent.ie/sport/soccer/premier-league/fergie-got-corner-idea-42-years-ago-1600556.html The Irish Independent], retrieved Feb 2009.</ref>, such as by [[Mladen Petric]] and [[Ivan Rakitic]] at [[FC Basel]]<ref name="ManU" />, as well as United manager [[Alex Ferguson]] saying he first saw it performed by [[Glasgow Celtic|Celtic]] 42 years previously, and even himself tried it at [[Aberdeen FC|Aberdeen]].<ref name="Celt" /> The strategy is, however, rare, as its great strength is the element of surprise.

===Scoring a goal direct from a corner===
It has been permitted to score direct from a corner kick since the [[International Football Association Board|IFAB]] meeting of 15 June 1924 authorised it for the following season.<ref name="Barnade">
{{cite web |url=http://www.clarin.com/diario/2004/10/02/deportes/d-07101.htm |title=El gol olímpico cumple 80 |last=Barnade |first=Oscar |date=October 2004 |work=[[Clarín (newspaper)|Clarín]] |language=Spanish |accessdate=2009-11-17 }}
</ref><ref>
{{cite web |url=http://ssbra.org/html/laws/IFABarc/pdf/1924/1924min.pdf |title=Minutes of the AGM of the IFAB |date=15 June 1924 |publisher=SSBRA |page=3 |accessdate=29 November 2009 |location=London}}
</ref>  The first such goal was scored by [[Billy Alston]] in Scotland on 21 August.<ref name="Barnade"/>  The first in England was by [[Huddersfield Town F.C.|Huddersfield's]] [[Billy Smith (footballer born 1895)|Billy Smith]].  It remains a rare occurrence, often accomplished by fluke rather than intent, and with the goalkeeper usually blamed for an error.<ref name="Freddi">
{{cite web |url=http://www.wsc.co.uk/content/view/2569/29/ |title=Gol olimpico |last=Freddi |first=Cris |date=March 2003 |work=[[When Saturday Comes]] |accessdate=2009-11-17}}
</ref>

This restart occurs when the ball leaves the field of play by crossing the goal line without a goal being scored, and having been last touched by a defending player, including the goalkeeper.

#### Procedure

When taking a corner kick, the ball is placed so that part of it touches the corner arc closest to where the ball went out of play. The corner arc is located at the intersection of the goal line and touchline and has a radius of one yard. All defending players must be at least ten yards (9.15 meters) from the ball until the corner kick is taken. The corner kick is taken as soon as the ball is kicked and moves.

A goal can be scored directly from a corner kick, but only against the opposing side; an own goal cannot be scored. Additionally, a player cannot be penalized for being offside by playing the ball directly from a corner kick.

#### Infringements

Opposing players must retreat the required distance as stated above. If they fail to do so, it may constitute misconduct and be punished by a caution (yellow card). It is also an offense for the kicker to touch the ball a second time until it has been touched by another player. This is punishable by an indirect free kick to the defending team from where the offense occurred. If the second touch is also a more serious handling offense, it is punishable by a direct free kick or penalty kick, as appropriate.

### Tactics in Taking and Defending a Corner

A common tactic for the attacking team is to position several players close in front of the goal and have the corner taker cross the ball for them to head into the goal. The defending team may choose to form a wall of players to force the ball to be played to an area that is easier to defend. However, this is not done often because defending players must remain at least ten yards from the ball until it is in play.

Defending teams also have the option of placing a player beside one or both of the goalposts to provide additional protection to the goal. This strategy aims to cover more of the goal area and maintain the ability to play an offside trap. Some teams will only place a player on one post, while it is unusual for a team to not have a player beside either post.

Another decision for the defending team is how many players to use in defending a corner. It has become increasingly common for defending teams to withdraw every player into a defensive area. However, some coaches argue against this strategy because it allows the attacking team to commit almost every player to attacking the goal, except the goalkeeper and perhaps one defender. Withdrawing all players into a defensive area also means that if the ball is cleared from an initial cross, it is more likely that the attacking team will regain possession and start a new attack.

An alternative strategy for the attacking team is to take a short corner. The ball is kicked to a player located within ten yards of the kicker, creating a better angle of approach toward the goal. An example of this was when Maniche scored a spectacular goal for Portugal against Holland in Euro 2004.

Although the goal was initially disallowed due to the linesman raising his flag, the routine has been considered legal on previous occasions.

It has been permitted to score directly from a corner kick since the International Football Association Board (IFAB) meeting of 15 June 1924 authorized it for the following season. Scoring directly from a corner remains a rare occurrence, often accomplished by fluke rather than intent, and with the goalkeeper usually blamed for an error.

This type of goal is called an "Olympic goal" in Latin America, dating back to 2 October 1924 when Argentina's Cesáreo Onzari scored against Uruguay, who had just won the 1924 Olympic title. The expression is also used in the United States, reflecting Latin influence.

## Overview of the Divizia B 1994–95 Season

The **Divizia B 1994–95 season** marked the 55th year of this division, which serves as the second tier of the Romanian football league system. This season featured 36 teams divided into two series, with each series consisting of 18 teams. The structure of the league allowed for promotion and relegation based on the final standings at the end of the season.

### Promotion and Relegation Rules

At the conclusion of the season, the winners of each series were promoted directly to the top-tier **Divizia A**. The runners-up from each series participated in a playoff to determine the second team to be promoted. Conversely, the bottom two teams from each series were relegated to the third-tier **Divizia C**, along with the 15th and 16th placed teams that did not succeed in the playoff.

## Standings Summary

### Seria I

In **Seria I**, **Selena** emerged as the champions, securing a direct promotion to **Divizia A**. They had an impressive record of 22 wins, 5 draws, and 7 losses, with a goal difference of 76-30. **Dacia Unirea Brăila** finished second but was penalized 8 points and excluded from the promotion playoff due to disciplinary issues. **Politehnica Iaşi** secured the second promotion spot after winning the playoff.

The bottom four teams faced relegation:

'''Mohamed Ahmed Ben Bella''' (''Muhammad Ahmad Bin Balla'') ('''{{lang-ar|أحمد بن بلّة}}''') (born [[December 25]] [[1918]]<ref>Shown as 1916 in some sources, but his father changed his year of birth from 1918 to enable him to leave school early and help him on his farm – [http://i-cias.com/e.o/benbella.htm].</ref>, [[Maghnia]], [[Algeria]]) was the first [[President of Algeria]].
==Youth==
Ben Bella was born in a small village in western Algeria during the height of the [[France|French]] colonial period to a [[Sufi]] [[Muslim]] family. He attended school in [[Tlemcen]] and was disturbed by the discrimination towards Muslims by his European teacher.  He failed his ''brevet'' exam, and subsequently dropped out of school.

==Service with French Army==

Ben Bella volunteered for service in the [[French Army]] in 1936. The Army was one of the few avenues of advancement for Algerian Muslims under colonial rule and voluntary enlistment was common. Posted to [[Marseille]] he played center mid-field for [[Olympique de Marseille]] in 1939–1940<ref>[http://www.om-passion.com/effectif_saison_1939_425_ben-bella.html Ben Bella profile on om-passion, unofficial Olympique de Marseille site]</ref>. He was offered a professional spot on the team, but rejected the offer.

Ben Bella's eldest brother had also served in the French Army during [[World War I]] and died of his wounds. Two other brothers died at young ages. In 1940 Ben Bella enlisted again and was awarded the ''Croix de Guerre''. He was demobilised after the fall of France but joined a regiment of [[1st Moroccan Infantry Division (France)|Moroccan tirailleurs]] (infantry) with whom he saw service throughout the Italian campaign. Ben Bella was promoted to the rank of [[warrant officer]] and received the ''Medaille Militaire'' for bravery. He refused to accept an officer's commission after learning of the harsh French repression that followed a Muslim rising in the small Algerian town of Setif in May 1945.

==Before independence==
[[Image:Khider - Lacheraf - Aït Ahmed - Boudiaf - Ben Bella.jpg|right|thumb|300px|Ben Bella (right) after his arrest by the French army]] 
Following election as a municipal councillor Ben Bella became a founder member of an underground organisation pledged to fight colonial rule, known as the ''[[Organisation Spéciale]]''. This was the immediate predecessor of the [[Front de Libération Nationale]]. Arrested in 1951 and sentenced to eight years imprisonment Ben Bella escaped from Blida prison, making his way to Tunisia and then Egypt.

At the outbreak of the Algerian War in 1954 Ben Bella was based in Cairo where he had become one of the nine members of the Revolutionary Committee of Unity and Action which headed the ''Front de Liberation Nationale''. He was arrested by the French in 1956, after his airplane had been controversially intercepted and brought to France, and released in 1962. His arrest led to the resignation of [[Alain Savary]], opposed to [[Guy Mollet]]'s policies. While in prison he was elected a vice-premier of the Algerian [[provisional government]]. Ben Bella's first language was [[French language|French]], not [[Arabic language|Arabic]]{{Citation needed|it might as well have been Berber or Algerian Arabic, see talkpage|date=February 2009}}.  He learned Arabic while in prison. While in Egypt, Ben Bella met the Egyptian president, [[Gamel Abdel Nasser]]. When Abdel Nasser brought Ben Bella to speak for the first time to an Egyptian audience, he broke into tears because he could not speak [[Arabic language|Arabic]]. It has been said that he refused to teach his own daughter French because he wanted her to learn Arabic first and not be in the same position he was. Like many [[Arab]] militants of the time, he would come to describe himself as a "[[Nasserism|Nasserist]]" and developed close ties to Egypt even before independence was achieved. Abdel Nasser's material, emotional and political support of the Algerian movement would come to cause him troubles, as it played a major role in France's choice to wage war on him during the 1956 [[Suez Crisis]].

Due to Pakistan's support to the cause of Algerian struggle for self determination and independence, Ben Bella was given a Pakistani diplomatic passport in order to make his foreign travels possible in the face of the international hunt down by the French and their allies.<ref>ipripak.org/factfiles/ff81.pdf </ref><ref name="mushahidhussain.com">http://www.mushahidhussain.com/articles/article3_promoting.htm</ref><ref>www.foreignaffairscommittee.org/includes/content_files/Pak-%20Africa%20Relations.pdf </ref> Ben Bella also traveled on a Pakistani diplomatic passport during the years of his exile from Algeria in 1980's. <ref name="mushahidhussain.com"/>

==Algerian independence==

After [[Algeria]]'s independence, Ben Bella quickly became more popular. In June 1962, he challenged the leadership of Premier [[Benyoucef Benkhedda]]; this led to several disputes among his rivals in the FLN, which were quickly suppressed by Ben Bella's rapidly growing number of supporters, most notably within the armed forces. By September, Bella was in control of Algeria by all but name, and was elected as premier in a one-sided election on [[20 September]], which was recognized by the United States on [[September 29]]. [[Algeria]] was admitted as the 109th member of the [[United Nations]] on [[8 October]] [[1962]]. 

In 1963 he was elected President in an uncontested election, and also led Algeria's costly but ultimately victorious defense against [[Moroccan]] invasion in the [[Sand war]]. After stabilizing the country, Ben Bella embarked on a series of popular but somewhat anarchic land reforms to the benefit of landless farmers, and increasingly turned to socialist rhetoric.  His policy of Autogestion, or self-management, was adopted after the peasants seized former French lands.  In balancing factions within the Algerian government, notably the FLN army, the former guerrillas and the state bureaucracy, his rule became increasingly autocratic. Eccentric and arrogant behaviour towards colleagues is said to have alienated many former supporters, and, while he promoted the development of his own cult of personality, by 1964 he was dedicating more time to foreign affairs than local political developments.  In 1965, Ben Bella was deposed by army strongman and close friend [[Houari Boumédiènne]] in 1965, and placed under house arrest until 1980, when he was granted exile in [[Switzerland]]. He lived for 10 years in [[Lausanne]], but was allowed to return to his homeland in 1990.

Ahmed Ben Bella was awarded the title [[Hero of the Soviet Union]] on [[April 30]] [[1964]] <ref>{{ru icon}}[http://www.warheroes.ru/hero/hero.asp?Hero_id=1069 Biography] at the website on Heroes of the Soviet Union and Russia</ref>

# Mohamed Ahmed Ben Bella: A Key Figure in Algerian Independence

## Early Life and Military Service

Mohamed Ahmed Ben Bella, born on December 25, 1918, in Maghnia, Algeria, grew up during the French colonial period. His early life was marked by the discrimination faced by Muslims in French-occupied Algeria. Ben Bella attended school in Tlemcen but left after failing his brevet exam. In 1936, he volunteered for the French Army, a common path for Algerian Muslims seeking advancement. During his military service, he played for Olympique de Marseille and was later awarded the Croix de Guerre for his bravery in the Italian campaign during World War II. He refused an officer's commission after learning about the French repression following a Muslim uprising in Setif in 1945.

## Pre-Independence Struggle

Ben Bella became involved in the fight against colonial rule, founding the Organisation Spéciale, a precursor to the Front de Libération Nationale (FLN). In 1951, he was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison but escaped to Tunisia and then Egypt. During the Algerian War of Independence, which began in 1954, Ben Bella was a key leader in the FLN. He was arrested by the French in 1956 and released in 1962, after which he was elected vice-premier of the Algerian provisional government. His first language was French, and he learned Arabic while in prison. Ben Bella developed close ties with Gamel Abdel Nasser, the Egyptian president, who supported the Algerian independence movement.

## Algerian Independence and Presidency

After Algeria gained independence in 1962, Ben Bella quickly rose to prominence. He challenged the leadership of Premier Benyoucef Benkhedda and won the support of the armed forces. In September 1962, he was elected premier, and the United States recognized Algeria as a sovereign nation. In 1963, Ben Bella was elected President in an uncontested election. He led Algeria's successful defense against Morocco in the Sand War and implemented land reforms that benefited landless farmers. However, his rule became increasingly autocratic, and he alienated many former supporters with his eccentric and arrogant behavior. In 1965, he was deposed by army strongman Houari Boumédiènne and placed under house arrest until 1980, when he was granted exile in Switzerland.

## Recent Activities and Legacy

Ben Bella has remained active in politics and advocacy. He was elected President of the International Campaign Against Aggression on Iraq and has described himself as a moderate Islamist. Despite his past as a leader of a one-party state, he now advocates for democracy in Algeria. He has criticized the militant voices rising in the Islamic world, attributing them to a faulty interpretation of Islam. Ben Bella is widely respected for his role in the anti-colonial struggle and is seen by many Arab intellectuals as a significant figure in the region.

This summary covers the key aspects of Mohamed Ahmed Ben Bella's life and contributions, highlighting his pivotal role in Algeria's independence and his subsequent political career and activism. [Data: Provided Text (entire text)]

'''Alexander "Alex" Smithies''' (born March 5, 1990 in [[Huddersfield]], [[England]]) is a [[professional]] [[association football|footballer]] with [[Football League One|League One]] side [[Huddersfield Town F.C.|Huddersfield Town]]. An [[academy]] [[goalkeeper (association football)|goalkeeper]] who first came into prominence during the [[2007-08 in English football|2007–08]] season, after second choice goalkeeper [[Simon Eastwood]] injured his foot and appeared on the Town bench during September 2007. Alex is now the first-choice 'keeper. 

==Career==
===Early Life===
Smithies grew up in Golcar, in the Colne Valley area of Huddersfield.  He attended Colne Valley High School.
===Club===
Smithies made his first team début as a 76th minute [[Substitute (football)|substitute]] for [[Matt Glennon]], who was sent off during Huddersfield Town's 4–1 defeat by [[Southend United F.C.|Southend United]] at [[Roots Hall]] on 5 December 2007. He made his first full start in the 4–0 defeat at [[Leeds United A.F.C.|Leeds United]] on 8 December, after Glennon lost his appeal against his dismissal and Town were refused permission to loan an emergency goalkeeper, because Smithies was registered as a professional. His next match for the Terriers would be in their 1–0 defeat against [[Darlington F.C.|Darlington]] in the [[Football League Trophy 2008-09|Football League Trophy]] on 7 October 2008. His next league appearance would also be his first at the [[Galpharm Stadium]] for a first-team match. Caretaker manager [[Gerry Murphy]] dropped regular keeper [[Matt Glennon]] for the young custodian and again, he didn't disappoint, helping Huddersfield to a 2–1 victory over [[Walsall F.C.|Walsall]] on 6 December 2008. He was only beaten by a superb long-range effort from Walsall [[midfielder]] [[Alex Nicholls (footballer)|Alex Nicholls]]. His first clean sheet for the club came on Smithies return to Roots Hall in a 1–0 win for Huddersfield over [[Southend United F.C.|Southend United]] on 13 December 2008. It was even more remarkable thanks to the penalty save made by Smithies from [[James Walker (footballer born 1987)|James Walker]] 10 minutes from time. On April 2, 2009 he was assesed by "Sky Sports Scout", a service offered by [[Sky Sports]] for finding the best young talent in the country.  He was given a rating of 65/80 and labelled as "already on his way to the top."<ref>http://www.skysports.com/story/0,19528,11979_5096081,00.html</ref>

===International===

He joined the [[North York Rockets]] of the [[Canadian Soccer League (1987%E2%80%931992)|Canadian Soccer League]] in 1990 and remained with the club through the league's demise in 1992 to the club's last year, played in the [[Canadian National Soccer League|National Soccer League]] (NSL), in 1993. He played in the summer of 1994 with the [[St. Catharines Roma]] (of the same league which however was by then renamed to the Canadian National Soccer League). Radziński returned to Europe, joining [[K.F.C. Germinal Beerschot|Germinal Ekeren]] in [[Belgium]] in 1994. From there he eventually signed for Belgian giants [[R.S.C. Anderlecht|Anderlecht]] for whom he scored 57 goals in 90 appearances – including five [[UEFA Champions League]] strikes in his last season with the Belgian champions - before moving to [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] for around [[Pound sterling|£]]4.5 million, the highest transfer fee paid for a Canadian up to that time. At Everton, Radziński scored 25 times in 91 Premiership outings before requesting a transfer, eventually securing a three year deal with [[Fulham F.C.]] worth £1.75 million. Radzinski wasn't as prolific at Fulham as he was in his previous side, but won over the fans with several crucial goals. Radzinski was released at the end of the [[FA Premier League 2006-07|2006-07 season]] by new manager [[Lawrie Sanchez]], totalling 17 goals in 117 appearances. On [[August 28]] 2007, he signed for [[Greece|Greek]] team [[Skoda Xanthi]], on a free transfer. One year later, on [[August 30]] 2008 he signed a 1 year contract for the [[Belgian Second Division]] club [[Lierse S.K.|Lierse]], although his previous contract still applied until 2010. Lierse first had their eye on [[Peter Utaka]], but when he was transferred to [[Odense Boldklub|Odense]], they chose to attract Radzinski. Radzinski had disclosed to the press his belief that members of Skoda Xanthi had been involved in [[match fixing]] and was seeking a transfer. ==International career== Radzinski made his debut for the [[Canada men's national soccer team|Canadian national team]] in a June 1995 friendly match against [[Turkey national football team|Turkey]]. # Tomasz Radziński: A Multifaceted Career in Football

## Biography

Tomasz Radziński, born on December 14, 1973, in Poznań, Poland, is a Polish Canadian football striker. He currently plays for Lierse S.K. in the Belgian Second Division. Standing at 1.74 meters tall, Radziński has had a long and varied career, playing for numerous clubs across different countries. His journey began in his native Poland with Cujavia Inowroclaw and VfL Osnabrück in Germany before he moved to Canada to play for North York Rockets and St. Catharines Roma. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

## Club Career

### Early Years in Canada

Radziński started his professional career in Canada, playing for the North York Rockets from 1990 to 1993. After the Canadian Soccer League's demise, he continued with the club through its last year in the National Soccer League. In 1994, he briefly played for St. Catharines Roma in the Canadian National Soccer League. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

### European Career

In 1994, Radziński returned to Europe, joining Germinal Ekeren in Belgium. This marked the beginning of his successful European career. He then moved to R.S.C. Anderlecht, one of Belgium's biggest clubs, where he scored 57 goals in 90 appearances, including five in the UEFA Champions League. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

### Premier League Experience

In 1998, Radziński made a significant move to Everton F.C., becoming the highest-paid Canadian player at the time with a transfer fee of around £4.5 million. At Everton, he scored 25 goals in 91 appearances before requesting a transfer. He then signed with Fulham F.C. for £1.75 million, where he scored 17 goals in 117 appearances. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

### Later Career

After leaving Fulham, Radziński signed with Greek team Skoda Xanthi in August 2007. One year later, he joined Lierse S.K. in Belgium, where he remains active in the Belgian Second Division. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

## International Career

Radziński has been a key figure for the Canadian national team since making his debut in a friendly match against Turkey in June 1995. Over his international career, he earned 46 caps and scored 10 goals. He participated in 17 FIFA World Cup qualification matches, showcasing his versatility and skill on the international stage. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

### Notable International Goals

Some of his notable international goals include:
- Scoring twice against Switzerland in a friendly match in St. Gallen, Switzerland, on May 15, 2002.
- Scoring against Belize in Kingston, Ontario, during the 2006 World Cup Qualification on June 13, 2004.
- Scoring against Mexico in Edmonton, Canada, during the 2010 World Cup Qualification on October 10, 2008. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

## Honors

Throughout his career, Radziński has achieved several honors, particularly during his time in Belgium. He won the Belgian First Division title twice with R.S.C. Anderlecht in the 1999-2000 and 2000-01 seasons. Additionally, he won the Belgian Cup in 1997. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

## Conclusion

Tomasz Radziński's career is a testament to his adaptability and talent as a footballer. From his early days in Poland and Germany to his success in Canada and Europe, Radziński has left a lasting impact on the sport. His contributions to both club and international football have solidified his place in the annals of football history. [Data: Infobox Football biography]

Davids started his career at [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]] in 1991, making his debut on 6 September in a 5–1 home win over [[RKC Waalwijk]]. He helped the [[Amsterdam]] club to three domestic [[Eredivisie]] titles, as well as international success with the 1992 [[UEFA Cup]] and the 1995 [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]]. In the [[1996 UEFA Champions League Final]], he missed Ajax's first penalty in the shootout, which they ultimately lost to [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]]. While at Ajax, he was nicknamed ''"The Pitbull"'' by Ajax manager [[Louis van Gaal]] due to his fierce style of play and bite in the midfield. 

Davids moved to [[Italy]] in 1996 to play for [[A.C. Milan|AC Milan]]. He did not see much playing time at Milan, and moved on to league rivals [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]] in December 1997 for a £5.3 million transfer fee.<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/internationals/scotland/3265413.stm David v Goliath?]</ref> Six successful years in [[Turin]] followed, with Davids helping the side to the [[Serie A]] title in 1998, 2002 and 2003. Also, Juventus manager [[Marcello Lippi]] once described him as ''"my one-man engine room."'' On 17 May 2001, Davids was suspended by [[FIFA]] when he tested positive for the banned [[anabolic steroid]], [[nandrolone]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/international/3006500/Davids-and-Couto-hit-with-FIFA-bans.html|title=Davids and Couto hit with FIFA bans|date=2001-05-31|accessdate=2009-10-09|publisher=Telegraph}}</ref>
He was often inspirational in Europe, playing 15 times as the club made it all the way to the [[UEFA Champions League 2002-03]] final before losing to Milan on penalties. 

In September 2003 Davids joined [[FC Barcelona]] on loan in January 2004 as the Spanish club enjoyed a successful resurgence of form, finishing second to [[Valencia CF]] in the league. Then, he permanently moved on to Italian club [[Internazionale Milano F.C.|Internazionale]] on a three-year contract.<ref>[http://www.inter.it/aas/news/reader?L=en&N=14623 inter.it], ''Edgar Davids joins Inter, 11 July 2004''</ref> When Inter terminated the remaining years of his contract in August 2005, he moved to [[England]] on a [[free transfer (soccer)|free transfer]] to play for [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]].<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/t/tottenham_hotspur/4719445.stm], Tottenham complete Davids signing , 3 August 2005''</ref> He had a successful stay at Tottenham and instantly became a fans favourite. His first and only goal was in a 2–1 away win against [[Wigan Athletic F.C.|Wigan Athletic]].<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/4450908.stm], Wigan 1-2 Tottenham , 26 November 2005''</ref> Davids played for Tottenham in the [[FA Premier League 2005–06|2005–06]] and the [[FA Premier League 2006–07|2006–07]] seasons, both in which Tottenham finished in 5th position. 

[[File:Edgar Davids 3.jpg|thumb|Davids during his second period at Ajax.]]
Davids signed once more for Ajax on 28 January 2007<ref>[http://www.nos.nl/nos/artikelen/2007/01/art000001C742BF711B18BC.html nos.nl], ''Davids signs for Ajax. 28 January 2007''</ref> and played his first match against Ajax's rivals [[Feyenoord]] on 4 February.<ref> {{cite web|title=Tactical Formation|work=Football-Lineups.com

He was one of the key midfielders in the run for the Dutch championship that was lost on one single goal to [[PSV Eindhoven|PSV]] on the final day of the league. He also played a major role in Ajax's cup campaign. He secured the [[KNVB Cup]] for Ajax by scoring the final penalty in a thrilling penalty shoot-out against [[AZ (football club)|AZ]].

Prior to the start of the 2007–08 season, Davids' leg was broken in a pre-season friendly against [[Go Ahead Eagles]], sidelining him for around three months.<ref name="Ajax midfielder Davids breaks leg">{{cite news| title = Ajax midfielder Davids breaks leg| url = http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/europe/6910718.stm| publisher = BBC Sport| date = 22 July 2007}}</ref> In May 2008, Davids said he would leave Ajax when his contract expired on 30 June.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/transfers/summer-sales-trans

The **1921 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team** represented the University of Nebraska in the 1921 college football season. Under the leadership of new head coach Fred Dawson, who came from Princeton, the team aimed to reclaim its place in the Missouri Valley Intercollegiate Athletic Association (MVI AA). This season marked Nebraska's return to the MVI AA after a two-year hiatus as an independent team. With eighteen returning lettermen, the highest number in the program's history at that time, the team had high aspirations for achieving a conference title.

### Before the Season

In preparation for the season, the coaching staff underwent some changes. Former head coach Henry Schulte stepped down to focus on coaching other sports at Nebraska but remained involved with the team as the linemen coach. Fred Dawson took over as the new head coach, bringing his experience from Princeton. The team faced a new challenge due to a league rule that limited preseason practices to only two weeks before the first game, requiring significant effort to prepare after the summer break.

### Schedule

The 1921 season saw the Nebraska Cornhuskers play eight games, with a record of 7 wins, 1 loss, and 0 ties. Here is a summary of their schedule:

'''Sotirios "Sotiris" Kyrgiakos''' ({{lang-el|Σωτήρης Κυργιάκος}}) (born on 23 July 1979 in [[Trikala]], [[Greece]]) is a [[Greeks|Greek]] international [[Association football|football]] player currently playing as a [[Defender (association football)#Centre back|centre back]] for [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] in the [[Premier League]].<ref name="LFC-sign">{{cite web|url=http://www.liverpoolfc.tv/news/drilldown/N165520090821-1750.htm|title=KYRGIAKOS COMPLETES REDS SWITCH }}</ref>

==Club career==
===Panathinaikos===
Kyrgiakos made his first football steps with a local team, Thyella Megalochoriou. It did not take long for him to be recognized. At the start of the 1996-97 season he became a member of the [[Panathinaikos FC|Panathinaikos]] football academy. He lived and played football at the Paiania athletic complex, the club’s training ground.

In the wake of the 1999-2000 season he became a member of [[Agios Nikolaos]], a second division club and won the respect of president Lampros Maris whom Sotirios considers as his second father. He stayed with Agios Nikolaos for two years and in 2001 he took part in the pre-season camp at [[OFI Crete]]. 
The centre-back injuries at his parent club, Panathinaikos, just before the 3rd Qualifying round matches with [[SK Slavia Praha|Slavia Prague]] for the [[UEFA Champions League 2000–01|2000–01 Champions League]] meant that he had to return to Paiania and become a regular member of the starting line-up.

===Rangers===
The following January, he joined Rangers on loan during [[2004-05 in Scottish football|season 2004-05]] with a view to a permanent deal at the end of the season. With his new club he won a second consecutive championship and also the [[Scottish League Cup]] scoring two goals in the 5-1 win against [[Motherwell F.C.|Motherwell]] in the final.<ref>{{cite web 
|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_div_1/4359199.stm
|title=Rangers 5-1 Motherwell 
|publisher=[[BBC]] 
|date=20 March 2005 |accessdate=5 November 2009}}</ref> He initially failed to agree terms with Rangers and held talks with [[Everton F.C.|Everton]], [[Portsmouth F.C.|Portsmouth]] and [[FC Schalke 04|Schalke]] and the Italian club [[Genoa C.F.C.|Genoa]] before finally agreeing a one year deal with [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] <ref>[http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/2354086/Rangers-finally-sign-Kyrgiakos.html Gers sign Kyrgiakos]</ref>. He scored a famous winning goal against [[FC Porto]] in the [[UEFA Champions League]] that year,<ref>{{cite web 
|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/europe/4236960.stm
|title=Rangers 3-2 Porto
|publisher=[[BBC]] 
|date=13 September 2005 |accessdate=5 November 2009}}</ref> and ended the season with three goals after also scoring against Peterhead in the FA Cup<ref>{{cite web 
|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_cups/4584896.stm
|title=Rangers 5-0 Peterhead 
|publisher=[[BBC]] 
|date=7 January 2006 |accessdate=5 November 2009}}</ref> and Dunfermline in the league.<ref>{{cite web 
|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_prem/4836940.stm
|title=Rangers 1-0 Dunfermline Athletic 
|publisher=[[BBC]] 
|date=25 March 2006 |accessdate=5 November 2009}}</ref> He was released in May 2006 after the contract ran out <ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/r/rangers/4758643.stm Gers release Soto]</ref>.

===Eintracht Frankfurt===
In June 2006 Sotiris signed a 2 year deal with [[Eintracht Frankfurt]]<ref>[http://www.uefa.com/footballeurope/news/kind=2/newsid=433279.html Kyrgiakos heads to Frankfurt]</ref>. In his first season, he proved to be a fan favourite with some great performances and crucial goals which helped the team avoid relegation. In his second season with the club with more excellent performances he helped the team finish in 9th position. On 1 July 2008, after his 2 year deal expired, Kyrgiakos decided not to renew his contract with the German club, and so was released.

===AEK Athens===
On 1 August 2008, Sotiris agreed to sign for [[AEK Athens F.C.|AEK Athens]] on a five year deal <ref>[http://www.aekfc.gr/index.asp?a_id=74&n_id=4309 AEK FC sign Kyrgiakos]</ref>. Sotiris Kyrgiakos has reportedly been earning 1.6 Million Euros per year, helping the team to reach the final of the [[Greek Cup]].

===Liverpool===
On 21 August 2009 it was announced that he had signed a two-year deal with the option of a further year for [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]], for a reported fee of £2 million, becoming the first Greek player to sign for Liverpool. Kyrgiakos wears the number 16 shirt at Anfield.<ref name="LFC-sign"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/l/liverpool/8211133.stm|title=Liverpool agree fee for Kyrgiakos }}</ref>

He made his league debut against [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton]] on 29 August 2009 in which Liverpool won 3-2 .<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.independent.co.uk/sport/football/premier-league/gerrards-late-winner-makes-point-to-benitez-1779309.html|title=Gerrard's late winner makes point to Benitez|date=29 August 2009|work=The Independent|accessdate=30 August 2009}}</ref>

==International career==
Kyrgiakos made his senior international debut on 13 February 2002 against [[Sweden national football team|Sweden]], and scored his first goal against [[Norway national football team|Norway]] 1 year later on 13 February 2003.
He was unlucky to miss their [[UEFA Euro 2004|Euro 2004]] victory through injury, which ironically was a knee injury sustained against [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] team-mate [[Stefan Klos]]. He scored three goals in their [[UEFA Euro 2008 qualifying Group C|Euro 2008]] qualifiers and was selected in the final squad to represent [[Greece]] in the [[Euro 2008|final tournament]] <ref>[http://en.euro2008.uefa.com/news/kind=1/newsid=702185.html#greeces+papastathopoulos+drops Papastaopoulos doesnt make final cut]</ref>.
