[[Serbia national football team|Serbia]] }} '''Radomir Antić''' ([[Serbian Cyrillic]]: Радомир Антић; born 22 November 1948 in [[Žitište]]) is a [[Serbia]]n former football defender and current football manager for the [[Serbia national football team|Serbian national team]]. Following a 17-year playing career he found his true calling in coaching. He is the only individual who has managed [[FC Barcelona]], [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]], and [[Atlético de Madrid|Atlético Madrid]]. Additionally, Antić is one of only two men to have managed both FC Barcelona and Real Madrid, long-time bitter rivals. (The other one is [[Enrique Fernández Viola]]). ==Playing career== Antić was born in [[Žitište]] to a Serbian family that settled in the small [[Banat]] town shortly before his birth (his father Jovan is from [[Janja]] village near [[Bijeljina]], his mother Milka from [[Grmeč]] region).[http://www.pressonline.rs/page/stories/sr.html?view=story&id=67952§ionId=37 Politički intervju - Radomir Antić: Imam taktiku za bolju Srbiju, ''Press'', June 7, 2009] The family then moved to [[Titovo Užice]] when Radomir was six years old.[http://www.blic.rs/sport.php?id=119120 Roki dobio spomenik, a Antić bilbord, ''Blic'', November 4, 2009] He started his playing career with [[FK Sloboda Užice]] (1967-1968) and then moved to the club where he would play most of his career, [[FK Partizan]] (1968-1976). In the summer of 1976, he signed for [[Fenerbahçe S.K.|Fenerbahçe]] in [[Turkey]]. He spent two seasons in [[Istanbul]] before moving to [[La Liga]] where he played for [[Real Zaragoza]]. In 1980, Antić moved on to [[Luton Town F.C.|Luton Town]], staying until 1984. Known in England as '''Raddy''', in May 1983, he scored the goal that saved Luton Town from relegation from the top division, the goal coming just four minutes from time in the final league match of the [[1982–83 Football League|season]]; the game was against [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]], who themselves were relegated as a result.[http://uk.youtube.com/watch?v=XyAUkaC6nsI Manchester City vs. Luton Town, May 1983] Almost 32 years of age when he arrived at Luton, Antić already looked to coaching as a career option once his playing days are finished. While an active player in England, he enrolled in and completed the coaching college in Belgrade (Viša trenerska škola). In that regard he often cites [[David Pleat]], his manager at Luton, as an influence on his later coaching style.[http://www.kurir-info.rs/clanak/sport/kurir-17-11-2009/moj-ucitelj-dejvid-plit Moj učitelj Dejvid Plit, ''Kurir'', November 17, 2009] ==Managerial career== After finishing his playing career at the age of 36, Antić started a career in coaching as an assistant with [[FK Partizan]] (1985-87), working under head coach [[Nenad Bjeković]]. Partizan won the [[1985–86 Yugoslav First League|1985-86 league]] title amid a huge match-fixing controversy. In early July 1987, [[Fahrudin Jusufi]] was brought in as the new head coach and initially Antić continued his assistant role. For the pre-season training ahead of the 1987-88 season, the team went abroad where Jusufi and Antić got into a row over player personnel issues that resulted in Antić being essentially demoted to the position of Partizan under-16 youth team (cadet squad) coach. ===Real Zaragoza=== Antić's first head coaching job was with [[Real Zaragoza]]. In addition to formerly playing for the club, his appointment owed a lot to being recommended for the job by countryman [[Vujadin Boškov]], who successfully led [[U.C. Sampdoria|Sampdoria]] at the time, but still enjoyed a lot of clout in Spain having led Zaragoza (coached Antić there for two years) and other La Liga clubs during the late 1970s and early 1980s. The squad was a fairly modest one without any really big names; the most notable players being the aging Spanish international midfielder [[Juan Antonio Señor|Juan Señor]] and forward [[Miguel Pardeza]] who came up through Real Madrid's youth system as part of ''[[Quinta del Buitre]]''. The club also had some young assets: a pair of 22-year-olds [[Francisco Villarroya]] and [[Juan Vizcaíno]] who were well on their way to becoming future Spanish internationals as well as eccentric Paraguayan goalie [[José Luis Chilavert]] who came to the club the same summer Antić did. Antić's La Liga coaching debut came on 4 September 1988 in a game versus [[Valencia CF]] that ended in a scoreless draw. The initial period was rough with the club hovering in and around the relegation zone, followed by a period of slight improvement, but still firmly tied up in the lower half of the table. The sudden and somewhat unexpected improvement came during last eight league matches of the season as Antić's Zaragoza started posting win after win, rapidly climbing up the table, finishing the [[1988–89 La Liga|season]] in 5th place, thus qualifying for the [[UEFA Cup]]. He ended up spending two full seasons (1988-1990) managing a club he also turned out for as a player. ===Real Madrid=== [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] came calling in March 1991 and Antić took over from club legend [[Alfredo di Stéfano]] with the club occupying 7th spot in La Liga standings. Antić led the team in the last 12 league games of the [[La Liga 1990–91|1990-91 season]]; Real finished third in the league, qualifying for [[UEFA Cup]]. Antić also spent the first half of the [[La Liga 1991–92|1991/92 season]] (19 league matches) coaching the Spanish giants. With [[Emilio Butragueño]], [[Míchel (footballer)|Míchel]], [[Fernando Hierro]], [[Manuel Sanchís Hontiyuelo|Manuel Sanchís]], and [[Gheorghe Hagi]] as the club's established stars, Antić brought in [[Robert Prosinečki]], prominent member of the [[Red Star Belgrade]]'s [[European Cup 1990-91|1991]] [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] winning side, as well as promising 21-year-old [[Luís Enrique Martínez García|Luís Enrique]] from [[Sporting de Gijón]]. The way Antić got fired mid-season in January 1992, showed the full range of club politics as well as the dog-eat-dog nature of top club coaching. He was enjoying a good run as the club's coach when then Real president [[Ramón Mendoza]] brought [[Leo Beenhakker]] into the organization in a vaguely defined role of a sporting director. In a matter of weeks Antić was sacked and replaced with Beenhakker. At the time of Antić's firing, Real was holding the top spot in La Liga by a 7-point margin and was also smoothly through to the [[UEFA Cup 1991-92|UEFA Cup]] quarterfinals. ### Biography and Playing Career

Radomir Antić, born on November 22, 1948, in Žitište, Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia (now Serbia), is a former football defender and current football manager for the Serbian national team. His playing career spanned 17 years, during which he played for several notable clubs including FK Partizan, Fenerbahçe, Real Zaragoza, and Luton Town. Notably, while playing for Luton Town, he scored a crucial goal in 1983 that saved the team from relegation. This moment marked a significant achievement in his playing career, showcasing his skill and importance to the team. After retiring from playing at the age of 36, Antić transitioned into coaching, completing a coaching course in Belgrade and citing David Pleat, his manager at Luton, as a key influence on his coaching style.

### Managerial Career

#### Early Coaching Years

Antić began his managerial career as an assistant coach with FK Partizan under Nenad Bjeković. However, his tenure was short-lived due to a disagreement with Fahrudin Jusufi, who became the head coach in 1987. This disagreement led to Antić being demoted to the role of the under-16 youth team coach. Despite this setback, he soon found success as a head coach.

#### Real Zaragoza

His first head coaching job was with Real Zaragoza in 1988. The club had a modest squad, but under Antić’s guidance, they improved significantly towards the end of the season, finishing fifth in La Liga and qualifying for the UEFA Cup. This success marked the beginning of a successful managerial career for Antić.

#### Real Madrid

In 1991, Real Madrid appointed Antić as their head coach, replacing Alfredo di Stéfano. Under his leadership, Real Madrid finished third in La Liga and qualified for the UEFA Cup. However, his tenure at Real Madrid was cut short in January 1992 when he was fired and replaced by Leo Beenhakker. Despite the abrupt end to his time at Real Madrid, Antić left a lasting impact on the club.

#### Other Clubs

Antić has managed several other prominent clubs, including Atlético Madrid, Real Oviedo, and FC Barcelona. He is unique in that he is the only person to have managed FC Barcelona, Real Madrid, and Atlético Madrid. This accomplishment highlights his versatility and adaptability as a coach, capable of handling the demands of different teams and leagues.

### Legacy

Throughout his career, Antić has demonstrated exceptional skills both as a player and a coach. His ability to turn around struggling teams and lead them to success is a testament to his talent and dedication. Today, he continues to contribute to football as the manager of the Serbian national team, carrying forward the legacy he built during his playing and coaching years.

The club plans to move into a new 22,000 seater stadium located at [[Fossetts Farm Stadium|Fossetts Farm]] in the near future, but no substantial work has yet commenced. ==History== {{main|History of Southend United F.C.}} == Rivalry == [[Image:Southend Players taunt colchester fans .jpg|thumb|left|Southend players taunt the Colchester fans.]] The club has a local rivalry with fellow [[Essex]] side [[Colchester United F.C.|Colchester United]]. The two clubs were promoted from League One at the end of the 2005–06 season after a long battle for top spot was eventually won by the Shrimpers. The rivalry extends back many years. At the end of the 1989–90 season Southend's promotion from the [[Fourth Division]] coincided with Colchester's fall from the [[Football League]] and the clubs had to wait almost 15 years before meeting once again in competition when they met in the Southern Final of the Football League Trophy; the Shrimpers triumphed 4–3 on aggregate to secure their first ever appearance in a national cup final. The two clubs met again in and [[Essex derby]] match in the same competition the following season, with Southend emerging as the victors once more after a [[penalty shootout]]. The 2008/09 season saw the return of the Essex Derby to League One on November 1 2008 the sides drew 3-3 at [[Roots Hall]] in a non stop action packed encounter. [[Peter Clarke]] gave Southend the lead as early as the 7th minute, [[Francis Laurent]] then put Southend 2-0 up after just 13 minutes. Colchester mounted a comeback with Johnnie Jackson, Mark Yeates and Andy Woldsworth giving Colchester a 3-2 advantage, the points and the bragging rights looked to be heading to Colchester but [[Jean Francois Christophe]] equalised for Southend in the 95th minute with the last kick of the game to ensure both sides shared the points. Southend hold the most recent victory in the Essex Derby on 21 February 2009 [[Franck Moussa]] scored his first professional goal which proved to be the difference between the two sides. Southend hold 29 victories over their near neighbours in all competitions compared to Colchester's 23, there have been 17 draws. The two sides will meet again on Boxing Day 2009 at [[Roots Hall]]. ==Stadium== The club has had three stadia: the Kursaal, the Greyhound Park, and the rented out Writtle Street, after many years of good service the [[club]] moved to a renovated amusement park on the Kursaal and played there until 1955 and their current stadium [[Roots Hall]]. Roots Hall was the club's first stadium and was built on a council [[landfill]] site in 1954/55 with simple fencing to hold back spectators. Roots Hall has been the home of Southend United since August 1955 after the site was purchased in 1952. It took ten years to fully complete the building of Roots Hall, the first game being played here on [[20 August]] [[1955]], a 3-1 [[Division Three]] (South) [[victory]] over [[Norwich City FC|Norwich City]], but the ground was far from complete. The main East Stand had barely been fitted and ran only 50 [[yards]] of the touchline, whilst only a few steps of terracing encircled the ground, with the North, West and the huge South Bank still largely unconcreted. The North Stand had a single-barrelled roof but this only ran the length of the penalty area whilst the West Bank was only covered at its rear by a similar structure. Although the ground was far from finished, during the inaugural season this was the least of the club's worries, for the pitch at Roots Hall showed the consequences of having been laid on top of thousands of tonnes of compacted rubbish. Drainage was somewhat of a problem, and the wet winter had turned the ground into a quagmire. The pitch was completely re-laid in the [[summer]] of 1956 and a proper drainage system, which is still in place, was constructed whilst the West Bank roof was extended to reach the touchline, creating a unique double-barrelled structure. The terracing was finally completed soon after, but the colossal task of completely terracing the South Bank, all of its 72 steps, was not completed until 1964. The North Bank roof was extended in the early 1960s, and the East Stand was extended to run the full length of the [[pitch]] in 1966. [[Floodlights (sport)|Floodlight]]s were also installed during this period. Roots Hall was designed to hold 35,000 spectators, with over 15,000 on the South Bank alone, but the highest recorded attendance at the ground is 31,090 for an [[FA Cup]] third round tie with [[Liverpool FC|Liverpool]] in January 1979. Until 1988 Roots Hall was still the newest ground in the Football League, but it was then that the ground saw a significant change. United had hit bad times in the mid 1980s and new chairman Vic Jobson sold virtually all of the South Bank for development, leaving just a tiny block of 15 steps. In 1994 Jobson self-designed a new stand at the South End{{Citation needed|date=March 2009}}. Seats were installed onto the original terracing whilst a second tier was added, with the upper level giving some of the best views in the country. The West Bank had already become seated in 1992 upon United's elevation to [[Division Two]] whilst the East Stand paddock also received a new seating deck, bolted and elevated from the terracing below. In 1995 the West Stand roof was extended to meet up with the North and South Stands, with seating installed into each corner, thus giving the Roots Hall we see today, with a capacity of just under 12,500. Southend United currently play in the 12,392 all-seater [[Roots Hall]] stadium, which has been their home since 1955. The future of this location has been in doubt since it was sold to property developers in 1998. Planning permission has been granted for a new 22,000 seater stadium to be located near to the team's training ground at [[Fossetts Farm Stadium|Fossetts Farm]]. On 24 January 2007, Southend Borough Council unanimously agreed to give [[planning permission]] for the new [[stadium]] at the proposed [[Fossetts Farm]] site with Rochford District Council following suit 24 hours later. The application was subsequently submitted to Ruth Kelly, Secretary of State for Communities and Local Government, for government approval. However, the application was unexpectedly "called in" at the beginning of April 2007, a move which at best delays the development by some considerable time and at worst might jeopardise the whole project entirely. The inquiry began in September 2007. In October 2007 a "final" inquiry began where [[chairman]] [[Ron Martin (businessman)|Ron Martin]] called for supporters to show in numbers at Southends local governing headquarters. # Overview of Southend United Football Club

**Southend United Football Club**, commonly known as **The Shrimpers**, **The Seasiders**, or **The Blues**, is an English football club based in Southend-on-Sea, Essex. Founded in 1906, the club currently competes in League One, the third tier of English football. The club is managed by Steve Tilson and chaired by Ron Martin. Their home ground is Roots Hall, which has a capacity of 12,306. The club plans to relocate to a new 22,000-seat stadium at Fossetts Farm in the near future, although construction has not yet begun.

## History and Achievements

Southend United has a rich history, including several promotions and relegations throughout the decades. The club has faced numerous challenges, particularly in the mid-1980s when financial difficulties led to the sale of parts of the stadium. Despite these setbacks, the club has continued to compete at high levels, with notable achievements such as reaching the FA Cup third round and securing promotions to higher divisions.

## Rivalry with Colchester United

Southend United shares a fierce local rivalry with Colchester United, another Essex-based club. This rivalry dates back many years and has intensified over the years due to competitive matches and close finishes. A memorable moment in the rivalry occurred during the 2008-09 season when the two teams drew 3-3 in a thrilling encounter at Roots Hall. Another significant victory for Southend came on February 21, 2009, when Franck Moussa scored the winning goal against Colchester. Over the years, Southend has held a slight edge in head-to-head matchups, with 29 victories compared to Colchester's 23, and 17 draws.

## Stadium History and Future Plans

### Roots Hall

Roots Hall, the current home of Southend United, has a storied history. Originally built in 1954-55, the stadium was constructed on a landfill site and initially lacked many amenities. Over the years, the stadium underwent significant renovations, including the installation of floodlights, the conversion of terraces to seats, and the addition of new stands. Despite its age, Roots Hall remains a beloved venue for fans, with a capacity of just under 12,500.

### Future Stadium at Fossetts Farm

In recent years, Southend United has been working towards building a new stadium at Fossetts Farm. The project has faced several hurdles, including planning permissions and government approvals. In 2007, the borough and district councils approved the plans, but the application was later "called in," delaying the project. After a series of inquiries and public support, the project received the green light in March 2008. However, as of now, no substantial work has commenced on the new stadium.

## Conclusion

Southend United Football Club continues to be a prominent fixture in Essex football, with a passionate fan base and a rich history. While the club faces challenges such as stadium relocation and financial stability, it remains committed to competing at the highest levels of English football. The rivalry with Colchester United adds an extra layer of excitement and passion to the local football scene, ensuring that Southend United remains a beloved club for years to come.

'''Zlatan Ibrahimović''' (born 3 October 1981) is a [[Sweden|Swedish]] [[association football|football player]] of [[Bosnia and Herzegovina|Bosnian]]<ref name=Hawkey>{{cite news|url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/article757217.ece |title=The Big Interview: Zlatan Ibrahimović |first=Ian |last=Hawkey |publisher=''[[The Sunday Times]]'' |date=2005-12-11| accessdate=2009-04-13}}</ref> and [[Croatia]]n<ref name=Hawkey/> parentage who plays [[Forward (association football)|striker]] for [[Spain|Spanish]] [[La Liga]] club [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]] and the [[Sweden national football team|Swedish national team]].

Ibrahimović started his career at [[Malmö FF]] in the late [[1990s|90's]] under [[Roland Andersson]]. He was signed by [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]], and made a name for himself under [[Ronald Koeman]]. Years later, he signed with [[Juventus]] for [[Euro|€]]16 million. Zlatan gained fame and popularity in the [[Serie A|Italian top flight]] while having a striking partnership with [[Alessandro Del Piero]]. After playing for the ''bianconeri'', he made his move to league giants [[Internazionale]] in 2006. His record breaking performances led him to awards such as the [[Oscar del calcio]], the [[Guldbollen]], and being named in the 2007 [[UEFA Team of the Year]]. In the [[List_of_Spanish_football_transfers_summer_2009|summer of 2009]], ''Ibracadabra'' transfered to [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]], while continuing to break records.

As of February 2009, Ibrahimović, along with [[Kaká]], were the highest salaried football players in the world with an annual pay of [[Euro|€]]9 million.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.futebolfinance.com/en/os-50-maiores-salarios-de-jogadores-de-futebol-20082009/| title=The 50 highest salaries of football players 2008/2009| publisher=www.futebolfinance.com| accessdate=2009-02-11}}</ref> Ibrahimović won the ''[[Capocannoniere]]'' on 31 May, 2009 with 25 domestic goals during [[Serie A 2008-09|the season]]. He has been named as one of the best players of his generation by being nominated for the [[FIFA World Player of the Year]] and [[Ballon d'Or]] due to his playing style, technique, and goal scoring abilities.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.thelocal.se/22982/20091030/| title=Ibrahimovic nominated for FIFA award| publisher=www.thelocal.se| accessdate=2009-30-10}}</ref> Ibrahimović currently holds the record for the second [[Transfer_(football)#Highest_fees|highest transfer fee]] in football history, with a total of €69 million for his transfer from [[Internazionale]] to [[FC Barcelona|Barcelona]].

Twice footballing [[coach (sport)|manager]] of the year, [[Jose Mourinho]], said in an interview to [[The Sun (newspaper)|The Sun]] on [[5 March]], [[2009]], “I think there are four outstanding players in the world - Ibrahimovic, [[Cristiano Ronaldo]], [[Lionel Messi]] and [[Kaká]]. At the moment, I think I have the best in the four - the best player in the world [Zlatan Ibrahimovic].” <ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.tribalfootball.com/inter-milan-boss-mourinho-ibrahimovic-best-world-230874| title=Inter Milan boss Mourinho: Ibrahimovic best in world| publisher=www.tribalfootball.com| accessdate=2009-05-03}}</ref>

==Early life==
Ibrahimović was born in [[Malmö]] to a [[Bosniaks|Bosnian]] father, Šefik Ibrahimović, and a [[Croats|Croatian]] mother, Jurka Gravić,<ref name=Hawkey/> who emigrated to Sweden, where they first met. Ibrahimović grew up in [[Rosengård]], a Malmö neighbourhood known for its immigrant communities, along with his three sisters and two brothers. After receiving his football boots, Ibrahimović began playing football at the age of six, alternating between local junior clubs [[FC Rosengård|Malmö BI]] and [[FBK Balkan]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.evolvia.se/ZlatanIbrahimovi%C4%87/tabid/54/Default.aspx. |title=Zlatan Ibrahimović |accessdate=2009-05-28 |publisher=Evolvia }} {{sv icon}}</ref><ref name="Sydsvenskan">{{cite web |url=http://sydsvenskan.se/sport/article96251/raquoRosenberg---for-mig-ar-han-hogerbacklaquo.html |title=»Rosenberg - för mig är han högerback« |accessdate=2009-05-28 |publisher=[[Sydsvenskan]] }} {{sv icon}}</ref> While in his early teens, he was a regular in his hometown club [[Malmö FF]].<ref name="Sydsvenskan"/> At the age of 15, Ibrahimović was close to quitting his football career, in favor of working at the docks in Malmö, but his manager convinced him to continue playing.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://sydsvenskan.se/sport/article6845.ece |title=Så blev Zlatan stor |date=2001-06-23 |accessdate=2009-05-28 |publisher=[[Sydsvenskan]] |last=Jönsson |first=Jan }} {{sv icon}}</ref> Ibrahimović successfully completed junior high school in the ninth grade, and though he was admitted to Borgarskolan, he soon dropped out of high school to focus on his football career.

==Club career==
===Malmö FF (1996-2001)===

In his first three years in the league, he did not get much playing time, and was very inconsistent when he did get on the field. Johnson scored just seven goals for Dallas in those seasons, while missing a lot of time with US youth national teams. Johnson came into his own at the end of 2003 at the [[2003 FIFA World Youth Championship|FIFA World Youth Championship]] in the [[United Arab Emirates]]. He scored four goals, three from the penalty spot, and notched one assist to win the tournament's [[Golden Shoe]] as the top scorer,{{cite press release |url=http://www.fifa.com/tournaments/archive/tournament=104/edition=6537/awards/index.html |title=FIFA World Youth Championship UAE 2003 Awards |publisher=[[FIFA]] |year=2003 |accessdate=2006-12-06}} becoming the youngest player to achieve that feat in MLS history. Johnson received his first cap and scored his first goal for the senior [[United States men's national soccer team|United States team]] against [[El Salvador national football team|El Salvador]] on October 9, 2004, becoming one of a small group of American players to get his first international goal in a World Cup qualifier. He then scored a [[hat-trick]] in his second appearance, all in a 17-minute spree against [[Panama national football team|Panama]], just four days later. Johnson totaled seven goals in his first six World Cup qualifiers and is already third on the U.S. all-time scoring list in World Cup qualifiers, earning himself limited playing time during the [[2006 FIFA World Cup]]. In January 2005, [[S.L. Benfica]] offered what would have been an MLS-record $5 million [[transfer fee]] for Johnson, but Johnson and the league both rejected the offer.{{cite news |first=Brian |last=Trusdell |title=Eddie Johnson sticking with MLS |url=http://www.usatoday.com/sports/soccer/mls/2005-03-11-johnson-portuguese-offer_x.htm |agency=[[Associated Press|AP]] |work=[[USA Today]] |date=2005-03-11 |accessdate=2007-07-07}} In May 2005, Johnson suffered an injury to the toes of his right foot that sidelined him until August of that year. After returning to MLS in August – he scored only five goals during the season – and making a brief re-appearance with the national team on September 7, 2005, Johnson reinjured his toes in mid-September and was sidelined until January 2006. With Dallas in [[salary cap]] trouble, Johnson was traded to the Kansas City Wizards on February 14, 2006 for two [[allocation (MLS)|allocations]].{{cite news |title=FC Dallas acquires allocations for Johnson |url=http://soccernet.espn.go.com/news/story?id=358613&cc=5901 |work=[[ESPNsoccernet]] |date=2006-02-14 |accessdate=10 March 2009}} In August 2006, MLS had reached an agreement with Spanish club [[Real Sociedad]] for a year-long loan but the plan fell through because the new ownership of the Wizards were not happy with sending Johnson.{{cite news |first=Grant |last=Wahl |date=2006-09-01 |url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2006/writers/grant_wahl/09/01/kc.wizards/index.html |title=Wizards' watershed week |work=[[CNN Sports Illustrated]] |pages=2 |accessdate=2006-11-16}} The loan would have made Johnson the first American [[outfield]] player and second American overall to play in [[La Liga]], following goalkeeper [[Kasey Keller]]. In November 2006 it was announced that Johnson would be training with English [[Premier League]] club [[Reading F.C.|Reading]] during the MLS [[Season (sports)#Offseason|offseason]], but he did not sign with the club.{{cite news |title=Wizards striker Johnson planning trip to Reading |url=http://soccernet.espn.go.com/news/story?id=392473&cc=5901 |agency=AP |work=ESPNsoccernet |date=2006-11-17 |accessdate=10 March 2009}} In 2006 and early 2007, Johnson suffered a decline in form, scoring only twice in the [[2006 MLS season]] and failing to make an impact with the national team. However, Johnson returned to form with the start of the [[2007 MLS season]], notching twelve goals and three assists in his first eleven games. In the month of July 2007, Johnson saw increased speculation over a transfer to the Premier League. [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]] had been most vocal, with Derby manager [[Billy Davies]] confirming that he would explore the U.S. market.{{cite news |title=Johnson Gaining Interest In Europe |url=http://www.kptv.com/soccer/13677356/detail.html |agency=[[The Sports Network (wire service)|Sports Network]] |work=[[KPTV]] |publisher=[[Meredith Corporation]] |location=[[Kansas City, Missouri|Kansas City]], [[Missouri]] |date=2007-07-13 |accessdate=2009-03-10}} However, after MLS accepted a $6 million bid from Derby, Johnson reportedly nixed the deal as he preferred to finish his season in Kansas City.{{cite news |first=Dent |last=McSkimming Jr. |title=Eddie Johnson Transfer News |url=http://www.soccerbuzzonline.com/eddie-johnson-transfer-news/ |work=Soccer Buzz |publisher=451 Press |date=2007-07-17 |accessdate=2007-07-25}} Johnson revealed his contract is structured to give him final say over whether he is purchased by 15 designated clubs.{{cite web |url=http://www.teamtalk.com/football/story/0,16368,12878_2614692,00.html |title=Johnson spurns switch to Rams |accessdate=2009-03-10 |date=2007-07-25 |work=[[TEAMtalk]] |publisher=[[365 Media Group]] |archiveurl=http://web.archive.org/web/20070930022353/http://www.teamtalk.com/football/story/0,16368,12878_261

'''Nathan John Porritt''' (born 9 January 1990)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.findmypast.com/post84BMDSearchStart.action?redef=0&searchType=B |title=Search 1984 to 2006 – Birth, Marriage and Death indexes |publisher=Findmypast.com |accessdate=2009-04-16}}</ref> is an English professional [[association football|footballer]] who plays as a [[winger]] for [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]].

==Early life==
Porritt was born in [[Middlesbrough]], [[Teesside]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mfc.premiumtv.co.uk/page/Squad/ProfilesDetail/0,,1~44839,00.html |title=Profiles Nathan Porritt |publisher=Middlesbrough F.C |accessdate=2008-05-10}}</ref> At the age of ten, he joined [[Middlesbrough F.C.]]'s youth academy while continuing his education at [[The King's Academy]].<ref name=NEcho060921>{{cite news |url=http://www.thisisthenortheast.co.uk/display.var.930426.0.unwelcome_fame_for_rising_star_porritt.php |title=Unwelcome fame for rising star Porritt |work=The Northern Echo |date=21 September 2006 |accessdate=2008-05-10}}</ref>

==Club career==
Secret filming for [[BBC]] [[Panorama (TV series)|Panorama]]'s programme ''[[2006 allegations of corruption in English football|"Undercover: Football's Dirty Secrets"]]'', aired in September 2006, exposed an agent acting without Middlesbrough's permission in offering the then 15-year-old Porritt to club representatives, including [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]]'s youth director [[Frank Arnesen]], in contravention of [[the Football Association]]'s rules.<ref name=NEcho060921/><ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/5363514.stm |title=Boro report agent to authorities |publisher=BBC Sport |date=23 September 2006 |accssdate=2009-08-31}}</ref>

Porritt signed a two-year scholarship with Middlesbrough in the summer of 2006,<ref name=NEcho060921/> and signed his first professional contract with the club on 10 June 2008.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.mfc.premiumtv.co.uk/page/News/NewsDetail/0,,1~1326239,00.html |title=Nathan Signs New Deal |publisher=Middlesbrough F.C |date=10 June 2008 |accessdate=2009-08-30}}</ref>

### Early Life and Background

Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, commonly known as Cristiano Ronaldo, is a Portuguese professional footballer who plays as a winger or forward for Spanish club Real Madrid and captains the Portuguese national team. Born on February 5, 1985, in Funchal, Madeira, Portugal, Ronaldo is the youngest child of Maria Dolores dos Santos Aveiro and José Dinis Aveiro. He has one older brother, Hugo, and two older sisters, Elma and Liliana Cátia. His given name "Ronaldo" was inspired by former U.S. President Ronald Reagan, who was his father's favorite actor [Data: Sources (1)].

### Early Career

Ronaldo's journey in football began at a very young age. At the age of eight, he played for the amateur team Andorinha, where his father worked as the kit man. In 1995, he moved to CD Nacional, another local club, where he spent two seasons before joining Sporting Clube de Portugal (Sporting CP) in 1997. This move marked the beginning of his professional career, as he quickly progressed through the ranks, playing for Sporting's U-16, U-17, U-18, B-team, and eventually the first team [Data: Sources (2, 3)].

### Health Challenges

During his early years at Sporting CP, Ronaldo faced a significant health challenge. At the age of 15, he was diagnosed with a racing heart, a condition that could have ended his football career. However, after undergoing successful surgery, he was able to resume training just a few days later, demonstrating his resilience and determination [Data: Sources (4)].

### Professional Career

#### Sporting CP

Ronaldo's performances at Sporting CP caught the attention of several clubs, including Liverpool, but it was Manchester United manager Alex Ferguson who ultimately signed him in 2003. Before moving to Manchester United, Ronaldo made 25 appearances for Sporting CP, scoring 3 goals [Data: Sources (5)].

#### Manchester United

At Manchester United, Ronaldo quickly established himself as one of the world's best players. Over his six-year tenure, he made 196 appearances and scored 84 goals, helping the club win numerous titles, including the FA Cup and the UEFA Champions League. His success at Manchester United also translated to the international stage, where he represented Portugal in major tournaments such as the UEFA Euro 2004 [Data: Sources (6, 7)].

#### Real Madrid

In 2009, Ronaldo transferred to Real Madrid in a deal worth £80 million, making him the most expensive player in football history. Since then, he has continued to excel, winning multiple Ballon d'Or awards and leading Real Madrid to numerous domestic and European titles [Data: Sources (8, 9)].

### International Career

On the international front, Ronaldo has been a key figure for the Portuguese national team since 2003. As of the latest records, he has made 68 appearances and scored 22 goals for Portugal, contributing significantly to the team's success in various tournaments [Data: Sources (10)].

### Achievements and Recognition

Throughout his career, Ronaldo has received numerous accolades, including being named the FIFA World Player of the Year, FIFPro World Player of the Year, and winning the Ballon d'Or multiple times. His exceptional performances have earned him comparisons with legendary players like George Best and Denis Law, with Johan Cruyff stating that Ronaldo is even better than these iconic figures [Data: Sources (11, 12)].

In summary, Cristiano Ronaldo's journey from a young player in Madeira to one of the world's most celebrated footballers is a testament to his talent, hard work, and resilience. His contributions to both club and country continue to inspire fans and players alike.

'''Antônio Augusto Ribeiro Reis Junior''' (born 30 January 1975 in [[Recife]]), commonly known as '''Juninho''' or '''Juninho Pernambucano''',<ref>His nickname comes from a combination of the Brazilian diminutive "Juninho" which is commonly applied to any person with the name "Junior" and "Pernambucano" meaning someone born in the north-eastern Brazilian state of [[Pernambuco]]. He is sometimes referred to as "Pernambucano" in southern France.</ref> is a [[Brazil]]ian [[football (soccer)|footballer]], currently playing as a midfielder for [[Qatari|Qatar]] club [[Al-Gharafa Sports Club|Al-Gharafa]]. He became a free agent and joined Al-Gharafa after winning 7 consecutive Ligue 1 titles with Olympique Lyonnais, finishing third in the 08-09 season. He scored 100 goals in 344 games for the [[Olympique Lyonnais]]<ref>http://www.olweb.fr/fr/Accueil/100007/Article/50317/Juninho-ses-chiffres-lyonnais</ref>. He scored six goals in 40 games for the [[Brazil national football team|Brazilian national team]], before retiring from international football after the [[2006 FIFA World Cup]].

==Club career==
===Early career===
After a long period of tests, and a time in the futsal (indoor football) division of [[Sport Club do Recife|Sport Recife]], he started his career in 1993. Soon he joined the main team of Sport Recife, helping form the so called "Gold Generation of the Futsal" with other great players from the indoor division. In 1994 Juninho won the [[Campeonato Pernambucano]] and the [[Copa do Nordeste]]. He participated in many remarkable games, including the 5-2 in the São Paulo of Tele Santana, World Champions in 1993. Juninho left Sport Recife, but never denied loving it since he was a kid, when he saw Sport Recife win the [[Brazilian Championship]] of 1987.

He moved to [[Club de Regatas Vasco da Gama|CR Vasco da Gama]] in 1995, and won several trophies with the club, including the [[Campeonato Brasileiro Série A|Brazilian Championship]] in 1997 and 2000, the [[Copa Libertadores]] in 1998, the [[Copa Mercosur]] in 2000, as well as the 2000 [[Bola de Ouro#Bola de Prata|Brazilian Silver Ball]] award as one of the best Brazilian midfielders of the season. In that time, he was part of an incredible forward squad, playing with some top level international players, as [[Romário]], [[Edmundo]], [[Juninho Paulista]], [[Felipe Jorge Loureiro|Felipe]] and [[Pedro Paulo de Oliveira|Pedrinho]].

====King of São Januário====
Before joining Lyon, Juninho played for [[CR Vasco da Gama|Vasco da Gama]] in Brazil. While there, he won the [[Brazilian Championship]] twice (1997-2000) and two continental cups (the [[Copa Libertadores]] in 1998 and the [[Copa Mercosul]] in 2000), becoming a favourite of the Vasco fans.{{fact|date=March 2007}}

Since that time he has been known as ''Reizinho de São Januário'' (The Little King of [[Estádio São Januário|São Januário]])<ref>[http://www.juninhopaulista.com/Reportagens/2000/12/distintivos_com_br.htm << Distintivos.Com.Br >><!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> or ''Reizinho da Colina'' (The Little King of the Hill),<ref>[http://globoesporte.globo.com/ESP/Noticia/Impressao/0,,AL1138149-5187,00.html GloboEsporte.com na Copa do Mundo 2006 - Exclusivo: todos os jogos em vídeo ao vivo - ARTICLE IMPRIMIR - FERAS DO PARREIRA: Raio-X de Juninho Pernambucano<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> a reference to Vasco da Gama Stadium's name ([[Estádio São Januário|São Januário]]) or nickname (Stadium of the Hill). ## Juninho: The Attacking Midfielder from Brazil

**Antônio Augusto Ribeiro Reis Junior**, better known as **Juninho** or **Juninho Pernambucano**, is a Brazilian former professional footballer who played as an attacking midfielder. Born on January 30, 1975, in Recife, Brazil, Juninho has had a storied career spanning various clubs and leagues, including a significant stint with Olympique Lyonnais in France.

### Early Career and Rise to Fame

Juninho began his professional career in 1993 with Sport Recife, where he quickly made a name for himself. His talent and skill were evident early on, leading to his move to CR Vasco da Gama in 1995. At Vasco da Gama, Juninho experienced tremendous success, winning multiple titles, including the Brazilian Championship in 1997 and 2000, the Copa Libertadores in 1998, and the Copa Mercosur in 2000. His performances earned him the nickname "Reizinho de São Januário" (Little King of São Januário), reflecting his status as a fan favorite and key player for the club.

### Transition to Europe: Lyon

In 2001, Juninho made a significant move to Europe, joining French club Olympique Lyonnais. This transition marked a pivotal moment in his career. Prior to his arrival, Lyon had never won the French Ligue 1 championship. However, under Juninho's leadership, the club achieved unprecedented success, securing the Ligue 1 title in his first season and going on to win it seven consecutive times. Juninho's contributions extended beyond scoring goals; he was renowned for his precise set pieces, passing abilities, and leadership qualities. His impact was so profound that he was named the team captain by manager Gérard Houllier.

### Legacy and Retirement

Juninho's tenure at Lyon came to an end in 2009 when he decided to leave the club as a free agent. Despite the mutual agreement to terminate his contract, the departure was emotional for both Juninho and the club. Following his time at Lyon, Juninho signed with Al-Gharafa Sports Club in Qatar, where he continued his career until his retirement.

Throughout his career, Juninho accumulated impressive statistics. He scored 100 goals in 344 appearances for Olympique Lyonnais and netted six goals in 40 matches for the Brazilian national team. His contributions to both club and country have cemented his legacy as one of the greatest Brazilian footballers of his generation.

## Summary

Juninho's journey from the streets of Recife to the heights of European football showcases his exceptional talent and dedication. From his early days at Sport Recife and CR Vasco da Gama to his dominant years at Olympique Lyonnais, Juninho has left an indelible mark on the sport. His legacy as a master of set pieces, a reliable scorer, and a respected leader continues to inspire football fans around the world.

'''Guus Hiddink''' ({{IPA-nl|ˈɣys ˈɦɪdɪŋk}}; born 8 November 1946) is a former [[Netherlands|Dutch]] [[Association football|footballer]] and current [[Coach (sport)|manager]]. He is recognised for winning [[Treble (association football)|the European treble]] ([[Eredivisie]], [[Dutch Cup]] and [[European Cup]]) with [[PSV Eindhoven]]; leading [[Korea Republic national football team|South Korea]] to a fourth place finish in the [[2002 FIFA World Cup]]; managing the [[Netherlands national football team|Netherlands]] into the same position in the [[1998 FIFA World Cup]], losing to eventual runner-up [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]] on penalties; leading [[Australia national football team|Australia]] to the second round at the [[2006 FIFA World Cup]], their first appearance in the tournament for 32 years; leading Russia to the semi-finals of [[UEFA Euro 2008|Euro 2008]], Russia's best performance since the breakup of the [[Soviet Union national football team|Soviet Union]]; and reviving [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] by winning the [[FA Cup]] in 2009 against Everton. He is currently the manager of [[Russia national football team|Russia]]. Hiddink previously managed [[De Graafschap]], [[PSV Eindhoven]], [[Fenerbahçe S.K.|Fenerbahçe]], [[Valencia CF|Valencia]], the [[Netherlands national football team|Netherlands]], [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]], [[Real Betis]], [[Korea Republic national football team|South Korea]], [[Australia national association football team|Australia]], and [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]].

==Playing career==
Hiddink was born in [[Varsseveld]] and started his career as a player in the youth side of amateur club SC Varsseveld. He turned professional after signing on for Dutch club [[De Graafschap]] in 1967. Hiddink played at the [[Doetinchem]] club under manager [[Piet de Visser]]. In 1973, Hiddink and manager de Visser earned promotion to the [[Eredivisie]], the top league in Dutch football.<ref>{{cite news | title=Oeuvreprijs naar Piet de Visser| url=http://www.net2client.com/ZZZ/08/04101/Uitslagen_2004.htm?MCT7evlngrp3%C3%BE | publisher=Rinus Michels Awards 2005 | date=28 May 2005 | accessdate=17 January 2007 |language=Dutch }}</ref> Ever since, the careers of the two Dutchmen have intersected: de Visser scouted numerous South American players, such as PSV players [[Ronaldo]], [[Romário]] (who played under Hiddink at PSV from 1988 until 1990) and current Chelsea defender [[Alex Rodrigo Dias da Costa|Alex]], for Hiddink's PSV. Also, de Visser, in his role as personal advisor to [[Roman Abramovich]], was influential in bringing Hiddink to the [[Russia national football team]] and more recently to [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] as caretaker manager following the dismissal of Brazilian [[Luiz Felipe Scolari]]. It was de Visser who introduced Hiddink to Abramovich during a meeting in [[Eindhoven]] in 2004.<ref>{{cite news | title=Will the Kremlin demand the final say in Hiddink's future at Chelsea?| url=http://www.dailymail.co.uk/sport/football/article-1145538/Will-Kremlin-demand-final-say-Hiddinks-future-Chelsea.html | publisher=Daily Mail | date=14 February 2009 | accessdate=14 February 2009}}</ref> He spent most of his playing career at De Graafschap, including three years under de Visser, and remains a fan of the club. He joined [[PSV Eindhoven|PSV]] in 1970, but after failing to win a permanent position in the team, he rejoined De Graafschap after just one year and remained there until 1976. He also had stints in [[England]] with [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] from July to December 1976 (though he did not make a first team appearance), and in the [[United States]] with [[Washington Diplomats]] and [[San Jose Earthquakes (NASL)|San Jose Earthquakes]], before returning home to sign for [[N.E.C. (football club)|NEC]]. In 1981, he rejoined De Graafschap and retired a year later. He generally played as a [[Midfielder (association football)|midfielder]] during his playing days.

==Managerial career==
===Early club career===
Having honed his coaching skills with De Graafschap as an assistant manager, he took over the managerial role at [[PSV Eindhoven]] in 1987 (after also holding the assistant manager position there from 1983 to March 1987). Hiddink took over at PSV in March, 1987, while the team was first in the [[Eredivisie 1986-87|League]]. It was at PSV where he led the team to its first ever [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] triumph in 1988 (and [[The Treble]]) affirming the Eindhoven club's ranking as one of the three giants of Dutch football, alongside rivals [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]] and [[Feyenoord]]. He also won three [[Eredivisie]] titles with the club in between 1987 and 1990.

He also had a coaching stint at [[Turkey|Turkish]] club [[Fenerbahçe S.K.|Fenerbahçe]] in 1990 but was dismissed after one year before joining [[Spain|Spanish]] giants [[Valencia CF|Valencia]]. His outspoken nature was demonstrated when during a league game at Valencia's [[Estadio Mestalla]], he ordered a racist banner to be removed from one of the stands.

{{0}}72 {{0}}(19) | pcupdate = 16:30, 29 November 2009 (UTC) | ntupdate = 16:25, 19 November 2009 (UTC) }} '''{{Audio|Bastian Schweinsteiger.ogg|Bastian Schweinsteiger}}''' (born 1 August 1984 in [[Kolbermoor]]) is a [[Germany|German]] [[Association football|footballer]] who plays as a [[midfielder]] for [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] and [[Germany national football team|Germany]]. ==Career== ===Club career=== Schweinsteiger signed for Bayern Munich as a youth team player on 1 July 1998 and rose through the club's youth sides. A talented youth ski racer, he had to decide between pursuing a professional career in skiing or football at the age of 14. Having won the German youth championship in July 2002, Schweinsteiger quickly earned a place in the reserves, producing a string of solid third division displays. A left midfielder, who can also play on the right, he has a hard shot, great dribbling skills and is a specialist at [[Set piece (football)|set pieces]]. He can also play as a defensive midfielder or just behind the strikers. After just two training sessions with the first team, coach [[Ottmar Hitzfeld]] gave Schweinsteiger his debut as a late substitute in a [[UEFA Champions League]] game against [[RC Lens]] in November 2002, and the youngster made an immediate impact, creating a goal for [[Markus Feulner]] within minutes. He signed a professional contract the following month and went on to appear in 14 Bundesliga games in 2002–03, helping Bayern to a league and cup double. The next season he played 26 [[Fußball-Bundesliga|Bundesliga]] games. Schweinsteiger scored his first Bayern goal against VfL Wolfsburg in September 2003. Surprisingly sent back to Bayern's amateurs by new coach [[Felix Magath]] at the beginning of the 2004–05 season despite his international exploits of the summer in the [[Confederations Cup]], Schweinsteiger swiftly returned to play a role in the double-winning campaign and scored in Bayern's Champions League quarter-final first-leg defeat at [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]]. Over the next three seasons, up until the end of 2007–08, Bastian made 135 appearances in all competitions for Bayern Munich ([[UEFA Champions League]], [[German Bundesliga|Bundesliga]] and German Cup), scoring 10 goals in the process. On 15 August 2008, Schweinsteiger scored the first [[Fußball-Bundesliga|Bundesliga]] goal of the [[Fußball-Bundesliga 2008–09|2008–09 season]]. He extended his contract at Bayern until 2012 on 18 November 2008. ===International career=== He made his international debut in 2004 in a friendly against [[Hungary national football team|Hungary]]. Bayern's number 31 earned rave reviews for his [[UEFA Euro 2004|Euro 2004]] performances in Portugal, showing combative skills and even setting up the opening goal for once Bayern teammate [[Michael Ballack]] in Germany's 2-1 loss against the [[Czech Republic national football team|Czech Republic]]. He scored his first two international goals on 8 June 2005 against [[Russia national football team|Russia]] and scored his first goal at a major tournament against [[Tunisia national football team|Tunisia]] on June 18, 2005 at the [[Confederations Cup 2005|Confederations Cup]] in Germany. This was followed up by two strikes in the [[2006 FIFA World Cup knockout stage#Third place|third place play-off]] game at the [[2006 FIFA World Cup|2006 World Cup]], also in his home country. He nearly scored a hat-trick as he caused [[Armando Petit]]'s own goal to make the score 3-1. During [[UEFA Euro 2008 qualifying Group D|Euro 2008 qualifiers]], he scored two goals en route to a 13-0 win over [[San Marino national football team|San Marino]] in San Marino. He scored the third goal in Germany's 4-1 win over [[Slovakia national football team|Slovakia]] in Bratislava. At the age of 22, he had already played 41 matches for the German national team, a record for any German player at the time. This record was soon broken, however, by [[Lukas Podolski]] who was capped 44 times at the age of 22. At the same age, [[Lothar Matthäus]] (the German all-time record holder with 150 caps) had only played 13 times for the German national team. To this day [[Germany national football team|Germany]] have never lost a game when he has scored. In the [[UEFA Euro 2008|Euro 2008 group stage]] he was sent off in Germany's second match of the tournament against [[Croatia national football team|Croatia]], which ended in a 2-1 defeat. As in Germany's quest to win European Cup, he was again instrumental against [[Portugal national football team|Portugal]] by scoring the first goal in Germany's Euro 2008 Quarter-final match against them. He also assisted goals by [[Miroslav Klose]] and [[Michael Ballack]] from free kicks. Germany ended up winning the match 3-2 to advance to the semi-finals. He also scored his country's first goal in the 3-2 semi-final victory against [[Turkey national football team|Turkey]]. ## Overview of the FIFA World Cup

The **FIFA World Cup**, also known as the **Football World Cup** or simply the **World Cup**, is an international football competition organized by the **Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA)**. It is held every four years and features the men's national teams of FIFA member countries. Since its inception in 1930, the World Cup has become the most widely viewed sporting event globally, with billions tuning in to watch the matches. For instance, the 2006 final had an estimated 715.1 million viewers worldwide. [Data: Wikipedia (2006 FIFA World Cup Final)]

### Current Format and Qualification Process

The current format of the World Cup involves 32 teams competing in the finals, which take place over approximately one month. Prior to the finals, a qualification phase occurs over the preceding three years, determining which teams will participate alongside the host nation(s). This ensures a diverse and competitive field of teams from around the globe.

### Historical Success

Over the course of 18 tournaments, only seven nations have emerged victorious. Brazil holds the record for the most World Cup wins, with five titles, and they are the only team to have participated in every tournament. Other notable champions include Italy (four titles), Germany (three titles), Uruguay and Argentina (two titles each), and England and France (one title each).

## History of the FIFA World Cup

### Early International Competitions

The first international football match was played between Scotland and England in Glasgow in 1872. The first international tournament, the inaugural edition of the **British Home Championship**, took place in 1884. Initially, football was primarily played within the United Kingdom, but as the sport gained popularity globally, it was included as a demonstration sport in the 1900 and 1904 Summer Olympics, and again in the 1906 Intercalated Games.

### FIFA's Early Attempts

Following FIFA's founding in 1904, there was an attempt to organize an international football tournament in Switzerland in 1906. However, this effort was largely unsuccessful. In 1908, football became an official competition at the Summer Olympics in London, with England winning the gold medal. This success was repeated in 1912 in Stockholm.

### The Sir Thomas Lipton Trophy

In 1909, Sir Thomas Lipton organized the **Sir Thomas Lipton Trophy** tournament in Turin, featuring club teams representing different nations. Despite the FA of England declining to send a professional team, West Auckland, an amateur side from County Durham, won the tournament and defended their title in 1911.

### Olympic Football Tournaments

In 1914, FIFA recognized the Olympic football tournament as a "world football championship for amateurs." This led to the first intercontinental football competition at the 1920 Summer Olympics, where Belgium emerged victorious. Subsequently, Uruguay won the Olympic football tournaments in 1924 and 1928.

### The First FIFA World Cup

The first FIFA World Cup was held in 1930 in Uruguay, with the final match taking place at the **Estadio Centenario** in Montevideo. This marked the beginning of what would become the most prestigious and widely watched football tournament in the world.

This historical context provides a comprehensive understanding of how the FIFA World Cup evolved into the global phenomenon it is today. [Data: Wikipedia (History of the FIFA World Cup)]

Mertesacker had an unlucky start for his home club, breaking his nose and conceding an own goal soon after, but he established himself as one of the most promising young defenders in the [[Fußball-Bundesliga|Bundesliga]]. For a while at Hannover 96, his played under his father, Stefan Mertesacker. His type of game was unusually clean, him being rarely booked (as of July 2006, only twice in 74 games) while regularly neutralizing his opponents. The slender Mertesacker was soon dubbed "the Defense Pole" (''die Abwehrlatte'') by German tabloids. During his time at Hannover 96, he was good friends with [[Robert Enke]], and along with Michael Ballack, presented the laurel during the memorial in honour of Enke's death. The [[Fußball-Bundesliga 2007–08|2007–08 season]] was a mixed bag for Mertesacker. He started in nearly all of Bremen's league and European fixtures and received his first red card in his professional career in a 6-3 loss against [[VfB Stuttgart]]. He scored four goals, including a crucial equalizer against [[VfL Wolfsburg]], as Bremen finished runners-up in the league and sealing a place in next season's [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]]. In September, he returned to the starting line-up and was ever present for the rest of the season until injury forced him off in the [[2008-09 UEFA Cup#Semi-finals|UEFA Cup semifinal]] second leg against Bundesliga rivals [[Hamburger SV|Hamburg]]. With his quiet but effective game, he established himself as Germany's first choice centre-back, pairing up with [[Robert Huth]], [[Christoph Metzelder]], and later, [[Heiko Westermann]]. At the World Cup on home soil, Mertesacker paired with Metzelder in central defense. After Germany won the quarterfinal penalty shoot-out against Argentina, Mertesacker was attacked by Argentine [[Leandro Damián Cufré|Leandro Cufré]], an unused substitute. They also won the [[1980 Mundialito]], a tournament among former World Cup champions [[Uruguay]] hosted in 1980 to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the first World Cup. Uruguay won more international titles (19) in the 20th century than any other country in the world and still holds this record, albeit it is now shared with [[Argentina national football team|Argentina]]. Their success is amplified by the fact that the nation has a very small population. [[Uruguay]] is the only country in the world to win a [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]] with a general population of under 4 million inhabitants and is by far the smallest nation to do so. The second smallest country to have won the World Cup is [[Argentina]] with a total population of over 40 million people. Uruguay is also the smallest country ever to win any World Cup medals. In fact, only six nations with populations smaller than Uruguay's have ever participated in any World Cup: [[Northern Ireland]] (3 times), [[Wales]], [[Kuwait]], [[Jamaica]], [[Slovenia]] and [[Trinidad and Tobago]]. Uruguay is also the smallest nation to win Olympic gold medals in any team sport. Uruguay is also the smallest member nation of [[CONMEBOL]], South American Football Association. Nethertheless, Uruguayan national team also have won the [[Copa América]] 14 different times, a record it shares with Argentina. However, the level of the Uruguay national team has decreased lately as Uruguay has only qualified on one occasion in the last 4 World Cups, although it remains a strong team in South America, having reached third place and fourth place in the last two [[Copa América]] tournaments, respectively. ==History== Prior to 1916, Uruguay played more than 30 matches, of which all but one were against Argentina. The following year Uruguay hosted the competition, and retained the title by winning every game. The 1919 Copa America saw Uruguay's first defeat in the tournament, a 1-0 defeat in a playoff with Brazil which went to two periods of extra time, the longest Copa America match in history. In 1924 the Uruguay team traveled to Paris to become the first South American team to compete in the [[1924 Summer Olympics|Olympic Games]]. In contrast to the physical style of the European teams of the era, Uruguay played a style based around short passes,{{cite web | title=Football's debt to Uruguay|work=BBC Sport| url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport3/worldcup2002/hi/team_pages/uruguay/newsid_1907000/1907148.stm| dateformat=mdy |accessdate=15 October 2006}} and won every game, defeating [[Switzerland national football team|Switzerland]] 3-0 in the gold medal match. # Uruguay National Football Team Overview

## Basic Information

The **Uruguay national football team** represents Uruguay in international football competitions and is controlled by the Asociación Uruguaya de Fútbol. The team is nicknamed "Charrúas," "La Celeste Olímpica" (The Olympic Sky Blue), and "La Celeste" (The Sky Blue). The current coach is Oscar Tabarez, and the captain is Diego Lugano. Rodolfo Rodríguez holds the record for the most caps with 79, while Héctor Scarone is the top scorer with 31 goals. The home stadium is the Estadio Centenario.

## Historical Achievements

### World Cup Success

Uruguay has achieved significant success in the FIFA World Cup:
- **First World Cup**: Hosted and won the inaugural World Cup in 1930, defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final.
- **Second World Cup**: Won again in 1950, defeating hosts Brazil 2-1 in the final match, a result known as the "Maracanazo."

### Olympic Gold Medals

Before the creation of the World Cup, Uruguay won Olympic gold medals in men's football:
- **1924 Paris Olympics**: Defeated Switzerland 3-0 in the gold medal match.
- **1928 Amsterdam Olympics**: Defeated Argentina 2-1 in the final.

### Copa América Dominance

Uruguay has been highly successful in the Copa América:
- **Record Wins**: Has won the Copa América 14 times, sharing this record with Argentina.

### Other Notable Achievements

- **1980 Mundialito**: Won the tournament, celebrating the 50th anniversary of the first World Cup.
- **International Titles**: Holds the record for the most international titles (19) in the 20th century, shared with Argentina.

## Population and Size

Despite being one of the smallest countries in the world, Uruguay has achieved remarkable success in football:
- **Smallest World Cup Winner**: Uruguay is the only country to win a World Cup with a general population of under 4 million inhabitants.
- **Smallest Olympic Gold Medalist**: Uruguay is the smallest nation to win Olympic gold medals in any team sport.

## Recent Performance

While Uruguay has maintained a strong presence in South American football, its recent performance has seen some decline:
- **World Cup Qualifications**: Qualified for the World Cup only once in the last four tournaments.
- **Copa América**: Reached third place in the last Copa América and fourth place in the preceding tournament.

## Historical Context

### Early Matches and Tournaments

- **Early Matches**: Prior to 1916, Uruguay played over 30 matches, mostly against Argentina.
- **Copa América**: In the inaugural Copa América, Uruguay won the tournament by defeating Chile and Brazil and tying with Argentina. The following year, they retained the title by winning every game.

### Olympic Triumphs

- **1924 Paris Olympics**: Became the first South American team to compete in the Olympics, winning every game and defeating Switzerland 3-0 in the gold medal match.
- **1928 Amsterdam Olympics**: Defended their title by defeating Argentina 2-1 in the final.

### World Cup Hosting and Participation

- **1930 World Cup**: Hosted and won the first World Cup, defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final.
- **1934 World Cup**: Refused to participate due to the boycott of the 1930 World Cup by some European teams.
- **1938 World Cup**: Again refused to participate as France was chosen as the host, contrary to the agreement to alternate between South America and Europe.

### Post-1950 Performance

Since winning the World Cup in 1950, Uruguay's performance has been mixed, but they continue to be a strong force in South American football.

### Overview of UEFA Euro 2016

The 2016 UEFA European Football Championship, commonly known as Euro 2016, was set to be the 15th European Championship for national football teams sanctioned by UEFA. It was scheduled to take place in the summer of 2016. The host nation was to be selected in May 2010, following a bidding process that began on December 11, 2008. [Data: UEFA (786278, 754190, 808293)]

### Hosting Requirements

UEFA required the host nation or nations to provide nine stadiums, with an additional three as optional backups. The stadiums needed to meet specific seating capacities: two stadiums with 50,000 seats, three with 40,000 seats, and four with 30,000 seats. These requirements were confirmed by UEFA in a letter sent on July 1, 2009, with the stadiums needing to be ready by June 30, 2014. [Data: UEFA (786278, 754190, 808293)]

### Expanded Format

The tournament format was expanded from 16 to 24 teams, which was unanimously agreed upon by senior officials of all 53 UEFA member nations. The final tournament would consist of six groups of four teams, followed by a round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, and the final. This format would result in a total of 51 matches, compared to the previous 31, and would span 29 to 31 days. This change aimed to give middle-ranked countries a better chance to qualify for the finals. [Data: UEFA (754190)]

### Bids for Hosting Euro 2016

Four candidates representing five European national associations expressed interest in hosting Euro 2016:

#### Turkey

Turkey was one of the countries that submitted a bid to host Euro 2016. The Turkish Football Federation (TFF) officially submitted their candidacy brief on February 7, 2009. Turkey had several completed and under-construction stadiums that could potentially meet the UEFA requirements. Some of the notable stadiums included:

- **İstanbul**
  - Atatürk Olympic Stadium (capacity 82,000)
  - Şükrü Saracoğlu Stadium (capacity 53,500)
  - BJK İnönü Stadium (capacity 35,000)

- **İzmir**
  - İzmir Atatürk Stadium (capacity 65,000)

- **Ankara**
  - Cebeci İnönü Stadium (capacity 35,000)

- **Kayseri**
  - Kadir Has Stadium (capacity 35,000)

- **Trabzon**
  - Hüseyin Avni Aker Stadium (capacity 30,000)

- **Şanlıurfa**
  - Şanlıurfa GAP Arena (capacity 30,000)

Additionally, there were several stadiums under construction, such as the Türk Telekom Arena in Istanbul, the New Trabzon Stadium, and the New Antalya Stadium. [Data: Turkish Football Federation (6151)]

### Conclusion

The bid process for Euro 2016 was intense, with Turkey among the candidates showcasing their readiness to host the tournament. The expansion of the tournament to 24 teams was a significant change that aimed to increase participation and excitement. The final decision on the host nation would be made in May 2010, following a thorough evaluation of the bids based on the criteria set by UEFA. [Data: UEFA (786278, 754190, 808293)]

Additionally, the club has claimed four titles in the Taça de Moçambique (Cup of Mozambique) in 1982, 1989, 1996, and 2004. Ferroviário has also secured two titles in the Maputo Honour Cup in 2001/02 and 2005. These achievements highlight the club's dominance in Mozambican football over several decades.

Ferroviário de Maputo plays its home matches at Estádio da Machava, located in Maputo, Mozambique. Other notable performances include reaching the preliminary round in 2009 and the first round in 2006. Additionally, the club has competed in the CAF Confederation Cup twice, reaching the preliminary round in 2004 and the first round in 2005. Ferroviário has also participated in the CAF Cup seven times, with its best performance being a semi-final appearance in 1992.

The squad is predominantly composed of Mozambican players, reflecting the club's commitment to nurturing local talent and contributing to the development of football in Mozambique.

### Famous Players

Throughout its history, Ferroviário de Maputo has been home to numerous famous players who have contributed significantly to the club's success. Some notable figures include Simão Mate Junior, who played for the club from 2003 to 2007, and Alberto da Costa Pereira, a Portuguese player who had a significant impact during his time with the club. Other well-known players include Joaquim João, Mabjaia, Tchaka-Tchaka, Jojó, Luis Parruque, Tomá's Inguane, Paulito, Pinto Barros, Danito Cuta, and Zelde.

Ferroviário de Maputo stands as a symbol of football excellence in Mozambique, with a storied past and a strong presence in both domestic and international competitions. The Mexican national football team is currently ranked 15th in the [[FIFA World Rankings]].{{cite news|url=http://www.fifa.com/worldfootball/ranking/lastranking/gender=m/fullranking.html | publisher=[[FIFA]]| title=FIFA World Rankings - July 2009| accessdate=2009-07-01}} It also represents the [[Mexico women's national football team]]. Mexico has qualified for thirteen [[FIFA World Cup|World Cups]] and has qualified consecutively since 1994. Mexico's best progression was reaching the Quarterfinals in both the [[1970 FIFA World Cup|1970]] and [[1986 FIFA World Cup|1986]] FIFA World Cups, both of which were staged on Mexican soil. Mexico holds one [[FIFA Confederations Cup]], five [[CONCACAF Gold Cup]]s, three [[CONCACAF Championship]]s, one [[North American Nations Cup]] and two [[NAFC Championship]]s. Although Mexico is under the jurisdiction of [[CONCACAF]], the national football team has been regularly invited to compete in the [[CONMEBOL]] [[Copa América]] since [[Copa America 1993|Ecuador 1993]] finishing as runner-up twice and obtaining the third place medal on three occasions. ==History== ===Early years=== Competitive association football in [[Mexico]] was organized in the early 20th century by various [[European ethnic groups|European]] immigrant groups, notably [[Cornish people|Cornish]] miners from [[Cornwall]], [[England]], and in later years, [[Spain|Spanish]] exiles fleeing the [[Spanish Civil War]]. Though organized football was disrupted from 1910 to 1919 as a result of the [[Mexican Revolution]], a new football association had been established in [[Mexico City]] by 1922, and by the end of the year a national team had been organized from players in this league to represent Mexico in international friendlies. On January 1, 1923, Mexico played their first international friendly against [[Guatemala national football team|Guatemala]], which the Mexican team won 3–2.{{cite web | title=The Start; El Comienzo| publisher=[[Televisa]] | url=http://www.esmas.com/seleccionmexicana/historia/313563.html| accessdate=2008-05-01}} A series of international friendlies were played against the national representation of [[Guatemala national football team|Guatemala]] on December 9, 12, and 16 of 1923. The match on December 9 was played in ''Parque España'' and was won by Mexico with a final score of 2-1. On December 12, the match ended in a 2-0 win for Mexico, and the final game of the series ended in a 3-3 draw.{{cite web | title=History of the National football team| publisher=[[Femexfut]] | url=http://www.femexfut.org.mx/portalv2/(wor2cn45znbm4tnjnmy11j45)/default.aspx#top| accessdate=2008-05-01}} The manager for this team was Rafael Garza Gutiérrez "Récord", and the assistant coach was Adolfo Frías. The fourteen players selected for this friendly series include: Nacho de la Garza, Pedro "Perico" Legorreta, Manuel "Güero" Yáñez, Enrique "La Matona" Esquivel, Agustín Ojeda, Roberto Jardón, Carlos Garcés, Horacio Ortiz, Adeodato López, Mauro Guadarrama "La Venada" Alatorre, Cornelio Cuevas, and Alfredo "Fofo" García Besné. It would be another four years before the national team would be represented in international friendlies. In preparation for a friendly against [[Spain national football team|Spain]], the team played a friendly against their "B" squad on June 12, 1927, winning 4-2. On June 19, 1927, the Mexican squad faced a selection from [[Spain national football team|Spain]], drawing 3-3. During this series, the squad also played against the [[Uruguay]]an club [[Nacional de Montevideo]], losing 1-3. ===Formation of the Federación Mexicana de Fútbol=== On August 23, 1927, the official governing body of the sport of [[association football|football]] in Mexico was founded. From its inception, the federation has been the main body in charge of the promotion, administration, organization, management, and funding of the Mexican national football team as well as all football competition within Mexico. Club representatives from the federation's first division all vote on the direction, management, and coaching staff of the national football team. The [[Football at the 1928 Summer Olympics|1928 Summer Olympics]] were hosts to Mexico's first international tournament. Prior to the tournament, the Mexican squad held friendlies against a representative [[Asturias national football team|Asturias]] side as well as two friendlies against [[Spain national football team|Spain]]. These matches resulted in two draws and one loss. At the Olympic tournament, Mexico faced Spain in the Round of 16 on May 30, 1928, resulting in Mexico's defeat of 1-7.{{cite web | title=The First Olympics| publisher=[[Televisa]] | url=http://www.esmas.com/seleccionmexicana/historia/313563.html| accessdate=2008-05-01}} Mexico participated in the [[1930 FIFA World Cup]], having been grouped together with Argentina, Chile, and France. Mexico's first match was played against [[France national football team|France]] at [[Estadio Pocitos]]

D.C. United is an American professional soccer club based in Washington, D.C., participating in Major League Soccer (MLS), the top-tier soccer league in the United States. Founded in 1995, the club has a rich history and a significant presence in the soccer community. The team's home ground is the Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Stadium, which has a seating capacity of 45,596. However, the club has proposed building a new soccer-specific stadium to enhance the fan experience and meet the growing demands of the sport.

### Ownership and Management

The team is currently owned by D.C. United Holdings, a consortium led by William H.C. Chang. As of the latest update, the head coaching position is vacant, indicating a period of transition within the club's management structure.

### Achievements and Success

D.C. United is widely regarded as one of the most successful clubs in American soccer. The team has achieved numerous accolades, including winning the U.S. Open Cup twice and holding the record for the most MLS Cups and MLS Supporters' Shields, with four each. Notably, D.C. United was the first club to repeat both the MLS Supporters' Shield and the MLS Cup consecutively. In 1998, the team made history by becoming the first American club to win the CONCACAF Champions' Cup and the Copa Interamericana, showcasing their international prowess.

### International Competitions

Internationally, D.C. United has participated in various CONCACAF competitions, including the 2008 CONCACAF Champions' Cup and the 2008 SuperLiga. Additionally, they hold the distinction of being the only U.S.-based club to compete in a South American CONMEBOL competition, having played in the Copa Sudamericana in 2005 and 2007.

### Player Legacy

Several notable players have contributed to the success of D.C. United, including Jaime Moreno, Christian Gómez, and Marco Etcheverry. These players have not only excelled on the field but have also helped build a strong fan base for the club.

### Fan Base and Support

D.C. United boasts a dedicated fan base, with three supporters' clubs and consistently high attendance averages in MLS. The club's official nickname is the "Black-and-Red," reflecting the team colors of black and white with red accents. This branding aligns with the club's identity and resonates with fans who appreciate the team's historical significance and ongoing success.

### Historical Context

The formation of D.C. United was part of a broader initiative by the United States Soccer Federation to establish a professional soccer league in the country. Following the 1994 FIFA World Cup, MLS was founded, and D.C. United was one of the original teams selected to participate. The club's name draws inspiration from the "United" theme commonly seen in British soccer teams, although it does not reflect a merger of existing clubs.

### Early Years and Success

D.C. United's inaugural match took place on April 6, 1996, against the San Jose Clash. Under the leadership of Bruce Arena, the club experienced tremendous success in its early years, winning the first MLS Cup and U.S. Open Cup in 1996. The team continued its dominance in subsequent years, achieving another MLS Cup victory in 1997 and winning the CONCACAF Champions' Cup and Copa Interamericana in 1998.

### Transition Period

Following Bruce Arena's departure in 1998 to manage the U.S. men's national team, the club faced a period of transition. Despite winning the MLS Cup again in 1999 under Thomas Rongen, the team struggled in the following years. Piotr Nowak took over as head coach in 2004, bringing a new approach to the team's management and tactics.

### Conclusion

D.C. United remains a prominent figure in American soccer, with a legacy of success and a passionate fan base. The club continues to strive for excellence, both domestically and internationally, as it navigates the challenges and opportunities of modern professional soccer.

It is analogous to its [[UEFA|European]] counterpart, the [[UEFA Super Cup]]. Since the competition takes place in the mid-summer, it's disputed between the champions of the previous year's forementioned competitions. Because of this, some count the year of the championship by the qualification year rather than that of the competition itself. Thus, [[CONMEBOL]] states that [[Club Nacional de Football|Nacional]] from [[Uruguay]] won the first Recopa of 1989, whereas the [[Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation|RSSSF]] refers to that championship as Recopa 1988. ==Format== The Recopa is contested over a [[two-legged tie]], usually no more than two weeks apart. The first leg is held at the home field of the [[Copa Sudamericana]] champion, and the second leg is played at the home field of the [[Copa Libertadores]] champion. The teams accumulate points as per the results of the match (3 for a win, 1 for a draw, 0 for a loss). The team with the most points after both legs wins the Recopa. Ties in points will be broken first by goal difference, then by [[Away goals rule|away goals]], and lastly by a [[Penalty shootout (association football)|penalty shootout]] after regulation of the second leg. ==History== The tournament has been played since 1989. From 1989 to 1998, the match was played between the reigning champions of [[Copa Libertadores de America]] and the defunct [[Supercopa Sudamericana]], which was last disputed in 1997. The 1990 edition was played in [[Miami]], [[United States of America|USA]]. The 1991 edition was not played because [[Olimpia Asunción|Olimpia]] won both Copa Libertadores and Supercopa Sudamericana. From 1992 to 1997, the competition was played in [[Japan]].
