# Recopa Sudamericana Overview

The **Recopa Sudamericana** (also known as the South American Winners' Cup, Recopa, or Cup Winners' Cup) is an annual football match-up between the reigning champions of the previous year's Copa Libertadores and the Copa Sudamericana. This competition is organized by CONMEBOL and is similar to the UEFA Super Cup in Europe. The Recopa Sudamericana was first established in 1989 and has been contested sporadically since then. The current champions are LDU Quito from Ecuador, while Boca Juniors from Argentina holds the record for the most titles with four.

## Format

The Recopa is typically contested over two legs, usually no more than two weeks apart. The first leg is played at the home ground of the Copa Sudamericana champion, and the second leg is held at the home ground of the Copa Libertadores champion. Points are accumulated based on the results of each match (3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw, and 0 points for a loss). The team with the highest total points after both legs is declared the winner. In case of a tie in points, the winner is determined by goal difference, away goals, and finally, a penalty shootout if necessary.

## Historical Context

### Early Years (1989-1998)

From 1989 to 1998, the Recopa was contested between the champions of the Copa Libertadores and the defunct Supercopa Sudamericana. Notable editions include:
- **1989**: Nacional (Uruguay) defeated Racing (Argentina) in Montevideo and Buenos Aires.
- **1990**: Boca Juniors (Argentina) won against Atlético Nacional (Colombia) in Miami.
- **1991**: Olimpia (Paraguay) automatically became the champion as they won both the Copa Libertadores and Supercopa Sudamericana.
- **1992**: Colo-Colo (Chile) beat Cruzeiro (Brazil) in Kobe, Japan, via a penalty shootout.
- **1993**: São Paulo (Brazil) defeated Cruzeiro (Brazil) in a penalty shootout in São Paulo and Belo Horizonte.
- **1994**: São Paulo (Brazil) won against Botafogo (Brazil) in Kobe, Japan.
- **1995**: Independiente (Argentina) defeated Vélez Sársfield (Argentina) in Tokyo.
- **1 996**: Grêmio (Brazil) beat Independiente (Argentina) in Kobe, Japan.
- **1997**: Vélez Sársfield (Argentina) won against River Plate (Argentina) in Tokyo via a penalty shootout.
- **1998**: Cruzeiro (Brazil) defeated River Plate (Argentina) in Belo Horizonte and Buenos Aires.

### Hiatus and Revival (1999-2002)

The competition was not played from 1999 to 2002 due to various reasons including scheduling conflicts and financial issues.

### Recent Years (2003-Present)

The competition resumed in 2003 with the following notable editions:
- **2003**: Olimpia (Paraguay) defeated San Lorenzo (Argentina) in Los Angeles.
- **2004**: Cienciano (Peru) won against Boca Juniors (Argentina) in Fort Lauderdale via a penalty shootout.
- **2005**: Boca Juniors (Argentina) defeated Estudiantes (Argentina) in a home-and-away format.

## Key Competitors

Throughout its history, several clubs have emerged as dominant forces in the Recopa Sudamericana. Boca Juniors stands out as the most successful club with four titles. Other notable winners include:
- **Nacional (Uruguay)**: Won the inaugural edition in 1989.
- **São Paulo (Brazil)**: Won twice in 1993 and 1994.
- **Grêmio (Brazil)**: Won in 1996.
- **Cruzeiro (Brazil)**: Won in 1998.

These clubs have showcased their prowess in South American football, contributing to the rich history and tradition of the Recopa Sudamericana.

In summary, the Recopa Sudamericana continues to be a prestigious competition in South American football, bringing together the continent's top clubs in a battle for supremacy. Despite its intermittent nature, it remains a significant event in the football calendar, celebrated by fans and players alike.

### Overview of Feyenoord

Feyenoord is a renowned Dutch professional football club based in Rotterdam, the second-largest city in the Netherlands. Founded on July 19, 1908, Feyenoord has a rich history and is one of the "big three" clubs in the country, alongside AFC Ajax and PSV Eindhoven. This trio has dominated the Dutch football scene, winning almost every Dutch League Championship since 1965, with only a few exceptions. Feyenoord's home ground is the famous Feijenoord Stadion, also known as "De Kuip," which has a capacity of 51,577 spectators. The club is managed by Mario Been and chaired by Dick van Well. As of the 2008-09 season, Feyenoord finished 7th in the Eredivisie, the top tier of Dutch football.

### Location and Name Change

Feyenoord is located in the Feijenoord district of southern Rotterdam, named after the area where the club was originally founded. The club initially struggled with pronunciation issues among foreign fans due to the Dutch letter combination "ij." To address this, Feyenoord changed its name to "Feyenoord" in 1974, making it easier for international audiences to pronounce. Despite this change, the club remains deeply rooted in its local community and continues to be a significant part of Rotterdam's cultural identity.

### Historical Achievements

#### Early Years (1908-1939)

Feyenoord was founded as Wilhelmina in 1908 and went through several name changes before settling on SC Feijenoord in 1912. The club adopted its current colors—red and white shirts, black shorts, and black socks—in 1912. By 1917, Feyenoord had been promoted to the highest level of Dutch football, the 1e Klasse (1st Division). The club's early success was evident when they won their first national league championship in 1924. Over the next few years, Feyenoord continued to dominate, winning multiple division titles and national championships. Their first Dutch Cup victory came in 1930, and they added another in 1935. In 1937, Feyenoord moved to their iconic home ground, the Feijenoord Stadion, nicknamed "De Kuip."

#### Mid-Twentieth Century (1940-1969)

During World War II, Feyenoord faced challenges as the Nazis occupied De Kuip. The club had to play their matches at Sparta Rotterdam's Kasteel stadium or their old ground, Kromme Zandweg, when Kasteel was unavailable. Despite these difficulties, Feyenoord managed to win a division title and a national championship in 1940. However, the 1945 championship was canceled due to the ongoing war. Post-war, Feyenoord's performance declined, and they did not challenge for the national championship as they had in previous decades. Nonetheless, the club remained a significant force in Dutch football, contributing to the rich tapestry of the sport in the Netherlands.

### Conclusion

Feyenoord's history is marked by numerous achievements and milestones, making it one of the most successful and beloved clubs in Dutch football. From its humble beginnings in 1908 to its current status as a major player in the Eredivisie, Feyenoord has consistently demonstrated its commitment to excellence and its deep connection to the people of Rotterdam. The club's legacy continues to inspire generations of football fans and players alike.

He played football at various times with his local clubs [[Eadestown GAA|Eadestown]] in Kildare and [[Castlehaven GAA|Castlehaven]] in Cork. He also played football with both the [[Kildare GAA|Kildare]] and [[Cork GAA|Cork]] senior inter-county teams throughout the 1980s and 1990s. Tompkins captained Cork to the [[All-Ireland Senior Football Championship|All-Ireland]] title in 1990 and later served as manager of the team from 1996 until 2003. ==Biography== Larry Tompkins was born in Greenmount, Rathmore just outside [[Naas]], [[County Kildare]] in 1963. The youngest of seven children, he showed a keen interest in Gaelic football from an early age. Tompkins was educated at Rathmore [[national school (Ireland)|national school]] where he first played both [[hurling]] and football. He later attended [[Blessington]] secondary school in [[County Wicklow]] were he developed his football skills even further. Tompkins was captain of the Wicklow Vocational Schools team that won the Leinster championship in 1980. The team subsequently lost the All-Ireland final to [[Derry GAA|Derry]]. Tomkins later trained as a carpenter; however, at a time when unemployment was rife in [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]], he spent much of the early 1980s working in the [[United States]]. Tompkins returned to Ireland in 1987 and settled in [[Castlehaven]], [[County Cork]]. He currently owns and runs his own pub in the centre of [[Cork (city)|Cork]] city. ==Playing career== ===Club=== Tomkins began his club football career with his local club in [[Eadestown GAA|Eadestown]] and enjoyed much success. He won a junior ‘B’ title with the club in 1981, a victory which acted as a springboard for further success. The following year Tompkins added a junior ‘A’ title to his collection. Further success followed in 1983 when Eadestown, with Tompkins playing a key role, secured a county intermediate championship title. When Tompkins emigrated to the United States in the 1980s he played his club football with the [[Donegal GAA|Donegal]] club in [[New York]]. He enjoyed much success here and he captained the club to win the New York championship on two occasions. Famously, the club never lost a championship game when Tompkins was included on the team. It was in New York that Tompkins befriended the Collins’s from [[Castlehaven]], [[County Cork]]. They persuaded him to join their local club when he returned to Ireland. In 1987 Tomkins did just that and threw his lot in with [[Castlehaven GAA|’the ‘Haven’]]. Two years later his decision bore fruit. Tompkins was captain as Castlehaven defeated the famous [[St. Finbarr's GAA|St. Finbarr’s]] club to take the [[Cork Senior Football Championship|county senior championship]] title in Cork. Castlehaven later defeated [[St. Senan's GAA|St. Senan’s]] of Clare to take the [[Munster Senior Club Football Championship|Munster]] club title .{{cite web|url=http://munster.gaa.ie/teams/clubfootball.html|title=Club Championship Senior Football - Munster Final Winning Teams (1887-2007)|publisher=[[Munster GAA]]|date=|accessdate=2009-04-10}} Castlehaven’s great run of success came to an abrupt end in the All-Ireland semi-final when the club was defeated by eventual champions [[Baltingglass GAA|Baltinglass]].{{cite book| first=Des| last=Donegan| title=The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games| publisher=DBA Publications| year=2005| id= | page=207}} Five years later in 1994 Tompkins secured a second county championship winners’ medal following a victory over nearby rivals [[O'Donovan Rossa (football club)|O’Donovan Rossa]]. A second Munster club winners’ medal later followed for Tompkins as Castlehaven defeated [[Clomnel Commercials]] of Tipperary. Once again, ‘the ‘Haven’ were later defeated by [[Kilmacud Crokes]] in the All-Ireland semi-final.''The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games'' p. 208 1997 saw Castlehaven lose the county final to [[Beara GAA|Beara]], however, the club later represented Cork in the provincial series of games. A third Munster club title soon followed after a defeat of [[Fethard GAA|Fethard]] in the provincial decider. Castlehaven faced heartbreak again following a third defeat in the All-Ireland semi-final.''The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games'' p. 209 ===Minor & under-21=== Tomkins first came to prominence on the inter-county scene as a sixteen year-old in 1979. That year he was a member of the [[Kildare GAA|Kildare]] minor, under-21 and senior football teams. Tompkins spent three seasons with Kildare at minor level. He lined out against [[Meath GAA|Meath]] in the Leinster final in 1980, however, on that occasion ‘the Lilywhites’ were defeated on that occasion by 1-12 to 1-9.''The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games'' p. 154 That same year Tompkins lined out in the Leinster under-21 final with [[Dublin GAA|Dublin]] providing the opposition. An exciting game developed with both sides finishing level. A replay proved more conclusive with ‘the Dubs’ taking the title by 2-9 to 0-6.''The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games'' p. 162 Three years later in 1983 Tompkins played in a second Leinster under-21 final. [[Louth GAA|Louth]] provided the opposition on that occasion; however, victory went to Kildare by 1-13 to 1-8. It was Tompkins’s first [[Leinster Under-21 Football Championship|Leinster]] under-21 winners’ medal.''The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games'' p. 162 Kildare, however, were subsequently defeated in the All-Ireland semi-final. ===Senior=== By this stage Tompkins was a well-established player on the Kildare senior football team. It was an unhappy time for ‘the Lilywhites’ as they failed to even reach the Leinster final. An [[O'Byrne Cup]] title in 1982 was the best that the county could muster.''The Complete Handbook of Gaelic Games'' p. 217 By the mid-1980s Tompkins was recognised as Kildare’s top player, however, it wasn’t long before he had a disagreement with the Kildare county board. He had been living in New York but returned regularly to line out with Kildare. The county board had been paying for his flight tickets, however, they decided to stop this and Tomkins found the expense too great. As a result of this he never played with his native-county again and faced the prospect of prematurely ending a promising inter-county career. In 1987 Tompkins’s performances for Castlehaven brought him to the attention of the [[Cork GAA|Cork]] senior football selectors under legendary goalkeeper [[Billy Morgan (Gaelic footballer)|Billy Morgan]]. He earned a call up to the team and made his senior debut in the provincial championship that same year. The task ahead was enormous as Cork’s nearest neighbours, [[Kerry GAA|Kerry]], had won eleven of the last twelve Munster titles and had put Cork to the sword on most of those occasions. He has been a member of the [[England national football team|England]] squad, and has two [[cap (football)|cap]]s. ==Club career== ===Ipswich Town=== Wright was born in [[Ipswich]], [[Suffolk]] and joined [[Ipswich Town F.C.|Ipswich Town]] as a trainee in January 1995, making his debut as a 17-year-old in a 2–0 victory at home to [[Coventry City F.C.|Coventry City]] in May 1995.{{cite news| title = Sky falls in on Coventry| url = http://www.independent.co.uk/sport/sky-falls-in-on-coventry-1618504.html| publisher = The Independent| date = [[1995-05-07]]| accessdate = 2009-05-07}} He played a major role in Ipswich's [[1999-2000 in English football|1999–2000]] season when the club were promoted from the [[Football League First Division]] to the [[Premier League]] via the play-offs, defeating [[Barnsley F.C.|Barnsley]], and Wright saved an all-important penalty kick. He made a total of 289 league and cup appearances for Ipswich. ===Arsenal=== Wright joined Arsenal in July 2001 for an undisclosed fee, reported as £6m but is claims have suggest it was as low as £2m due to a clause in Wright's contract.{{cite news| title = Arsenal complete Wright signing| url = http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/a/arsenal/1420099.stm| publisher = BBC Sport| date = [[2001-07-05]]| accessdate = 2007-07-15}} He signed a five-year contract and was signed as manager [[Arsene Wenger]] envisaged him as a long-term successor to [[David Seaman]] and also as a more experienced competitor for the previous second choice goalkeeper [[Alex Manninger]] (who soon left the club). He made his debut against [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]] on 29 September, but despite an injury to Seaman which gave him an extended run in the team, his season soon fell apart. He punched the ball into his own net in a 4–2 home defeat to [[Charlton Athletic F.C.|Charlton Athletic]] and then limped off with injury in a [[UEFA Champions League]] match against [[Deportivo La Coruna]]. Wright later slipped to third-choice behind youth goalkeeper [[Stuart Taylor (footballer born 1980)|Stuart Taylor]] and only played [[FA Cup]] matches for the remainder of the season, although Seaman replaced him for the final, which Arsenal won 2–0 against [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]]. He made his last Arsenal appearance on the final day of the 2001–02 season, a 4–3 victory over [[Everton F.C.|Everton]]. He was substituted in the 85th minute for Taylor, which gave both goalkeepers enough appearances to qualify for a Premier League winners' medal that season. Wright made 22 appearances for Arsenal in total. ===Everton=== Although initially first-team keeper at Everton, a number of injuries, including a serious knee injury, hampered his playing aspirations. He lost his place at Everton and had to be content with being understudy to veteran [[Nigel Martyn]]. During [[2005-06 in English football|2005–06]] Martyn had a spell out with injury, but Wright promptly injured himself whilst warming up in a match against Chelsea and was out for the rest of the season. ### Career Overview

Ryan Michael Green, born on 20 October 1980 in Kidderminster, England, is a professional footballer who has played as a defender throughout his career. Currently, he plays for Hereford United F.C., wearing the number 2 jersey. Green began his career as a trainee with Wolverhampton Wanderers, turning professional in October 1997. He made his first-team debut for Wolverhampton Wanderers on 10 November 1998, in a 2–1 victory against Sheffield United at Molineux Stadium. Unfortunately, after only 70 minutes, he suffered a medial ligament injury that kept him sidelined for six months. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

Despite his early promise, Green struggled to establish himself at Wolverhampton Wanderers. In March 2001, he joined Torquay United on loan, where he played ten matches as Torquay successfully avoided relegation to the Conference. However, he scored an own goal in the final game of the season, a 3–2 win over Barnet, which did not affect Torquay's survival. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

In October 2001, Green moved to Millwall on a free transfer. He nearly joined Bradford City in 2002, but the move was prevented due to the financial impact of ITV Digital's collapse on Football League clubs. Instead, he joined Cardiff City on a monthly contract in November 2002 before moving to Sheffield Wednesday two weeks later. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

During his time with Sheffield Wednesday, Green faced numerous injuries. He made 33 league appearances in his first season but suffered a foot injury that sidelined him for several weeks. Further injuries, including a broken jaw and Achilles tendon issues, plagued him during the following season. Despite these setbacks, he managed to play 91 games for Sheffield Wednesday, scoring three goals. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

In May 2009, Green's contract with Sheffield Wednesday was not renewed, and he left the club. On 5 June 2009, he re-signed with Hereford United on a one-year deal for the 2009–2010 season. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

### International Career

Green's international career was brief but notable. He made his full international debut for Wales against Malta on 3 June 1998, becoming the youngest player ever to play for Wales at the age of 17 years and 226 days. This record was previously held by Ryan Giggs and was later surpassed by Lewin Nyatanga and currently held by Gareth Bale. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

Green's international career consisted of only two caps. His second and final appearance was against Tunisia. He also represented Wales at youth and under-21 levels. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

### Summary

Throughout his career, Ryan Green has played for several clubs, including Wolverhampton Wanderers, Torquay United, Millwall, Cardiff City, Sheffield Wednesday, and Hereford United. Despite facing numerous injuries, he has shown resilience and determination to continue playing at a high level. His international career, though short-lived, marked a significant milestone in Welsh football history. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

'''FC Spartak Moscow''' ({{lang-ru|Футбольный клуб «Спартак» Москва}}) is a [[football (soccer)|football]] club from [[Moscow]], [[Russia]]. They are nicknamed "Meat" because in Soviet era the club was owned by the Collective Production Farms (the [[kolkhoz]] and the sovkhoz) .

Spartak have won 12 [[Soviet Top League|Soviet championships]] (second only to [[Dynamo Kyiv]]) and 9 of 16 [[Russian Premier League|Russian championships]]. They have also won the [[Soviet Cup]] 10 times and the [[Russian Cup (football)|Russian Cup]] 3 times. Spartak have also reached the semi-finals of all three European club competitions.

The football club is a part of the [[Spartak (sports society)|Spartak Moscow sports society]]. Other teams  in the society include [[ice hockey]] club [[HC Spartak Moscow|Spartak Moscow]].

== History ==
=== Foundation ===
{{seealso|FC Presnya Moscow}}
In the early days of Soviet football many government agencies such as the police, army, and railroads created their own clubs.
In 1921 the Moscow Sport Circle (Moscow sport club of Krasnopresnensky district) (Russian: МКС, Московский кружок спорта), later named Krasnaya Presnya was formed by [[Ivan Artemyev]] and involved [[Nikolai Starostin]], especially in its football team.[4] The team grew, building a stadium, supporting itself from ticket sales and playing matches across Russia.[5] As part of a 1926 reorganisation of football in the USSR, Starostin arranged for the club to be sponsored by the food workers union and the club moved to the 13,000 seat Tomskii Stadium and was known as Pishcheviki . The team changed sponsors repeatedly over the following years as it competed with Dinamo Moscow, whose 35,000 seat Dinamo Stadium lay close by.

As a high-profile sportsman, Starostin came into close contact with Alexander Kosarev, secretary of the Komsomol (Communist Union of Youth) who already had a strong influence on sport and wanted to extend it.[6] In November 1934, with funding from Promkooperatsiia, Kosarev employed Starostin and his brothers to develop his team to make it more powerful. Again the team changed its name, this time to Spartak Moscow.[7] It took its name from the Roman slave rebel and athlete Spartacus

It became part of the Spartak Sports Society during its establishment on April 19, 1935

=== Soviet period ===
In 1935 Starostin proposed the name Spartak that was derived from [[Spartacus]], a [[gladiator]]-slave who led a rebellion against [[Ancient Rome|Rome]], and was inspired by eponymous book by [[Raffaello Giovagnoli]]. Starostin is also credited with the creation of the Spartak logo.<ref>[http://fcspartak.ru/content/ist/ History of Spartak], fcspartak.ru {{ru icon}}</ref> The same year the club became a part of newly created [[Spartak (sports society)|Spartak sports society]].
[[Image:Spartak Society logo.png|100px|thumb|right|Spartak's third logo]]

[[Czech Republic|Czech]] manager [[Antonin Fivebr]] is credited as the first head coach of Spartak, though he worked as a consultant in several clubs simultaneously<ref name=History1936>{{cite web |url= http://www.redwhite.ru/1936.html |title= History of Spartak 1936 |accessdate=2007-11-28 }}{{ru icon}}</ref>. In 1936 the [[Soviet Top League]] was established. The first Championship was won by [[FC Dynamo Moscow|Dynamo Moscow]], while in the second one held the same year Spartak came first. Before the [[World War II]] Spartak gained two more titles.

During 1950-s Spartak together with [[FC Dynamo Moscow|Dynamo Moscow]] dominated in the [[Soviet Top League]]. When the [[USSR national football team]] won gold medals on the [[Football at the 1956 Summer Olympics|Melbourne Olympics]], it consisted largely of Spartak players. Spartak captain [[Igor Netto]] was the captain of the national team from 1954 to 1963. In the 1960s, Spartak won two league titles, but by mid-60s Spartak was no more regarded as a leading Soviet club. The club was even less successful in the 1970s and in 1976 Spartak was relegated into the [[Soviet First League|lower league]].

During the following season, the stadium was still full as the club's fans stayed with the team during its time in the lower division. [[Konstantin Beskov]], who became the head coach (ironically, as a footballer Beskov made his name playing for Spartak's main rivals, [[FC Dynamo Moscow|Dynamo Moscow]]), introduced several young players, including [[Rinat Dasayev]] and [[Georgi Yartsev]]. Spartak came back the next year and won the title in 1979, beating [[FC Dynamo Kyiv|Dynamo Kyiv]] and thanks to Spartak supporters, the period is considered to be the start of the modern-style fans' movement in the Soviet Union.

On October 20, 1982, [[Luzhniki disaster|disaster struck]] during the [[UEFA Cup]] match between Spartak and [[HFC Haarlem]]. Scores of people were trampled. The official number of deaths is 66 but many people believe this number to be significantly higher.

In 1989 Spartak won the its last USSR Championship defeating 2-1 the main rival Dynamo Kyiv in the closing round. Spartak's striker [[Valeri Shmarov (footballer)|Valery Shmarov]] scored the "golden" [[Direct free kick|free kick]] with almost no time left. The next season Spartak reached [[European Cup 1990-91|European Cup]] semifinal consequently eliminating [[S.S.C. Napoli|Napoli]] (by penalties) and [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] (with 3-1 away victory) but losing to [[Olympique de Marseille]].

=== Modern period ===
A new page in the club’s history began when the USSR collapsed and its championship ceased to exist. In the newly created Russian league, Spartak, led by coach and president [[Oleg Romantsev]] dominated and won all but one title between 1992 and 2001. Year after year the team also represented Russia in the [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]].

Problems began in the new century. Several charismatic players ([[Ilya Tsymbalar]] and [[Andrey Tikhonov]] among others) left the club as a result of conflict with Romantsev. Later Romantsev sold his stock to oil magnate [[Andrei Chervichenko]], who in 2003 became the club president. The two were soon embroiled in a row that would continue until Romantsev was sacked in 2003 with the club suffering several sub-par seasons until Chervichenko finally sold his stock in 2004. The new ownership made a number of front office changes with the aim of returning the team to the top of the Russian Premier League.<ref>[http://www.uefa.com/footballeurope/news/Kind=4/newsId=310087.html All-star Spartak rise again], Eduard Nisenboim, ''uefa.com''</ref>

## Overview of FC Spartak Moscow

FC Spartak Moscow (Футбольный клуб «Спартак» Москва) is a prominent football club based in Moscow, Russia. Founded in 1922, the club has a rich history and has been a significant player in both Soviet and Russian football. Known by various nicknames such as "Meat," "Krasno-belye" (The Red-Whites), and "Narodnaya komanda" (The People's Team), Spartak has achieved numerous accolades and milestones throughout its existence.

### Nicknames and Founding

The club's nickname "Meat" originates from the Soviet era when the club was owned by collective production farms (kolkhoz and sovkhoz). This nickname reflects the agricultural roots of the club's sponsorship. Additionally, Spartak is often referred to as "Krasno-belye" due to its traditional red and white colors, and "Narodnaya komanda" highlighting its connection with the people of Moscow.

### Achievements

Spartak has a storied history of success, having won 12 Soviet championships (second only to Dynamo Kyiv) and 9 out of 16 Russian championships. The club has also claimed the Soviet Cup 10 times and the Russian Cup 3 times. Furthermore, Spartak has reached the semi-finals of all three major European club competitions, showcasing its international competitiveness.

### Current Status

Currently, Spartak plays its home games at the Luzhniki Stadium in Moscow, which has a capacity of 78,000 spectators. The club is managed by Valery Karpin (acting caretaker) and chaired by Leonid Fedun. Spartak competes in the Russian Premier League and held the 2nd position in the 2009 season.

## Historical Background

### Early Days and Formation

In the early days of Soviet football, many government agencies created their own clubs. The foundation of Spartak can be traced back to 1921 when the Moscow Sport Circle (Moscow sport club of Krasnopresnensky district) was formed by Ivan Artemyev and Nikolai Starostin. Initially known as Krasnaya Presnya, the club grew and built a stadium, supporting itself through ticket sales and competing across Russia.

### Transition and Reorganization

In 1926, as part of a reorganization of football in the USSR, the club was sponsored by the food workers union and renamed Pishcheviki. Over the years, the club changed sponsors frequently, competing with Dinamo Moscow, another prominent Moscow-based club. In 1934, with funding from Promkooperatsiia, the club was renamed Spartak Moscow, inspired by the gladiator Spartacus.

### Spartak Sports Society

Spartak officially joined the Spartak Sports Society on April 19, 1935. This organization included other sports teams, such as the ice hockey club HC Spartak Moscow. The club's logo and identity were developed under the leadership of Nikolai Starostin, who played a crucial role in shaping Spartak's early years.

### Soviet Period

#### Early Success

In 1936, the Soviet Top League was established, and Spartak quickly emerged as a dominant force. The club won its first championship in 1936 and continued to compete at the highest level throughout the 1940s and 1950s. During this period, Spartak produced notable players like Igor Netto, who captained the USSR national team from 1954 to 1963.

#### Golden Era

The 1950s and 1960s saw Spartak dominate the Soviet Top League alongside Dynamo Moscow. The club's success continued into the 1970s, although it faced a setback when it was relegated to the lower league in 1976. Under the guidance of Konstantin Beskov, Spartak returned to the top division and won the title in 1979, marking the beginning of a modern fan movement in the Soviet Union.

### Modern Period

#### Post-Soviet Success

Following the collapse of the USSR, Spartak adapted to the new Russian league system. Led by Oleg Romantsev, the club dominated the Russian Premier League, winning all but one title between 1992 and 2001. Spartak also excelled in European competitions, reaching the UEFA Champions League semifinals in 1990.

#### Recent Challenges

In the new millennium, Spartak faced internal conflicts and financial challenges. Key players left the club, and the management underwent significant changes. Despite these difficulties, the club continues to strive for success under new leadership and aims to reclaim its place at the top of Russian football.

This summary provides an overview of FC Spartak Moscow's rich history, achievements, and current status, reflecting its enduring legacy in Russian football.

'''John Robert Rudge''' (born 21 October 1944) is an [[English people|English]] former [[association football|football]] player and [[coach (sport)|football manager]]. He is currently working as the [[director of football]] at [[Stoke City F.C.|Stoke City]].

His playing career saw him start with [[Huddersfield Town F.C.|Huddersfield Town]], but find regular football with [[Carlisle United F.C.|Carlisle United]] in 1966. In 1969 he joined [[Torquay United F.C.|Torquay United]], before moving on to [[Bristol Rovers F.C.|Bristol Rovers]] three years later. He ended his career in 1977, after a three years spell with [[A.F.C. Bournemouth|Bournemouth]].

He managed [[Port Vale F.C.|Port Vale]] for a sixteen year period between 1983 to 1999, easily the longest spell in the [[History of Port Vale F.C.|club's history]]. He masterminded some of the club's most successful ever campaigns, but was sacked in January 1999. Following this he was made [[director of football]] at their [[Potteries derby|rivals]] - Stoke City.

==Playing career==
[[Wolverhampton]]-born Rudge began his professional career with [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]] [[Huddersfield Town F.C.|Huddersfield Town]] in [[Huddersfield Town F.C. season 1962–63|1962]]. They were mid-table in [[Huddersfield Town F.C. season 1963–64|1963–64]], coming close to promotion in [[Huddersfield Town F.C. season 1964–65|1964–65]] and [[Huddersfield Town F.C. season 1965–66|1965–66]]. Rudge was still a young player coming to grip with the game, and thus only made five league appearances.

In [[Huddersfield Town F.C. season 1966–67|1966]], he moved onto Second Division rivals [[Carlisle United F.C.|Carlisle United]]. They finished third in [[1966–67 in English football|1966–67]], but this was not enough for promotion. In [[1967–68 in English football|1967–68]] and [[1968–69 in English football|1968–69]] ''the Bluebirds'' gradually declined in strength. Rudge scored sixteen goals in fifty league games.

In 1969, he moved on to [[Football League Third Division|Third Division]] [[Torquay United F.C.|Torquay United]]. He stayed for three seasons; [[1969–70 in English football|1969–70]], [[1970–71 in English football|1970–71]] and [[1971–72 in English football|1971–72]]. Mid-table for his first two seasons, Rudge switched clubs after relegation in 1972. He scored 34 goals in 96 league games for ''the Gulls''. During 1969/70 and 1970/71 he was the [[List of Torquay United F.C. seasons|club's top scorer]] with sixteen and twenty goals respectively.

He spent [[1972–73 in English football|1972–73]] and [[1973–74 in English football|1973–74]] with [[Bristol Rovers F.C.|Bristol Rovers]]. Rovers were promoted in 1974 as Third Division runners-up. He made 70 league appearances for ''the Pirates'', scoring seventeen goals.

He saw out his playing days at [[A.F.C. Bournemouth|Bournemouth]]. They suffered relegation in [[1974–75 in English football|1974–75]], thus were a [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] club in [[1975–76 in English football|1975–76]] and [[1976–77 in English football|1976–77]]. He scored twice in 21 league games for ''the Cherries''.

==Coaching career==
Following his retirement as a player, Rudge was made a coach at old club Torquay United.<ref name="Kent">{{cite book|last=Kent|first=Jeff|title=Port Vale Personalities|publisher=Witan Books|page=256|date=1996|isbn=0952915200|url=http://www.amazon.ca/Port-Vale-Personalities-Jeff-Kent/dp/0952915200}}</ref> In January 1980 he was appointed as a coach at [[Port Vale F.C.|Port Vale]], in December of that year he was promoted to the position of assistant manager, under [[John McGrath (English footballer)|John McGrath]].<ref name="Kent" />

==Managerial career==
Following the sacking of McGrath in December 1983, Rudge was made [[caretaker manager]] at Port Vale.<ref name="HIStory" /> Under McGrath, the club had lost thirteen of their opening seventeen league games. The club had the third highest budget in the division, the weekly wage bill three times that of the home gate receipts and were rooted to the foot of the table, nine points from their nearest competitors.<ref name="HIStory" /> Rudge understated things somewhat when he said: "''We cannot change things overnight.''"<ref name="HIStory">{{cite book|last=Kent|first=Jeff|title=The Valiants' Years: The Story Of Port Vale|publisher=Witan Books|page=270|date=1990|isbn=0950898147}}</ref> However, player [[Tommy Gore]] noted "''the players are in a more determined mood.''"<ref name="HIStory" /> He was unable to prevent [[promotion and relegation|relegation]] [[1983-84 in English football|that year]], though the club did avoid picking up the wooden spoon. Though [[Mark Bright]] and [[Robbie Earle]] were signed to Vale before Rudge's appointment, he helped to nurture their talents, both were the first of many to develop into outstanding players under Rudge.

{{Quote|"Vale's reputation has been built on grit and determination and I will be looking to bring in the player who is willing to die for the cause."|Rudge prepares for his first full season as manager.<ref name="HIStory"/>}}

In reality, the task in [[1984–85 in English football|1984–85]] was to arrest the decline. Rudge achieved this aim, slashing the wage bill to offset the club's reduced income, ''the Vale'' finished 12th. Young striker [[Andy Jones (footballer)|Andy Jones]] was purchased for a few thousands pounds from [[Rhyl F.C.|Rhyl]].

In [[1985-86 in English football|1985-86]], promotion was the target. An eighteen game unbeaten run from January to April helped to win Vale a fourth place promotion place, seven points clear of fifth place [[Leyton Orient F.C.|Leyton Orient]]. At the end of the season, Rudge turned down an offer of the management job at [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]].

{{0}}47 (14) | pcupdate = 15:29, 08 November, 2009 | ntupdate = 17:00, 14 November 2009 (UTC) }} '''Robert Earnshaw''' (born 6 April 1981) is a [[Zambia]]n-born [[Wales national football team|Welsh international]] [[football (soccer)|football]] player. He is a striker presently playing for [[Nottingham Forest F.C.|Nottingham Forest]]. He is the only player to score a [[hat-trick]] in the Premier League, Championship, League One, League Two (or the divisions under their previous names), the League Cup, the FA Cup and for his country at International level. == Early life == Earnshaw, nicknamed "Earnie", was born on the outskirts of the north central Zambian mining town of [[Mufulira]] on 6 April 1981. When he was five, his family moved to [[Malawi]] where David Earnshaw took charge of another coal mine and his youngest son began school. Again, the family's stay was to be a short one. In September 1990, following the death of her husband, Rita moved the Earnshaw family to [[Bedwas]], a small Welsh town to the north of [[Cardiff]], where they lived initially with her sister. Earnshaw still has a house there.{{cite web|title=The Official Robert Earnshaw Website - My Early Life|url=http://robertearnshaw.com/early.php|accessdate=2009-10-13|publisher=Robert Earnshaw|year=2009|work=The Official Robert Earnshaw website}} "It was the first time I had been away from Africa." he recalls. "It was just completely different, from one extreme to another. It was much colder as well, just every little thing was different, everyone spoke English over here and although I could speak a little bit I had to learn. But when you're a kid you just get on with it." It was in Wales that he began playing football, kicking a ball around with friends between and after classes at [[Cardinal Newman RC School]], [[Pontypridd]], the school he moved on to after a spell at St. Helen's Primary. Cardinal Newman's was a [[rugby union]]-playing school so Earnshaw's first organised football match came at the age of 12 with local youth side [[Llanbradach]]. "We didn't win anything, we weren't the best," he says. "I only played one year and then I moved to GE Wales, which was a better team and we won a few local titles. I scored a lot of goals, 80 one season, 60 another when I was 14, 15, 16." == Playing career == ===Cardiff City=== Those goals grabbed the attention of then [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]] youth team coach [[Gavin Tait]], earning the youngster an invite to training, and, on 1 August 1997, a one-year YTS contract at [[Ninian Park]]. He came through the club's youth development programme and became a full-time professional in August 1998, despite the attentions of his heroes [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]]. Earnshaw made his mark immediately with a superb equaliser at [[Hartlepool United F.C.|Hartlepool United]] on the opening day of the season. Earnshaw was loaned to [[Greenock Morton F.C.|Greenock Morton]] by [[Frank Burrows]] to gain experience and toughen up. He also at one stage had a trial at [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]] under [[Bryan Robson]]. The experience gave Earnshaw the motivation to succeed and on his return he soon became one of the Bluebird fans' biggest heroes. He had already been capped by [[Wales national football team|Wales]] at youth and under-21 level, but his exploits in Cardiff City's promotion campaigns attracted the attention of national coach [[Mark Hughes]]. Earnshaw duly exploded onto the international scene, scoring the winning goal on his debut for Wales against Germany at the [[Millennium Stadium]] in May 2002; he was also named man of the match.{{cite news |date=2002-05-14 |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport3/worldcup2002/hi/team_pages/germany/newsid_1986000/1986443.stm |title=Earnshaw seals historic win |publisher=BBC Sport |accessdate=2007-04-28}} A few months later Earnshaw was named Young Welsh Footballer of the Year, and was named in the [[Professional Footballers' Association|PFA]] Division Two Team of the Year for 2002–03{{cite news | title = Wigan dominate PFA team | url = http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_div_2/2981569.stm | publisher = BBC Sport | date = 2003-04-28 | accessdate = 2008-10-09}} after a prolific season saw him score 35 goals in all competitions, with 31 scored in the league meaning he broke the 56-year old club record of [[Stan Richards (footballer)|Stan Richards]].{{cite news | title = Earnie sends records tumbling | url = http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/c/cardiff_city/2855393.stm | publisher = BBC Sport | date = 2003-03-22 | accessdate = 2008-10-12}} Earnshaw became a key member of the Wales squad during the Euro 2004 qualifying campaign. He staked his claim for a regular slot in the starting line-up with a hat-trick in the 4–0 friendly win over [[Scotland national football team|Scotland]] in February 2004. At the end of 2003–04, Earnshaw was named in the First Division team of the year.{{cite news |date=2004-04-25 |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/3628905.stm |title=Henry retains PFA crown |publisher=BBC Sport |accessdate=2007-04-26}} Several top clubs including Manchester United, [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] and [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] sent their scouts to look at Earnshaw as his reputation spread. He scored 87 goals in his 175 appearances for Cardiff City. ===West Bromwich Albion=== [[Image:robearnshaw.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Earnshaw in action for Wales]] In 2004 Earnshaw was transferred from Cardiff to [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] for £3 million, a fee that could have reached a maximum of £3.62 million with performance-related add-ons.{{cite news |date=2004-08-30 |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/c/cardiff_city/3607710.stm |title=Earnshaw signs for Baggies |publisher=BBC Sport |accessdate=2007-04-28}} His agent [[Mel Eves]] was fined 30,000 [[Swiss franc]]s (£12,250) by [[Fifa]] in July 2007 over his role in the transfer. Eves was found guilty of acting for both his client (Earnshaw) and the buying club (Albion) in the deal.{{Cite news | last = Conn | first = David | title = Agent fined £12,000 by FIFA for dual role in Earnshaw move | url = http://www.guardian.co.uk/football/2007/jul/17/newsstory.westbrom | publisher = [[guardian.co.uk]] | date = 2007-07-17 | accessdate = 2008-06-03}} Earnshaw made his Albion début in a 3–0 defeat at Liverpool on 11 September 2004, coming

During his tenure at Cardiff City, he scored 87 goals in 175 appearances, breaking the club's long-standing record set by Stan Richards. His time at West Bromwich Albion was marked by consistent performances and contributions to the team. [Data: Football player infobox (1)]

'''Zvjezdan Misimović''' (born 5 June 1982) is a [[Germany|German]]-born [[Bosnian]] [[association football|footballer]] who currently plays for [[VfL Wolfsburg|Wolfsburg]]. Misimović is the co-[[Captain (football)|captain]] of the [[Bosnia and Herzegovina national football team|Bosnia and Herzegovina national team]]. 

==Early life==
Misimović's parents are [[Bosnian]] ''[[gastarbeiter]]s'' who came to [[West Germany]] from [[Bosanska Gradiška]] during the late 1960s.

==Club career==
Known in Germany as ''Zwetschge'' (German word for [[damson|damson plum]]) due to similar pronunciation to his first name, Misimović played for [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] in the past, but joined [[VfL Bochum|Bochum]] at the start of the 2004–05 season and then moved on to [[1. FC Nuremberg|Nuremberg]] in July 2007. He led the Bundesliga in assists during the 2008–09 season with 18 (23 in all competitions). 

Misimović signed a four year contract to 2012 at [[VfL Wolfsburg|Wolfsburg]].

==International career==
===Youth level===
Misimović played for the [[Serbia national under-19 football team|FR Yugoslavia under-18 national squad]], appearing with them at the [[2001 UEFA European Under-18 Football Championship|2001]] [[UEFA European Under-18 Football Championship]] held in [[Finland]]. In that team, he played alongside [[Nemanja Vidić]] and [[Danko Lazović]].<ref>[http://arhiva.kurir-info.rs/Arhiva/2004/oktobar/07/SP-08-07102004.shtml Mešano "meso", ''Kurir'', October 7, 2004]</ref> 

Misimović later progressed to the [[Serbia and Montenegro national under-21 football team|FR Yugoslavia under-21 national team]], but appeared in only one match as the 85th minute substitute against [[France national under-21 football team|France]] in November 2002. Head coach of the under-21s at the time [[Vladimir Petrović Pižon]] soon cut Misimović, telling him he was overweight and slow.<ref>[http://www.novine.ca/arhiva/2008/1150/sport.asp Oteran iz Srbije, u Bundesligi postao zvezda, novine.ca, April 25, 2008]</ref><ref>[http://www.guardian.co.uk/football/blog/2009/sep/29/wolfsburg-manchester-united-champions-league Wolfsburg and Bosnia's dynamic duo get chance to make history of their own, Jonathan Wilson's blog @ guardian.co.uk, September 29, 2009]</ref>

===Senior===
By late 2003 and early 2004, 21-year-old Misimović was still unattached to any senior national team. He got approached by then teammate at [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] – [[Hasan Salihamidžić]] – about a possibility of playing for Bosnia.<ref>[http://www.sarajevo-x.com/clanak/090710128 Zvjezdan Misimović - mozak Ćirine ekspedicije, sarajevo-x.com, July 11, 2009]</ref> Misimović accepted and debuted for the national team of Bosnia and Herzegovina under head coach [[Blaž Slišković]] on 18 February 2004 in a friendly versus Macedonia. Misimović was used sparingly by Slišković during [[2006 World Cup]] [[2006 FIFA World Cup qualification - UEFA Group 7|qualifying]] campaign: he played full 90 in the opening home draws versus Spain and Serbia-Montenegro, but then come off the bench in the away loss to Belgium. Misimović then experienced a period of being in the starting lineup before being subbed off 10–20 minutes into the second half: 1-1 home draw with Lithuania (scored the leading goal), the away win at San Marino, and finally the away 1-1 draw versus Spain in Valencia (he again scored the leading goal before Spain tied in the 96th minute). For the deciding four qualifiers (home win versus Belgium, away win at Lithuania, home win versus San Marino, and the away loss to Serbia-Montenegro), Slišković moved Misimović to the bench, inserting him into action only during final 15–20 minutes.

[[Euro 2008]] [[UEFA Euro 2008 qualifying Group C|qualifying]] began in fall 2006 with Slišković still behind the bench and Misimović an established starter and scorer. After dismantling of Malta in the opening match came a shocking 1-3 defeat to Hungary at home that prompted Slišković's resignation, which he retracted couple of weeks later and stayed on. However, more heartbreak was to follow with a 2-2 draw at lowly Moldova as Misimović sparked a comeback by scoring a goal at 2-0 down. Four days later Bosnia got spanked 0-4 by Greece at home; this time Slišković's resignation was final. As qualifying winter break commenced, Bosnian team was in complete disarray with relations inside the organization strained to the maximum. In such circumstances 13 Bosnian national team players (including Misimović) announced in a letter published in ''[[Dnevni Avaz]]'' daily, that they would boycott all national team matches until four FA officials resigned.<ref>[http://www.sarajevo-x.com/sport/clanak/061031019 Reprezentativci BiH neće igrati dok ne odu Jelić, Dominković, Čolaković i Pašalić, sarajevo-x.com, October 31, 2006]</ref> New head coach [[Fuad Muzurović]] was announced in late December 2006, and under him Misimović truly came into his own and even got to be the captain of the national team.

After [[Meho Kodro]] replaced Muzurović as the new head coach in early January 2008, one of the changes he introduced was stripping Misimović of the captain's armband and giving it to [[Emir Spahić]]. On 8 April 2008, Misimović (still only 25 years of age at the time) announced his retirement from the national team, stating that he's doing so out of health concerns as he feels no longer able to keep up with the physical rigors of playing for both the club and the country.<ref>[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=15Q7X86SoNc Zvjezdan Misimović napušta reprezentaciju BiH, BHRT, April 8, 2008]</ref> However, many speculated that health had little to do with Misimović's sudden announcement. This was in essence confirmed two days later by the Bosnian national team general manager [[Elvir Bolić]] who said that Misimović may have softened his original stance and revealed that new head coach Meho Kodro will travel to Germany in order to visit the player personally and discuss the "real reasons" for his decision.<ref>[http://sportsport.ba/bh_fudbalp-977.htm Bolić: Misimović malo smekšao stav, sportsport.ba, April 10, 2008]</ref> On 12 April 2008, after speaking to Kodro, Misimović change

# Zvjezdan Misimović

## Early Life and Background

Zvjezdan Misimović was born on June 5, 1982, in Munich, West Germany. His parents were Bosnian gastarbeiters who migrated to Germany from Bosanska Gradiška during the late 1960s. Despite being born in Germany, Misimović has always maintained strong ties to his Bosnian heritage. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

## Club Career

### Early Years

Misimović started his professional career with Bayern Munich's reserve team, Bayern Munich II, where he played from 2000 to 2004. During this period, he made 102 appearances and scored 44 goals. He also had brief stints with the senior team of Bayern Munich, making three appearances between 2002 and 2004. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

### Move to Bochum and Nuremberg

In 2004, Misimović transferred to VfL Bochum, where he spent three seasons, making 92 appearances and scoring 21 goals. He then moved to 1. FC Nuremberg in July 2007, where he played for one season, making 28 appearances and scoring 10 goals. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

### Wolfsburg

In 2008, Misimović signed a four-year contract with VfL Wolfsburg, where he continued to play as an attacking midfielder and left winger. At Wolfsburg, he wore the number 10 jersey and became known for his creative playmaking abilities. During the 2008–09 season, he led the Bundesliga in assists with 18, contributing significantly to his team's success. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

## International Career

### Youth Levels

Misimović represented FR Yugoslavia at the under-18 and under-21 levels. He played for the under-18 team in the 2001 UEFA European Under-18 Football Championship in Finland. Later, he was part of the under-21 team but only made one appearance as a substitute. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

'''Darlington Football Club''' are an [[England|English]] [[association football|football]] team based in the town of [[Darlington]] and play in [[Football League Two|League Two]]. The club's nickname is The Quakers in reference to [[Religious Society of Friends|the religious movement]] that had a historic influence on the town. Darlington have remained in the bottom tier of the league since 1992; they are the division's second-longest inhabitants after [[Rochdale A.F.C.|Rochdale]]. Their local rivals are [[Hartlepool United F.C.|Hartlepool United]], [[Carlisle United F.C.|Carlisle United]] and [[York City F.C.|York City]].

Darlington Football Club was founded at Darlington Grammar School in 1883 and won the [[Durham Challenge Cup|Durham Senior Cup]] two (1895) and eight (1891) years later. In [[1919-20 in English football|1919–20]] the side managed to finish second in the North Eastern League and the following year were champions. This was a stroke of good luck as their victory coincided with the forming of the Northern Section of the [[Football League Third Division|Football League's Third Division]], which Darlington were elected to. Their first season in the Third Division was a successful one and they ended up in second place. In 1925, they were champions and won promotion to the [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]] but were relegated two seasons later.

===Post-War===
In [[1957-58 in English football|1957–58]] they attained their best ever [[FA Cup]] run, reaching the last 16. This was not enough to stop them being put into the new [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] with the reorganisation of the League and the end of the Third Division's Northern and Southern Sections. In 1966, they won promotion to the Third Division after finishing the season as runners-up, but were relegated the following year. In 1982, the club faced a financial crisis but survived thanks to fundraising efforts of the town. Three years later the club won promotion by finishing 3rd in the league under manager [[Cyril Knowles]]. Darlington spent two seasons in the Third Division, their finish of 13th in 1986 their highest position attained in the Football League since the introduction of the present four-division structure in 1958, but they were relegated [[1986-87 in English football|the following season]].

In 1989, the team finished bottom of the league and was relegated to the Conference. However, they were only there for one season before winning the [[Football Conference|Conference]] title and returning to the [[Football League]] under manager [[Brian Little (footballer)|Brian Little]], who had been appointed in January 1989. A second successive promotion followed in [[1990-91 in English football|1990-91]], this time to the Third Division as Fourth Division champions, but Little was then lured away to [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]] and he was succeeded by [[Frank Gray]]. Darlington were relegated in bottom place [[1991-92 in English football|the following season]], and Gray was dismissed.

After a comfortable 3-0 aggregate semi-final win over [[Hartlepool United F.C.|Hartlepool]], Quakers arrived in confident mood, however they wasted a host of chances and were again undone by a single goal, this time from [[Andy Clarke]].

The [[1999-2000 in English football|1999–00 season]] was a notable one for Darlington. It was the first season under the ambitious new chairman [[George Reynolds (business)|George Reynolds]], Also, they became the first team to lose a tie in the [[FA Cup#1990s|FA Cup]] and yet still qualify for the next round. ===2000-2007===
During the summer of 2002, Darlington made approaches to sign two world famous players - [[Paul Gascoigne]] and [[Faustino Asprilla]] - but both bids failed.

In 2003, as part of the Farewell to Feethams celebrations, the club programme ran a competition to decide which Darlington’s best ever team would be. The top 11 players that made the team were: [[Mark Prudhoe]], [[Ron Greener]], [[Craig Liddle]], [[Kevan Smith]], John Peverell, [[Andy Toman]], [[Alan Sproates]], [[David McLean (English footballer)|David McLean]], [[Alan Walsh]], [[Marco Gabbiadini]] and Colin Sinclair. Stefanos Borbokis was born on September 1, 1966, in Serres, Greece. He is a former Greek football player known for his versatility as both a forward and winger. During this period, he played 215 matches in the Alpha Ethniki league, scoring 28 goals [Data: Infobox Football biography (1)].

At PAOK FC, Borbokis was instrumental in several UEFA Cup campaigns. One notable match was his debut in the UEFA Cup, where he faced Diego Maradona’s Napoli FC. Although PAOK lost the tie 2-1 on aggregate, the experience was significant for Borbokis. Another memorable moment came during the 1991/92 UEFA Cup when he scored the winning goal against KV Mechelen in Belgium, securing a 2-1 victory and advancing to the second round. Additionally, he participated in the 1992 Greek Cup Final, where PAOK lost to Olympiakos FC over two legs with a score of 2-1 [Data: Infobox Football biography (1)].

### Other Clubs

In 1994, Borbokis moved to Edessaikos F.C., where he spent a single season. During this time, he helped the team reach the final four in the Greek Cup. After Edessaikos, he returned to Thessaloniki and played for Iraklis Thessaloniki F.C., Aris Thessaloniki F.C., and Apollon Kalamarias. Throughout his career, he accumulated a total of 380 appearances across these clubs, scoring 60 goals [Data: Infobox Football biography (1)].

## International Career

Borbokis represented the Greece national football team from 1988 to 1992, making a total of 29 appearances and scoring six goals. His international career peaked during the UEFA Euro 1992 qualifying campaign, where he scored in all three of Greece's victories—against Malta (4-0), Portugal (3-2), and Finland (2-0). '''Craig Stephen Noone''' (born 17 November 1987 in [[Liverpool]], [[Merseyside]]) is an [[England|English]] [[Association football|footballer]] who currently plays as a [[midfielder]] for [[Championship]] club [[Plymouth Argyle F.C.|Plymouth Argyle]].

==Career==
Noone, formerly a roofer by trade, began his football career as a youth team player with [[Skelmersdale United F.C.|Skelmersdale United]], and rose up through the ranks to make his first team debut in the [[2005-06 in English football|2005/2006 season]].

In the summer of 2007, Noone had a trial with [[Football in Belgium|Belgian]] club [[Royal Antwerp FC|Royal Antwerp]], but ultimately did not sign for them, and in October of the same year, [[Liam Watson (footballer)|Liam Watson]] took Noone to [[Burscough F.C.|Burscough]] on a two-year contract.

Nine months later, in July 2008, Watson signed the player once again, this time for [[Southport F.C.|Southport]], Watson having resigned from his post at Burscough. However, Noone played only one game for the club, and was signed by [[Football League Championship]] club [[Plymouth Argyle F.C.|Plymouth Argyle]] for an undisclosed fee, which could rise to in excess of [[Pound sterling|£]]100,000.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/p/plymouth_argyle/7560635.stm |title=Plymouth sign left-winger Noone |publisher=BBC Sport}}</ref>

==Plymouth Argyle==

On 30 August 2008, Noone made his debut for Plymouth as he came of the bench against Burnley in a league match, the game ended in a goalless draw. He scored his first goal for Plymouth on the 15th November 2008 in a 1-0 win away at Coventry City, coming off the bench to score an 87th minute winner.

After 10 substitute appearances for Plymouth, Noone made his first start for the club in the league match versus [[Southampton FC]] on Boxing Day 2008, where his team won 2-0. On 3 January 2009, Noone made his FA Cup debut coming off the bench for his sides 3-1 loss to Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium.

Noone was linked with a £800,000 move to either Sunderland or Wigan of the Premier League on the 6th January<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/gossip_and_transfers/7812907.stm|title=Noone linked with Premiership move |publisher=BBC Sport}}</ref>, which prompted a response from Mackems manager [[Ricky Sbragia]] saying that they were not considering making a bid for the winger.

'''Samuel "Sam" Baldock''' (born 15 March 1989 in [[Bedford, England]]) is an [[England|English]] professional [[football (soccer)|football]] [[striker]] who is currently contracted to [[Milton Keynes Dons F.C.|Milton Keynes Dons]]. 

He grew up in the village of [[Steeple Claydon]], [[Buckinghamshire]], while attending the [[Royal Latin School]] in [[Buckingham]].

==Club career==

Baldock joined MK Dons as a trainee in July 2004.<ref>[http://www.miltonkeynes.co.uk/mkdons/Saints-hit-sorry-Dons-for.856499.jp Saints hit sorry Dons for six (MK Citizen 16 September 2004)]</ref><ref>[http://www.miltonkeynes.co.uk/mkdons/Under-16s-beat-Spurs.907103.jp Dons under-16s beat Spurs (MK Citizen 17 December 2004)]</ref>  [[Danny Wilson (footballer)|Danny Wilson]] handed Baldock his first team debut on [[20 December]] 2005 in the 2–1 [[Football League Trophy]] loss to [[Colchester United F.C.|Colchester United]] as a late substitute in his only appearance of the season.<ref>[http://www.miltonkeynes.co.uk/sport/MK-Dons-1-Colchester-United.1291121.jp MK Dons 1, Colchester United 2 (MK Citizen 20 December 2005)]</ref>

[[Martin Allen]] as Dons manager for the 2006/07 season gave Baldock two further games in the first team in his only year in charge. Baldock failed to score as a substitute in either game as the Dons lost 4–1 away to [[Brighton & Hove Albion]] in the Football League Trophy and drew 1–1 at home to [[Mansfield Town]].

As [[Paul Ince]] took the role as manager, Baldock became more involved in matches, first making a substitute appearance in the [[FA Cup]] away to [[Crewe Alexandra]], before making 5 substitute appearances in League Two. He also made his full debut in the Football League Trophy victory over [[Gillingham FC]], and made 2 further appearances as a substitute, including one in the [[Football League Trophy 2007-08|Trophy]] final at [[Wembley Stadium]], helping MK Dons win their first ever trophy.

As new manager [[Roberto Di Matteo]] joined MK Dons as manager, Baldock made his break-through season as he become a regular in the first-team, scoring his first senior goal in the Dons' 2–1 loss against [[Reading F.C.|Reading]] in a friendly match at [[stadium:mk]] on 19 July 2008. He then made his first competitive start in the [[MK Dons]] opening Day [[Coca Cola League One]]  defeat to [[Leicester City]] on 9 August 2008. During the season he got known by the fans as "Super Sam".

Baldock's first competitive goal came as the Dons beat [[Norwich City]] 1-0 in the [[Football League Cup]] at [[stadium:mk]] on 12 August 2008. Baldock's continued presence in the first team led to him featuring in the League One top scorers charts.

==International career==

On 26 August 2009, Baldock was called up to an initial 30-man squad for the [[2009 FIFA U-20 World Cup]] in [[Egypt]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.miltonkeynes.co.uk/sport/Baldock-suprised-by-England-call.5591201.jp|title=Baldock suprised [sic] by England call|publisher=MK Citizen|date=2009-08-26|accessdate=2009-09-12|author=James Chard}}</ref> Later, on 11 September, he made the final squad of 21 players, MK Dons chairman [[Pete Winkelman]] commented: "The standard of players he will now be rubbing shoulders with underlines what a wonderful talent he is."<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.mkdons.com/page/NewsDetail/0,,10420~1794084,00.html|title=Baldock set for U20 World Cup|publisher=Milton Keynes Dons|date=2009-09-11|accessdate=2009-09-12}}</ref>

The club is nicknamed "''The Grecians''". For the 2009-10 season City's home kit is supplied by [[Carbrini Sportswear]] and it consists of red and white shirts, white shorts, and white socks{{cite news | url=http://www.footballshirtculture.com/09/10-kits/exeter-city-2009-2010-carbrini-home-kit.html | title=Exeter City 09/10 Carbrini Home Kit| publisher=www.footballshirtculture.com| accessdate=13 July 2009 }}. == History == [[Image:Brazil v Exeter City (1914).jpg|right|thumb|350px|The match against Brazil]] ===Early history=== Exeter City FC was formed from two predecessor clubs: - '''[[Exeter United F.C.|Exeter United]]''' and '''St Sidwell's United'''. Exeter United was a football club from Exeter, Devon, that played between 1890 and 1904. In 1904, Exeter United lost 3-1 to local rivals St Sidwell's United and after the match, it was agreed that the two clubs should become one. The new team took the name 'Exeter City' and continued to play at Exeter United's ground, St James Park, where Exeter City still play today. The team was formed from the cricket team of the same name and thus the first football team with the moniker 'United'. St Sidwell's United (which had also been known as St Sidwell's Wesleyans and St Sidwell's Old Boys) was a club that had formed from the regulars who frequented the Foresters Inn in Sidwell Street, Exeter; although the [[public house]] was always known as the Drum and Monkey. The team played in St Sidwell's old colours of green and white. On 10 September 1904, Exeter City played its first ever competitive match: - a 2-1 victory at St James over [[110th Battery]] of the [[Royal Artillery]], in the [[East Devon League]]. The attendance was 600, and the winning goal scored by Sid Thomas, who was to serve the club in various capacities for 70 years. City topped the East Devon League with 11 wins, 2 draws, 1 defeat in its 1st season, and transferred to the Plymouth & District League for next 3 seasons. In 1908, Exeter City AFC became a limited company. City became a full-time professional team, and applied successfully for membership of the Southern League, replacing [[Tottenham Hotspur]]. A wooden grandstand was erected, and the club entered into a leasing arrangement over the ground. On 3 October 1908, City got its record highest FA Cup win: - Exeter City 14 [[Weymouth F.C.|Weymouth]] 0. The match was in the 1st Qualifying Round. James ("Daisy") Bell scored 6 goals, and 10 of Exeter's 14 goals came in the first half. City changed to its current colours of red and white in 1910. This was after having had a poor start to the season (only 2 wins out of 11). The result of the game was a 0-0 draw, but 5 consecutive League wins came for the club in December. City made an historic tour of South America in 1914, during which time it played 8 matches against teams in [[Argentina]] and [[Brazil]]. That was the last match of the tour, which yielded 5 wins, 1 draw and 2 defeats. The only other loss was in a match that kicked off 12 hours after the players got off the boat. [[Image:Exeter City vs Altrincham.JPG|right|thumb|350px|Exeter City vs Altrincham, a Conference National fixture played on 19 August 2006.]] ===Football League (1920-2003)=== City's historic first match in the Football League took place on Saturday 28 August 1920, when [[Brentford F.C.|Brentford]] was the visiting team to St James Park. # Exeter City Football Club Overview

Exeter City Football Club, commonly referred to as "The Grecians," is an English football club based in Exeter, Devon. Founded in 1904, the club has a rich history and has been a prominent figure in English football for over a century. The club plays its home games at St James Park, which has a capacity of 9,036 (3,806 seated). As of the 2008–09 season, Exeter City rejoined the Football League after a stint in the Conference National, achieving automatic promotion to League One for the 2009–10 season. [Data: Exeter City FC (1)]

## Historical Background

### Formation and Early Years

Exeter City FC was formed from the merger of two predecessor clubs: Exeter United and St Sidwell's United. Exeter United, which existed from 1890 to 1904, merged with St Sidwell's United in 1904 following a 3-1 defeat. The new club, named Exeter City, continued to play at St James Park, the former ground of Exeter United. The club's first competitive match was a 2-1 victory over 110th Battery of the Royal Artillery in the East Devon League on September 10, 1904. [Data: Exeter City FC (2)]

### Transition to Professionalism

In 1908, Exeter City AFC became a limited company and transitioned to a full-time professional team. The club joined the Southern League, replacing Tottenham Hotspur, and constructed a wooden grandstand at St James Park. On October 3, 1908, Exeter City recorded its highest-ever FA Cup win, defeating Weymouth 14-0 in the First Qualifying Round. [Data: Exeter City FC (3)]

### Color Change and International Tour

In 1910, the club changed its colors from green and white to the current red and white stripes. This change followed a poor start to the season, and the new kit brought better results. In 1914, Exeter City embarked on a historic tour of South America, playing eight matches against teams in Argentina and Brazil. One notable match was against the Brazil national team, with conflicting reports suggesting either a 2-0 loss or a 3-3 draw. [Data: Exeter City FC (4)]

### Entry into the Football League

In 1920, Exeter City was invited to become a founder member of the Football League Third Division. The club's first match in the Football League took place on August 28, 1920, against Brentford, which Exeter won 3-0. Over the years, Exeter City has achieved significant milestones, including reaching the sixth round of the FA Cup twice, in 1931 and 1980. [Data: Exeter City FC (5)]

## Recent Achievements

In the 1990 season, Exeter City secured its only major trophy by winning the Fourth Division Championship. The club's success continued into the 2000s, with a return to the Football League in 2008 after a period in the Conference National. Exeter City's journey back to the Football League culminated in automatic promotion to League One for the 2009–10 season. [Data: Exeter City FC (6)]

## Current Status

As of the 2008–09 season, Exeter City was positioned second in League Two, securing promotion to League One. '''Gonzalo Antonio Fierro Caniullán''' (born March 21, 1983) is a Chilean footballer, who currently plays as a right winger for the Brazilian club [[Clube de Regatas do Flamengo|Flamengo]].

==Career==
===Colo-Colo===
He spent the rest of his years at Chilean club [[Colo-Colo]] where he received the name, "El Joven Pistolero" (the young sniper). In 2005 he scored eleven goals and gave numerous assists while playing with other prominent players such as [[Humberto Suazo]], the world's top international scorer in 2007 and the Mexican League's top scorer in 2008, [[Matias Fernandez]], who preceded [[Carlos Tevez]] as the Americas's best player in 2007 and [[Alexis Sánchez (footballer)|Alexis Sánchez]] who went on to become an idol in world-renown club [[River Plate]] and is now at Italy's premier club, [[Udinese]].  However he still seemed to find the back of the net scoring ten goals so far in 2008.  In his initial years, Fierro scored a dozen goals in the Chilean League as well as two 30 meter rockets in the [[Copa Sudamericana 2006]].  He scored three more goals at the [[Copa Libertadores 2007]] and was a regular starter at the [[Copa Libertadores 2008]] where he scored against [[Maracaibo]], arguably Venezuela's best club and was a key man in the historical 2-0 win against Diego Maradona's club, [[Boca Juniors]] where he took a penalty.  

===Flamengo===
On August 26, 2008, Fierro joined [[Brazilian Série A]] club [[Clube de Regatas do Flamengo|Flamengo]]<ref name="flamengo">{{cite web | title = Flamengo contrata atacante chileno Fierro | url=http://www1.folha.uol.com.br/folha/esporte/ult92u438205.shtml | accessdate = 2008-08-26 | date=2008-08-26 | publisher=[[Folha de S. Paulo|Folha Online]] |language = Portuguese }}</ref>. He became the first [[Chile]]an player in the club's history<ref>[http://www.flamengo.com.br/flapedia/Estrangeiros Estrangeiros do Flamengo]@Flapédia {{pt icon}}</ref>. On April 5, 2009, Gonzalo played his first match as a starter on the [[Campeonato Carioca|Rio de Janeiro State League]] 1-1 draw against rivals [[Fluminense Football Club|Fluminense]]<ref> {{cite web | title = Fla-Flu decidido no fim garante novo confronto entre os rivais nas semifinais | url=http://globoesporte.globo.com/Esportes/Noticias/Futebol/Campeonato_Carioca/0,,MUL1074107-9835,00.html | accessdate = 2009-03-05 | date=2009-03-05 | publisher=[[Globoesporte.com]] |language = Portuguese }}</ref>.

Fierro had his second chance in the first team only on July 12, 2009, this time against [[Campeonato Brasileiro Série A|Brazilian Série A]] defending champions [[São Paulo Futebol Clube|São Paulo]] in [[Morumbi Stadium]], he was the choice to replace [[Ibson]] after the end of his loan<ref>[http://globoesporte.globo.com/Esportes/Noticias/Times/Flamengo/0,,MUL1226091-9865,00.html Motivado por telefonema especial, Fierro teme comparação com Ibson] (globoesporte.com) {{pt icon}}</ref>. In this match he scored his first goal ever for [[Clube de Regatas do Flamengo|Flamengo]] with only three minutes of playing receiving a pass from [[Adriano Leite Ribeiro|Adriano]]<ref>[http://espnbrasil.terra.com.br/flamengo/noticia/61158_CUCA+APOSTA+NO+CHILENO+FIERRO+NO+FLAMENGO+CONTRA+O+SAO+PAULO Cuca aposta no chileno Fierro no Flamengo contra o São Paulo] (espn.com.br) {{pt icon}}</ref><ref>[http://globoesporte.globo.com/Esportes/Noticias/Futebol/Brasileirao/Serie_A/0,,MUL1227113-9827,00.html Na volta do Imperador ao Morumbi, São Paulo reage e empata com o Flamengo] (globoesporte.com) {{pt icon}}</ref>.

Bielsa had so much faith in Fierro's abilities that he immediately took him into his new process, nominated him to play the two hosts of Euro 2008, Austria and Switzerland, where Chile won 2-0 and lost 2-1 in a game where Chile was inexplicably denied a legitimate goal.  In a tour of Asia in 2007 where Chile played the two hosts of the [[2002 World Cup]], Fierro played and scored against South Korea in a 1-0 win and played the 90 minutes in the tie against Japan 0-0. In the [[2010 FIFA World Cup qualification (CONMEBOL)|2010 World Cup Qualifiers]], Fierro started in the 0-2 loss to Argentina, the 2-0 win against Peru, the historical 2-2 tie against Uruguay in Montevideo, and the 0-3 loss against Paraguay. Due to his demanding season he stayed out in the 2-0 win against Bolivia in La Paz, and the 3-2 win against Venezuela in Caracas. Fierro then played against Euro 2008's most entertaining squad, Turkey, in a tight 1-0 loss in [[Istanbul]] and has been nominated to play Brazil as well as Colombia on September 7 and September 10 of this year.

His debut for Flamengo came in a Rio de Janeiro State League match against Fluminense on April 5, 2009. [Data: Infobox football biography 2 (1)]

- **Primera División Chile Champion**: Clausura 2002, Apertura 2006, and Clausura 2006. [Data: Infobox football biography 2 (1)]

'''Aaron James Ramsey''' (born 26 December 1990)<ref>{{cite news |title=Official Player Profile |url=http://www.cardiffcityfc.premiumtv.co.uk/page/ProfilesDetail/0,,10335~39793,00.html |publisher=cardiffcityfc.co.uk |date=2007-08-22 |accessdate=2007-08-22 }}</ref> is a [[Wales|Welsh]] international [[association football|footballer]], who plays as an attacking [[central midfielder]] for [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]], but can also play on either wing or at fullback.

==Career==
===Cardiff City===
After impressing in an [[Urdd Gobaith Cymru|Urdd]] tournament as a youngster he signed for [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]], who beat off competition from [[Newcastle United F.C.|Newcastle United]], as a schoolboy at the age of eight, working his way through the club's youth system.  After a few more years he eventually made his Cardiff City debut in the last home game of the [[The Football League 2006-07|2006–07 Championship season]], coming on to replace [[Paul Parry]] in the final minute of the 1–0 defeat to [[Hull City A.F.C.|Hull City]] on 28 April 2007. In doing so, Ramsey became the youngest player to ever play for Cardiff City, aged just 16 years and 124 days,<ref>{{cite news |title=Jones hails record-breaker Ramsey |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/c/cardiff_city/6607983.stm |publisher=BBC Sport |date=2007-04-30 |accessdate=2007-04-30 }}</ref> beating the previous record holder [[John Toshack]]. In June 2007, Cardiff City turned down a bid of over £1m for Ramsey from a [[London]]-based Premier League club.<ref>{{cite news |title=Cardiff reject £1m bid for Ramsey |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/c/cardiff_city/6244228.stm |publisher=BBC Sport |date=2007-06-27 |accessdate=2007-06-27 }}</ref> The club was not named, but it was widely believed that they continued to watch Ramsey at every available opportunity during the 2007–08 season. Cardiff also turned down a £1m offer, although the deal was to start with a payment of £200,000 and rise depending on his future achievements, from [[Everton F.C.|Everton]].

"Rambo", as he is known to Cardiff City fans, made his first league appearance of the 2007–08 season on 6 October, when he came on as a late substitute for [[Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink]] in the 2–1 home win over [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]]. Ramsey signed his first professional contract in December 2007<ref>[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/c/cardiff_city/7165918.stm "Ramsey pens professional contract"] [[BBC Sport]] Retrieved on 11 February 2008</ref> and went on to make his first full professional start for Cardiff on 5 January in the [[FA Cup]] against non-league side [[Chasetown F.C.|Chasetown]] replacing the suspended [[Stephen McPhail]]. An impressive performance from Ramsey saw him head in the second Cardiff goal as they went on to win 3–1.<ref>{{cite news |title=Chasetown 1-3 Cardiff |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/fa_cup/7163953.stm |publisher=BBC Sport |date=2008-01-05 |accessdate=2008-01-05 }}</ref> Due to his performance against Chasetown, Ramsey was nominated for the Player Of The Round award, eventually losing out to [[Coventry City F.C.|Coventry's]] [[Michael Mifsud]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Mifsud takes the vote |url=http://www.thefa.com/TheFACup/TheFACup/NewsAndFeatures/Postings/2008/01/Potr_MifsudThirdRound.htm |publisher=TheFA.com |date=2008-01-14 |accessdate=2008-01-14 }}</ref> On 26 April, he scored his first league goal in a 3-3 draw against [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]].<ref>[http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/sport/football/article4103536.ece Factfile: Aaron Ramsey]</ref> He went on to make his first career league start three weeks later in a 3–1 win over [[Queens Park Rangers F.C.|Queens Park Rangers]] and began to establish himself in the first team making several more starts in the Cardiff side.
