The '''Sportfreunde Stuttgart''' is a [[Germany|German]] [[football (soccer)|football]] [[:Category:German football clubs|club]] from the city of [[Stuttgart]], [[Baden-Württemberg]].

==History==
===1874 to 1945===
The club was formed, as a gymnastics club, on 18 April 1874, under the name of '''Turnverein Heslach'''.<ref>[http://www.sportfreunde-stuttgart.de/sportfreunde.php?ID=12 Spfr. Stuttgart website - Club history] {{de icon}}, accessed: 22 March 2009</ref> In June 1889, the club changed its name to '''Turnverein Karlsvorstadt'''.

On 20 June 1896, a separate football club, the '''Fußballclub Karlsvorstadt''', was formed. In 1900, it merged with two other clubs, the ''F.C. Adler'' and the ''F.C. Askania'' to form the '''Stuttgarter Sportfreunde 1896'''.

The club was a founding member of the [[Südkreis-Liga]] in 1908, then the highest level of play in the Baden-Württemberg region.<ref>[http://www.fussball-historie.de/Sueddeutschland/Sued1909.html Southern German league tables 1908-09] {{de icon}} Hirschis Fussball Archiv, accessed: 22 March 2009</ref> The club existed there as a mid-table side but, in 1912-13, after a league reduction from 13 to eight clubs the previous season, it came last and was relegated. In this era, the club had [[Eugen Kipp]] in its ranks, who played 18 times for Germany between 1908 and 1913, 16 of those as a ''Sportfreunde'' player.<ref>''kicker Almanach 1990'' {{de icon}} Yearbook of German football, publisher: [[Kicker (sports magazine)|kicker]], published: 1989, page: 88, accessed: 22 March 2009</ref>

After the [[First World War]], on 2 August 1919, Turnverein Karlsvorstadt and Stuttgarter Sportfreunde 1896 merged to form the current club, '''Stuttgarter Sportfreunde 1896'''. The team made a return to the highest league in the region, which was now the [[Kreisliga Württemberg]] and came third in 1919-20.

''Sportfreundes'' most successful season came in 1921-22. It took out the title in its local division, the Kreisliga Württemberg having been split into two regional divisions. In the Württemberg-final, it managed to defeat [[Stuttgarter Kickers]] 1-0 and 3-2.<ref>[http://www.fussball-historie.de/Sueddeutschland/Wuerttemberg1922.html Württemberg league tables 1921-22] {{de icon}} Hirschis Fussball Archiv, accessed: 22 March 2009</ref> From there, it advanced to the Württemberg-Baden championship, where it overcame [[Karlsruher FV]] 1-0 and 1-1. Advancing to the [[Southern German football championship|Southern German championship]], it lost 0-1 to [[Borussia Neunkirchen]] in the semi-finals.<ref>[http://www.fussball-historie.de/Sueddeutschland/Sued1922.html Southern German league tables 1921-22] {{de icon}} Hirschis Fussball Archiv, accessed: 22 March 2009</ref>

The next season saw the club missing out on qualification for the new [[Bezirksliga Württemberg-Baden]] and ''Sportfreunde'' was relegated to the second tier, where it stayed until 1926, when it earned promotion. The club managed to survive for four seasons in the Bezirksliga but was relegated once more in 1930. A fifth place in 1927-28 was its best result. 

The club recovered from its temporary decline and, in 1933, it qualified for the [[Gauliga Württemberg]], the new highest level of play in the region. It belonged to this league for the duration of its existence, until 1945. It this time, the club produced good results and finished runners-up in the league three times, never quite making it to the German championship finals.

===1945 to 2008===
With the resumption of football in Germany after the [[Second World War]], ''Sportfreunde'' was grouped in the tier-two [[Landesliga Württemberg]], which it won in 1946-47. This earned the club promotion to the [[Oberliga Süd (1945-63)|Oberliga Süd]], where it played for one last season in the top flight. The club came a distant last in the league in 1947-48, conceding 100 goals and being relegated back to the Landesliga. ''Sportfreunde'' became a mid-table side in this league, failing to qualify for the new [[2nd Oberliga Süd]] in 1950 and thereby dropping another level to what was now the tier-three [[Amateurliga Württemberg]].

The team continued to struggle against relegation but in 1954, it dropped down another level. The club made a brief recovery, earning promotion to the [[Amateurliga Nordwürttemberg]] in 1961 but being relegated again in 1964. After this, ''Sportfreunde'' never reached the higher levels of Württemberg football agin, descending to the lower amateur leagues instead, to the extend that the new millennium saw it playing tier-eight football.

On 9 April 1987, the club changed its name to '''Sportfreunde Stuttgart 1874'''.

===Current===
The club was playing in the Kreisliga A Stutgart-Group 3 (IX) in 2008-09, struggling against relegation once more, finishing second-last and having to step down one level.<ref>[http://ergebnisdienst.fussball.de/landesverband/wuerttemberg/0809/013/052/101/350162/tabelle/ Kreisliga A Stutgart-Group 3 table 2008-09] Fussball.de, accessed: 22 March 2009</ref>

### Footballer of the Year

The Estonian Footballer of the Year award has been presented annually since 1992, recognizing the best Estonian footballer each year. Over the years, several players have stood out, with Mart Poom being the most decorated winner, having claimed the title six times [Data: Footballer of the Year (1993, 1994, 1997, 1998, 2000, 2003)].

Here’s a summary of the winners from 1992 to 2008:

- **1992**: Urmas Hepner played for Kumu Kuusankoski (Finland) and Kotkan Työväen Palloilijat (KTP, Finland).
- **1993**: Mart Poom represented FC Flora (Estonia) and FC Wil (Switzerland).
- **1994**: Mart Poom continued his success, playing for FC Wil (Switzerland) and Portsmouth (England).
- **1995**: Martin Reim was recognized while playing for FC Flora (Estonia).
- **1996**: Marek Lemsalu was honored during his time at 1. FSV Mainz 05 (Germany).
- **1997**: Mart Poom was again the recipient, this time representing Derby County (England).
- **1998**: Mart Poom retained his title with Derby County (England).
- **1999**: Andres Oper was awarded the title while playing for FC Flora (Estonia) and AaB Fodbold (Denmark).
- **2000**: Mart Poom secured another win with Derby County (England).
- **2001**: Indrek Zelinski was recognized for his performances with FC Flora (Estonia) and AaB Fodbold (Denmark).
- **2002**: Andres Oper and Raio Piiroja shared the honor; Andres Oper played for AaB Fodbold (Denmark) and Raio Piiroja for FC Flora (Estonia).

## Simon Ainge: Career Overview

Simon Ainge is an English footballer who primarily plays as a central defender. Born on February 18, 1988, in Shipley, West Yorkshire, England, Ainge began his professional career with Bradford City A.F.C., a Football League Two club. Standing at 1.85 meters tall, Ainge has had a varied career, playing for several clubs and spending time on loan.

### Early Career and Breakthrough

Ainge started his career in the youth system of Bradford City A.F.C., where he won a senior contract in March 2006. His breakthrough came in the 2006-07 season when he made his debut for Bradford City in a 2-1 defeat to Scunthorpe United in the Football League Trophy on October 17, 2006. He then made his first league appearance and his first start in an FA Cup match against Crewe Alexandra on November 4, 2006. During this period, Ainge received praise from his manager, Colin Todd, a former England international center back.

### Loan Spells and Development

Despite initial promise, Ainge's opportunities at Bradford City were limited in the following seasons. In 2007, he was given a trial at Scunthorpe United but returned to Bradford. In January 2008, he joined Halifax Town A.F.C. on loan for the remainder of the season. At Halifax, Ainge played 12 games, helping the team avoid relegation from the Conference by just one point. However, he received his first red card during a match against Burton Albion on April 15, 2008.

### Return to Bradford and Further Loan

After his loan spell at Halifax, Ainge returned to Bradford City and made his first start in over a year in a 1-1 draw with Luton Town on October 4, 2008. Despite this return, Ainge's opportunities remained limited, and he joined Cambridge United F.C. on loan in March 2009 for the final two months of the season.

### Current Club

As of the latest update, Simon Ainge plays for Guiseley A.F.C., a Northern Premier League Premier Division side. This move represents a continuation of his journey through various levels of English football.

The '''1970 FIFA World Cup''', the ninth staging of the World Cup, was held in [[Mexico]], from 31 May to 21 June. Mexico was chosen as [[FIFA World Cup hosts#1970 FIFA World Cup|hosts]] by [[FIFA]] in October 1964. The 1970 tournament was the first World Cup hosted in [[North America]], and the first held outside [[South America]] and [[Europe]]. In a match-up of two-time World Cup champions, the final was won by [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]], who beat [[Italy national football team|Italy]] 4–1. With their third World Cup triumph, Brazil were allowed to keep the [[Jules Rimet Trophy]] permanently.

The Brazilian team, featuring the likes of [[Pelé]] (who was in his fourth and final World Cup), [[Carlos Alberto Torres|Carlos Alberto]], [[Clodoaldo]], [[Gérson]], [[Jairzinho]], [[Roberto Rivelino|Rivelino]], and [[Tostão]], is usually regarded as the greatest attacking World Cup team ever. This tournament saw the return of free-flowing, attacking play after the physical battles of [[1962 FIFA World Cup|1962]] and [[1966 FIFA World Cup|1966]], and is still considered by many fans to be the finest World Cup in history.

==Qualification==
{{main|1970 FIFA World Cup qualification}}
[[Image:1970 world cup.png|thumb|right|350px|Qualifying countries]]
A total of 75 teams entered the qualifying tournament. Those who failed to qualify included France, Portugal, Hungary, Argentina and Spain. Meanwhile, Morocco became the first African nation to reach the World Cup finals since the Second World War.

==Summary==
===First Round===
The 1970 World Cup is now remembered as a classic – but, as usual, the tournament was preceded by disputes over the organisation of the event. This World Cup was the first one to be televised in colour. However, to fit into the European viewing schedules, some matches kicked off at noon. This was an unpopular decision with many players and managers because of the intense heat in Mexico at that time of day.
[[Image:1970Telstar.jpg|thumb|left|''[[Adidas Telstar|Telstar]]'', the official 1970 FIFA World Cup ball.]]
The format of the competition stayed the same as [[1966 FIFA World Cup|1966]]: 16 teams qualified, divided into four groups of four playing each other once in a [[round-robin tournament]] format. There were no seeds, instead the organizers formed geographical ‘sections’ from which the four groups were drawn in [[Mexico City]], on 10 January 1970.<ref>[http://www.fifa.com/mm/document/fifafacts/mcwc/ip-201_10e_fwcdraw-history_8842.pdf History of the World Cup Final Draw]</ref> The top two teams in each group advanced to the quarter-finals. However, for the first time in the World Cup finals, teams level on points at the end of the group stage were separated by [[goal difference]] (replacing play-offs and goal average) and where two or more teams had equal goal difference, by the drawing of lots. If a quarter-final or semi-final match resulted in a draw after extra time the referee would have drawn the name of the team to progress to the next round out of a hat.

Controversy surrounded the World Cup before a ball was even kicked. For England, the build-up to the tournament took a bizarre turn when their captain was accused of theft. While England were in Colombia for a pre-tournament friendly, [[Bobby Moore]] was arrested for allegedly stealing a bracelet from a jeweller's shop. He was released on bail to allow him to appear in the World Cup finals, and the charges were later quietly dropped.

In Group 1, hosts Mexico lived up to the expectations of an entire nation by advancing along with the Soviet Union.
Group 2 of the opening round produced just six goals in six games as [[Uruguay national football team|Uruguay]], reigning South America champions, and the reigning European champions, [[Italy national football team|Italy]], prevail over [[Sweden national football team|Sweden]] and surprise qualifier [[Israel national football team|Israel]] after a series of dull, uninspired games. [[Italy national football team|Italy]] would, however, show the true measure of its talent in the knock-out phase.

The first great moments of this memorable World Cup happened in Group 3, where two-time former World champion [[Brazil national football team|Brazil]] were pooled with the current world champions [[England national football team|England]] and solid European sides [[Czechoslovakia national football team|Czechoslovakia]] and [[Romania national football team|Romania]]. In the rematch of the 1962 World Cup final, they fell behind early in their opening game against Czechoslovakia, but fought back strongly and eventually won 4–1. [[Pelé]] scored one of their goals, but a goal attempt that in which Pelé audaciously attempted to lob a shot over Czechoslovak goalkeeper [[Ivo Viktor]] from the halfway line, missed the goal by a whisker. The "Clash of the Champions" between Brazil and England lived up to all expectations. The match is best remembered for a Pelé near-miss. His powerful close-range downward header was kept out by an amazing save from [[Gordon Banks]], who somehow managed to get down to the ball and flick it upwards and over the bar. In the end, a single Jairzinho goal was enough to win the game for Brazil. Romania ran Brazil close in their third game, but were finally beaten 3–2. England joined Brazil with two 1–0 victories over Romania and Czechoslovakia.
[[Image:WorldCup1970lposter.jpg|thumb|right|250px|The official 1970 FIFA World Cup poster.]]
In Group 4, [[Peru national football team|Peru]] and its attacking style created a sensation by beating established side [[Bulgaria national football team|Bulgaria]] 3–2 after trailing 0–2 at halftime. Morocco also got off to a bright start, taking the lead against West Germany in their first match, but the Germans came back to win 2–1. West Germany also went behind against Bulgaria in their second match, but a Gerd Muller hat-trick helped them fight back to win 5–2. Muller hit another hat-trick in the Germans' last group game, scoring all their goals in a 3–1 win over Peru. In the end, Peru eventually advanced along with [[West Germany national football team|West Germany]] after scoring three times in 11 second-half minutes to beat Morocco 3–0.

===Quarterfinals, Semifinals, and third-place match===
The quarter-finals saw a transformed Italy prevail 4–1 over Mexico after trailing 0–1. The host took the lead against Italy with a Jose Gonzales goal, but his team-mate Gustavo Pena equalised with an own goal before half-time. Italy then took over, and dominated the second half. Two goals from Luigi Riva and one from Gianni Rivera saw them go through 4–1. In Guadalajara, Peru's World Cup adventure ended in the quarter-finals, where they lost 4–2 to Brazil after an entertaining and dramatic match between two equally attacking teams.

The game between Uruguay and the Soviet Union was goalless until five minutes from the end of extra time, when Victor Esparrago struck to send the South Americans through. The last quarter-final, a rematch of the 1966 World Cup final between England and West Germany, produced one of the great matches of World Cup history. England suffered a serious blow before the game, when their great goalkeeper Gordon Banks was taken ill with food poisoning. ## Overview of the 1970 FIFA World Cup

The **1970 FIFA World Cup**, officially known as the **Mexico 70**, was held in Mexico from **May 31** to **June 21, 1970**. It marked the first World Cup hosted in North America and the first outside of South America and Europe. The tournament featured 16 teams divided into four groups, with the top two teams from each group advancing to the knockout stages. Brazil emerged victorious, defeating Italy 4–1 in the final, securing their third World Cup title and earning the right to keep the Jules Rimet Trophy permanently.

### Key Highlights

- **Host Country**: Mexico
- **Dates**: May 31 – June 21, 1970
- **Number of Teams**: 16
- **Champion**: Brazil
- **Runner-Up**: Italy
- **Third Place**: West Germany
- **Fourth Place**: Uruguay
- **Top Scorer**: Gerd Müller (Germany) with 10 goals

## Qualification Process

A total of 75 teams participated in the qualification process. Notable absentees included France, Portugal, Hungary, Argentina, and Spain. Morocco made history by becoming the first African nation to reach the World Cup finals since the Second World War.

## Tournament Format and Organization

The tournament followed the same format as the 1966 World Cup, with 16 teams divided into four groups of four. Each group played in a round-robin format, and the top two teams advanced to the quarter-finals. A new rule introduced in 1970 was the use of goal difference to separate teams level on points at the end of the group stage, replacing previous methods like play-offs and goal average.

### Controversies and Incidents

Before the tournament began, there were several controversies:
- **England's Captain Arrested**: Bobby Moore, England's captain, was arrested in Colombia for allegedly stealing a bracelet. He was released on bail and the charges were later dropped.
- **Heat and Scheduling Issues**: Matches were scheduled to kick off at noon to fit into European viewing schedules, causing discomfort due to the intense heat in Mexico.

## Group Stage Performances

### Group 1
- **Teams**: Mexico, Soviet Union, El Salvador, and Israel
- **Advancing Teams**: Mexico and Soviet Union

### Group 2
- **Teams**: Uruguay, Italy, Sweden, and Israel
- **Advancing Teams**: Uruguay and Italy
- **Notable Match**: Italy showed its true talent in the knockout phase despite a series of dull, uninspired games during the group stage.

### Group 3
- **Teams**: Brazil, England, Czechoslovakia, and Romania
- **Advancing Teams**: Brazil and England
- **Notable Matches**:
  - **Brazil vs. Czechoslovakia**: Brazil won 4–1, with Pelé scoring one goal.
  - **Brazil vs. England**: Known as the "Clash of the Champions," this match is remembered for Pelé's near-miss header saved by Gordon Banks. Brazil won 1–0 with a goal from Jairzinho.
  - **England vs. Romania**: England won 1–0.
  - **England vs. Czechoslovakia**: England won 1–0.

### Group 4
- **Teams**: Peru, West Germany, Bulgaria, and Morocco
- **Advancing Teams**: Peru and West Germany
- **Notable Matches**:
  - **Peru vs. Bulgaria**: Peru won 3–2 after trailing 0–2 at halftime.
  - **Morocco vs. West Germany**: West Germany won 2–1.
  - **West Germany vs. Bulgaria**: West Germany won 5–2 with a hat-trick from Gerd Müller.
  - **West Germany vs. Peru**: West Germany won 3–1 with another hat-trick from Gerd Müller.

## Knockout Stages

### Quarter-Finals
- **Italy vs. Mexico**: Italy won 4–1.
- **Peru vs. Brazil**: Brazil won 4–2.
- **Uruguay vs. Soviet Union**: Uruguay won 1–0 in extra time.
- **England vs. West Germany**: West Germany won 2–1 after coming back from a 2–0 deficit.

### Semi-Finals
- **Brazil vs. Uruguay**: Brazil won 3–1.
- **Italy vs. West Germany**: Italy won 4–3 after extra time.

### Third-Place Match
- **West Germany vs. Uruguay**: West Germany won 1–0.

### Final
- **Brazil vs. Italy**: Brazil won 4–1, securing their third World Cup title.

## Conclusion

The 1970 FIFA World Cup is often regarded as one of the finest tournaments in history, characterized by free-flowing, attacking play and memorable moments. The Brazilian team, featuring legends like Pelé, Carlos Alberto, and Jairzinho, is widely considered the greatest attacking World Cup team ever. This tournament marked a significant milestone in the history of international football, setting a high standard for future World Cups.

'''Wellington Phoenix FC''' is a professional [[Association football|football]] club based in [[Wellington]], [[New Zealand]], competing in the [[Australia]]n [[A-League]]. The club replaced the now-defunct [[New Zealand Knights F.C.|New Zealand Knights]] in the [[A-League 2007-08|2007-08 season]].

==History==
During the later stages of the [[A-League 2006-07|2006-07 season]], the [[Football Federation of Australia]] (FFA) removed the [[New Zealand Knights F.C.|New Zealand Knight's]] (NZK) A-League licence due to club's financial and administrative problems and poor on-field performance. After the resignation of the NZK board, FFA transferred the licence to New Zealand Soccer (NZS; now [[New Zealand Football]]), which administered the club for the rest of the season before its subsequent dissolution. 

FFA then provided NZS a provisional A-League licence to sub-let to a suitable New Zealand team to enter the A-League 2007-08 season. The FFA provided an application deadline to NZS, which was subsequently delayed to give more time for potential applicants in New Zealand to apply along with NZS support. 

While NZS was given a chance to apply with a new sub-licencee, a [[Townsville, Queensland|Townsville]]-based consortium, Tropical Football Australia (TFA) also expressed interest and prepared an A-league application to replace the place previously held by the Knights.<ref>[http://tvnz.co.nz/view/page/410965/1023055 Shock! A-League decision delayed], [[Television New Zealand|TVNZ]], 14 March 2007</ref> However, TFA eventually pulled out with the understanding of the FFA's preference to retain a New Zealand team for the league. TFA later resubmitted its bid in the following year as a potential A-League expansion franchise under the name of "Northern Thunder FC", which was later changed to "[[North Queensland Thunder]]"<ref>Fink, Jesse: [http://www.foxsports.com.au/story/0,8659,21407148-5000940,00.html Kiwis alive as Townsville pulls pin], [[Fox Sports (Australia)]], 28 March 2007</ref>, however this bid died after expansion for the [[A-League 2007-08|2007-08 season]] was cancelled. 

After much delay, the final money amount needed for the final application came from Wellington property businessman [[Terry Serepisos]] in the last moments of the bid giving much relief to the New Zealand football fans. Serepisos, the club's majority owner and chairman, provided [[New Zealand Dollar|NZD]] $1,000,000{{Fact|date=August 2007}} to ensure the beginnings of a new New Zealand franchise and a continuation of New Zealand's participation in the A-League. FFA finalised a three-year A-League licence to [[New Zealand Football]] who then sub-let the licence to the Wellington-based franchise.<ref>{{cite web
 |url=http://www.centurycity.co.nz/press_release.html
 |title=Century City Developments and Century City Football
 |publisher=Century City Developments
 |date=19 March 2007
 |accessdate=2007-03-25}}</ref> The Wellington franchise was confirmed on 19 March 2007.

The name for the new club was picked from a shortlist of six, pruned from 250 names suggested by the public, and was  announced on 28 March 2007.<ref>
[http://www.a-league.com.au/default.aspx?s=newsdisplay&id=7283&pageid=11 NZ franchise for A-League.]</ref><ref>{{cite news
 |url=http://www.news.com.au/heraldsn/story/0,21985,21463845-2883,00.html
 |title=NZ Phoenix to rise in A League
 |date=2007-03-28|publisher=[[News Corporation|News.com.au]]

# Wellington Phoenix FC Overview

Wellington Phoenix FC is a professional football club based in Wellington, New Zealand, competing in the Australian A-League. The club was established in 2007, replacing the defunct New Zealand Knights F.C. in the A-League. The Phoenix plays its home games at Westpac Stadium, which has a capacity of 34,500 spectators. Terry Serepisos is the majority owner and chairman, while Ricki Herbert serves as the manager. The club's colors are black and yellow, reflecting the traditional colors of Wellington, and the team's nickname includes "Phoenix" and "The Nix."

## History

### Formation and Early Challenges

During the 2006-07 season, the Football Federation of Australia (FFA) removed the A-League license from the New Zealand Knights due to financial and administrative issues, as well as poor on-field performance. This led to the dissolution of the Knights and the transfer of the license to New Zealand Soccer (now New Zealand Football). FFA then provided a provisional A-League license to New Zealand Soccer, which was intended to be sub-leased to a suitable New Zealand team.

A consortium from Townsville, Queensland, known as Tropical Football Australia (TFA), initially showed interest in acquiring the license but eventually withdrew, allowing the focus to remain on retaining a New Zealand team in the A-League. Wellington businessman Terry Serepisos stepped in at the last moment, providing NZD $1,000,000 to secure the club's formation. On March 19, 2007, the Wellington franchise was officially confirmed.

### Naming and Sponsorship

The club's name, "Wellington Phoenix," was chosen from a shortlist of six names, selected from over 250 suggestions made by the public. The name was announced on March 28, 2007, symbolizing a fresh start and the strong support from Wellington fans. In November 2007, Sony NZ Ltd became the team's principal sponsor, further solidifying the club's presence in the A-League.

### International Implications

Despite the club's success, there were concerns regarding its continued participation in the A-League due to AFC criteria. AFC President Mohammed Bin Hammam had stated that the Wellington team would need to move to Australia or disband by 2011. However, FIFA President Sepp Blatter clarified that the decision would ultimately lie with the FIFA Executive Committee, indicating that the club could continue playing in the A-League if both the Australian and New Zealand associations agreed.

## Seasons and Performance

### Season Highlights

The club has participated in several A-League seasons since its inception. Each season has been documented separately, highlighting the team's performance, key players, and significant events. For instance, the 2007-08 season marked the club's debut in the A-League, while subsequent seasons have seen varying levels of success and challenges.

## Club Crest and Colours

### Kit Design

The club's official colors are black and yellow, with the badge featuring a phoenix rising above a shield. Initially, the kit design was constrained by Reebok's requirements, leading to a predominantly black strip with yellow and white trim for the first two seasons. However, starting from the 2009-10 season, the club adopted a kit with yellow and black vertical stripes, aligning with fan preferences.

The away kit features black sleeves with yellow trim on a white background, with white shorts and socks. The team's sponsors included Sony on the front of the kit and Wellington Beds on the sleeve.

## Current Squad

### Key Players

As of the latest update, the squad includes notable players such as Mark Paston (GK), Manny Muscat (DF), Tony Lochhead (DF), Jonathan McKain (DF), Diego Walsh (MF), Tim Brown (MF), Leo Bertos (MF), and Paul Ifill (FW). These players contribute to the team's overall performance and strive to achieve success in the A-League.

In summary, Wellington Phoenix FC has established itself as a prominent football club in New Zealand, navigating through various challenges and achieving significant milestones in its journey within the A-League.

# Introduction and Overview

The **FIFA Club World Cup** is an annual international football competition organized by FIFA, featuring the champion clubs from each of the six continental confederations. Originally established in 2000, the tournament aims to bring together the best club teams globally, replacing the former Intercontinental Cup. Since 2007, the champions of Oceania have had to qualify through a playoff against the champion club of the host country. The competition has seen various venues, including Brazil, Japan, and the United Arab Emirates, with the latest editions planned for Abu Dhabi.

## Historical Context and Evolution

The inaugural tournament took place in Brazil in January 2000. Following this, plans for subsequent tournaments faced several setbacks due to financial issues, leading to a gap until 2005 when the competition was relaunched in Japan. In 2006, the tournament was officially renamed as the FIFA Club World Cup. Over the years, the structure and prize money have evolved, with the reintroduction of the fifth-place match in 2008 and an increase in total prize money to $16.5 million.

## Champions and Notable Performances

Since its inception, the FIFA Club World Cup has seen several notable performances and champions. Here’s a summary of the champions and some key details:

- **2000**: Corinthians (Brazil) defeated Vasco da Gama (Brazil) in a penalty shootout after a 0-0 draw.
- **2005**: São Paulo (Brazil) won against Liverpool (England) with a score of 1-0.
- **2006**: Internacional (Brazil) beat Barcelona (Spain) with a score of 1-0.
- **2007**: A.C. Milan (Italy) triumphed over Boca Juniors (Argentina) with a score of 4-2.
- **2008**: Manchester United (England) defeated LDU Quito (Ecuador) with a score of 1-0.

The Egyptian club Al-Ahly holds the record for the most appearances in the competition, having participated in three out of the five tournaments held (2005, 2006, and 2008).

## Honors and Awards

Each year, the FIFA Club World Cup recognizes outstanding individual and team performances through various awards:

- **Golden Ball**: Awarded to the best player of the tournament.
- **Silver Ball**: Second-best player.
- **Bronze Ball**: Third-best player.
- **Top Goalscorer**: Player with the highest number of goals.
- **Fair Play Award**: Given to the team demonstrating the best sportsmanship.
- **Winning Manager**: Recognizes the manager of the winning team.

For instance, in 2000, Edílson of Brazil was named the Golden Ball winner, while Romário was both the Bronze Ball recipient and the Top Goalscorer. In 2005, R. Ceni of Brazil received the Golden Ball award, and Liverpool was honored with the Fair Play Award.

## Future Prospects

With the 2009 and 2010 events scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi, the FIFA Club World Cup continues to grow in stature and importance within the global football calendar. The tournament serves as a platform for showcasing the best club teams worldwide and fostering international competition and camaraderie among football clubs.

# Early Life and Background

Rhan Hooper, born on January 9, 1988, in Charleville, Queensland, is an Indigenous Australian (Murri) footballer. His ancestry traces back to the Kooma tribe, and he grew up in Cunnamulla and Ipswich, Queensland. Hooper attended Bundamba State Secondary College during his teenage years. He was first introduced to Australian rules football while living in Melbourne, where he played with the Dandenong Stingrays and later returned to Ipswich to play for the Ipswich Eagles. His exceptional speed and tackling abilities caught the attention of Brisbane Lions talent scouts, leading to his recruitment.

# AFL Career

## Early AFL Years

Hooper was selected by the Brisbane Lions in the 2005 National Draft as the 41st overall pick. He quickly broke into senior AFL level, making his debut in the 2006 NAB Cup. In his first game against Essendon, he showcased his blistering pace and strong tackling skills, earning 7 tackles and scoring a goal. Despite initial success, Hooper faced challenges with his commitment to the sport. In late January 2007, the Lions announced they had stopped paying him due to a lack of enthusiasm for the work required to be a professional athlete. However, he returned to the team in June 2007 with a renewed commitment.

## Notable Performances and Challenges

Throughout the 2007 season, Hooper demonstrated his potential with several standout performances. He received a nomination for the 2007 AFL Army Award for a match-saving tackle against Richmond in Round 10. He also contributed crucially with 5 tackles against Melbourne in Round 15 and scored a bag of 4 goals against Carlton in Round 16. However, his career was marred by disciplinary issues. In Round 19, he was suspended for striking Rick Ladson of the Hawthorn Hawks, and this suspension was extended to three matches after he contested the original two-match ban.

## Suspension and Relocation

In December 2008, Hooper was suspended by the Brisbane Lions for 58 days for breaching his playing contract, including failing to attend pre-season training sessions. This was followed by a $40,000 fine in early 2009 for multiple breaches, including a second failure to attend training. Despite these issues, he was delisted by the Brisbane Lions at the end of the 2009 season, but was subsequently drafted by Hawthorn with the 58th overall pick in the 2009 National Draft.

# Summary

Rhan Hooper's AFL career has been marked by both significant achievements and notable challenges. His exceptional physical attributes and tackling skills have made him a valuable asset, but his inconsistent commitment to the sport has led to disciplinary actions and setbacks. Despite these hurdles, Hooper continues to play for the Hawthorn Football Club, showcasing his potential and resilience in the highly competitive world of Australian rules football.

'''Jerzy "Jurek" Dudek''' ({{IPA-pol|ˈjɛʐɨ ˈdudɛk}});  born 23 March 1973 in [[Rybnik]]) is a [[Poland|Polish]] [[Association football|football]]er who plays for [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] in ''[[La Liga]]'', as a [[Goalkeeper (association football)|goalkeeper]].

With an obscure career in his country, he went on to have successful spells in [[Netherlands|Holland]] and [[England]], winning the [[UEFA Champions League]] with [[Liverpool F.C.]] in 2005. Already well into his 30's, he still moved to [[Spain]], representing giants [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]], albeit with little impact.

==Club career==
===Early years===
Dudek began playing football at youth level at twelve for Górnik II Knurów. At sixteen, he made his debut in the oldest youth team of Górnik Knurów, before moving to Concordia Knurów in the Polish third division two years later. He set a goalkeeping record of 416 minutes in the third division without conceding a goal. 

After four years at the club, he moved to [[GKS 71 Tychy|Sokół Tychy]], making his debut against [[Legia Warsaw]]. He only played fifteen games before moving to Holland.

===Feyenoord===
Dudek left Poland in 1996 to join [[Feyenoord|Feyenoord Rotterdam]], but had to wait a year before he made his debut, then played 140 consecutive games for the club. He won his first trophy in 1998–99, along with the [[Johan Cruijff Shield|Dutch Super Cup]] later that year after defeating [[AFC Ajax|Ajax Amsterdam]]. 

Dudek was named the ''Dutch Goalkeeper Of The Year'', becoming the first foreign player to win the award, which he would retain the following season. He played his final game for Feyenoord on 26 August 2001, against Ajax.

===Liverpool===
Dudek joined Liverpool in late August 2001, and replaced [[Sander Westerveld]] as coach [[Gerard Houllier]]'s first-choice between the sticks. Dudek was a catalyst in Liverpool's 2005 Champions League success, performing a double save against [[A.C. Milan]]'s [[Andriy Shevchenko]] at the end of [[extra time]] in the final, after Liverpool had rallied from a 3–0 deficit to tie the match 3–3. He saved from [[Andrea Pirlo]] and Shevchenko in the ensuing [[penalty shootout]], which Liverpool won 3-2. During the shootout, he attempted to distract the Milan players with the "spaghetti legs" tactic that was used by former Liverpool goalkeeper [[Bruce Grobbelaar]] in the [[1984 European Cup Final]]. Being European Cup winners for the fifth time, Liverpool kept the trophy and received the UEFA badge of honour, and as a tribute to Dudek's heroics, a group of Liverpool fans, the ''Trophy Boyz'', recorded a successful novelty single called '[[Du the Dudek]]'. He became the third Polish footballer after [[Zbigniew Boniek]] (with [[Juventus F.C.|Juventus]]) and fellow goalkeeper [[Józef Młynarczyk]] ([[F.C. He received his second UEFA Goalkeeper of the Year nomination, but lost his starting position to new acquisition [[José Manuel Reina]] the next season, following an arm injury. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1)]

{{0}}1 (0) | pcupdate = 08:39, 11 November 2009 (UTC) | ntupdate = 17:51, 11 February 2009 (UTC) }} '''Gary James Cahill''' (born 19 December 1985 in [[Sheffield]], [[South Yorkshire]]) is an [[England|English]] [[Association football|footballer]] who currently plays for [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]]. ==Club career== Cahill started his career at AFC [[Dronfield]], a Sunday league team in [[Derbyshire]], where he played up until the age of 15, at that point whilst training with Derby County Academy, he signed for Aston Villa's academy. ==Aston Villa== Cahill previously played for [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]] on loan and during his spell, which began in November 2004, he was handed the accolades of Burnley's Player Of The Year and Young Player Of The Year and scored once in the league against Stoke City.{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_div_1/4129757.stm |title=Stoke 0-1 Burnley |publisher=[[BBC]] |date=3 January 2005 |accessdate=13 September 2009}} He made his Villa debut as a substitute in the 5–0 defeat at [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] and impressed on his first start in the local derby game against [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] at [[Villa Park]] on 9 April 2006. Just a week later he scored his first goal; an overhead kick against rivals [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham City]]. Villa went on to win the match 3–1.{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/eng_prem/4890642.stm |title= Aston Villa 3-1 Birmingham |publisher=[[BBC]] |date=16 April 2006 |accessdate=13 September 2009}} Cahill started the following season injured, but took advantage of an injury to [[Martin Laursen]] later in the season to force his way into the Villa team. ### Biography of Gary Cahill

**Gary James Cahill** (born 19 December 1985 in Sheffield, South Yorkshire) is an English footballer who currently plays as a defender for Bolton Wanderers. Standing at 6 feet 2 inches tall, Cahill has had a notable career spanning various clubs and levels of play. He began his professional journey at Aston Villa's academy and has since played for several clubs, including Burnley and Sheffield United on loan, before settling at Bolton Wanderers. Cahill wears the number 5 jersey for his current club [Data: Infobox Football biography (1)].

### Club Career

#### Early Years and Aston Villa

Cahill's early footballing experiences were with AFC Dronfield, a Sunday league team in Derbyshire, where he played until the age of 15. After training with Derby County Academy, he signed with Aston Villa's academy in 2000. His professional debut came in 2004 when he was loaned to Burnley, where he quickly made an impact, earning the titles of Burnley's Player of the Year and Young Player of the Year. During this loan period, he scored once in the league against Stoke City [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); Aston Villa (2)].

At Aston Villa, Cahill made his debut as a substitute in a 5-0 defeat against Manchester United. He then impressed in his first start in a local derby against West Bromwich Albion at Villa Park. Just a week later, he scored his first goal for Villa with an overhead kick against Birmingham City, helping his team secure a 3-1 victory [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); Aston Villa (2)].

#### Loan Spells and Transfer Speculation

In 2007, Cahill was loaned to Sheffield United for three months, where he made his debut in a 3-2 away defeat at Crystal Palace. He scored his first goal for Sheffield United in a 1-0 win against Stoke City. Upon returning to Aston Villa, speculation surrounded his future, with clubs like Birmingham City, Bolton Wanderers, and Turkish club Beşiktaş showing interest [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); Aston Villa (2)].

### Bolton Wanderers

Cahill joined Bolton Wanderers on a three-and-a-half-year deal in January 2008. He made his league debut for Bolton in a 2-0 victory over Reading. Over time, he became a firm favorite at Reebok Stadium and won the "Best Newcomer" award at the end of the season. In July 2008, he was given the number 5 shirt by manager Gary Megson. On 5 October 2008, Cahill scored his first goal for Bolton in a 3-1 victory against West Ham United [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); Bolton Wanderers (3)].

### International Career

Cahill represented England at the under-20 and under-21 levels. He earned his first under-21 cap in the inaugural match at the new Wembley Stadium, partnering Anton Ferdinand in the center of defense. He participated in the 2007 UEFA European Under-21 Football Championship, making one appearance. In 2009, he was called up to the senior England squad for a game against Kazakhstan after Rio Ferdinand's withdrawal. Additionally, he has been linked with a potential call-up to the Republic of Ireland squad due to his eligibility through a grandparent [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); International career (4)].

### Honors

Throughout his career, Cahill has received several awards and honors. At Aston Villa, he won the Goal of the Season award in 2005-06. While on loan at Burnley, he was named Player of the Year and Young Player of the Year for the 2004-05 season. At Bolton Wanderers, he was awarded Players' Player of the Year in 2008-2009 [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); Honours (5)].

This summary provides a comprehensive overview of Gary Cahill's career, highlighting his achievements and contributions to various clubs and teams [Data: Infobox Football biography (1); Aston Villa (2); Bolton Wanderers (3); International career (4); Honours (5)].

He is also heavily involved in the management side of [[horse racing]]. In 2003 Niall received the prestigious [[Beacon Fellowship]] Prize for his contribution to medical and children's charities. ==Early and personal life== Both Quinn's parents are from [[County Tipperary]].{{cite news |first=Declan |last=Bogue |title=What makes world beaters? |newspaper=Gaelic Life |date=4 September 2009}} His father as well as his mother's brothers played [[hurling]] for [[Tipperary GAA|Tipperary]]. He now lives in Tipperary. ==Football playing career== ===Gaelic games=== Niall Quinn played [[Gaelic football]] for [[Robert Emmets GAC]] in Perrystown, Dublin 12 [http://homepage.eircom.net/~pfur/quinn.html Niall Quinn]. He also played underage football and hurling for [[Dublin GAA]] (he played in the 1983 [[All-Ireland Minor Hurling Championship]] Final) and was offered a lucrative contract to play Australian Rules football before settling on a career playing soccer.[http://www.irelandshirts.com/profiles/niallquinnprofile.htm Niall Quinn] He played Gaelic football [http://archives.tcm.ie/irishexaminer/2002/03/07/story24400.asp Irish Examiner - 2002/03/07: Quinn game for Gaelic] for Co. Kildare club [[Eadestown GAA|Eadestown]] after his retirement, winning a junior C county title in 2008.[http://www.leinsterleader.ie/sport/Niall-Quinn-helps-Eadestown-to.4590113.jp Junior C victory] ===Club career=== He played as a youth for Irish club [[Manortown United]], which was based at Greentrees Park, adjacent to Robert Emmets GAC (it not being unusual in Dublin to play two separate codes of football). He signed professional forms with English club [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] in 1983. He scored on his first-team debut against [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] in December 1985, against the mighty pairing of Hanson and Lawrenson earning himself the nickname "Mighty Quinn" and made the headlines on the back page of Sunday World Ireland's biggest selling tabloid- the original plate of which is still in his mother's home, but his form for the rest of that season was decidedly patchy. Prior to being recruited to the Arsenal youth team Quinn played in the 1983 [[All-Ireland Minor Hurling Championship]] final with [[Dublin GAA|Dublin]]. Quinn took time to find form, but by [[1986-87 in English football|1986-87]] had become a regular in the Arsenal side, helping them reach and then win the 1987 [[Football League Cup|League Cup]] final. However, the arrival of fellow centre-forward [[Alan M. Smith|Alan Smith]] that summer forced Quinn out of the Arsenal first team, and he became a fringe player. In all he scored 20 goals in 94 matches for the Gunners. He missed out on a league title winner's medal in 1989 after failing to appear in enough games. [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]] signed Quinn for £800,000 in March 1990. He scored 22 times in his first full season, and he went on to spend six years at the club, scoring 78 goals in 245 appearances; his time at City was hampered by a [[cruciate ligament]] injury in [[1993-94 in English football|1993-94]]. His most notable game for City was 20 April 1991 when he scored early on and saved a [[Dean Saunders]] penalty as City beat [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]] 2-1, relegating Derby in the process.[http://football.guardian.co.uk/theknowledge/story/0,13854,1330963,00.html The Guardian] City goalkeeper [[Tony Coton]] had been sent off before half time for fouling Saunders to concede the penalty. At this time teams rarely, if ever, named goalkeepers as substitutes, so Quinn replaced Coton in goal. Quinn finished his career with a highly successful spell at [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]], joining the north-east club in 1996, although he missed six months of his first season due to a knee injury - similar to the one which ruined his World Cup chances three years earlier. His partnership with striker [[Kevin Phillips (footballer)|Kevin Phillips]] was one of the most prolific in the [[Football League]] and helped the club to promotion to the [[FA Premier League|Premiership]]. Quinn also has the distinction of being the first player to score at Sunderland's [[Stadium of Light]], against Manchester City in 1997. He became a local legend at Sunderland, winning both the Sunderland and North East Sportswriters' Player of the Year awards in 1999 after scoring 21 goals in Sunderland's record-breaking Division One title-winning season. ===International career=== Quinn made his debut for the [[Republic of Ireland national football team|Republic of Ireland]] in 1986, and went on to earn 92 [[cap (football)|caps]] . He retired as his country's all-time scorer with 21 goals; this record was surpassed by [[Robbie Keane]] in October 2004. Quinn played for his country at two [[Football World Cup|World Cups]], in [[Football World Cup 1990|1990]] and [[Football World Cup 2002|2002]]; he missed the [[1994 FIFA World Cup]] because of injury. Quinn was also a member of the Irish squad that participated in the [[1988 European Football Championship]] playing just once, as a substitute in Ireland's 1-0 win over England in Stuttgart. Quinn famously scored the equaliser against the [[Netherlands national football team|Netherlands]] in the [[Football World Cup 1990|1990 World Cup]] which allowed Ireland to progress to the second round of that tournament. In the 2002 tournament, his header set up [[Robbie Keane]]'s late equaliser against [[Germany national football team|Germany]], which was the only goal Germany conceded before the final. ==Song== Niall also had his own song entitled "Niall Quinn's Disco Pants". The song was originally created by Manchester City fans during a night out on a pre-season tour in Penola, Italy. It was 1992. There had been a bust-up with City team-mate Steve McMahon and Quinn had removed his torn and bloodied shirt and was dancing with Rick Holden wearing just a pair of cut-off jeans. He was "hardly aware" that there were a group of hardcore City fans watching and they treated him to "the first performance of the song that will follow me till the end of my career."

# Niall Quinn: A Multi-Faceted Sports Figure

## Early Life and Background

Niall William Quinn, born on October 6, 1966, in Perrystown, Dublin, Ireland, is a former Irish international footballer and current chairman of Sunderland AFC. Known affectionately as "Saint Niall," Quinn has had a significant impact on both football and horse racing. On his first-team debut against Liverpool in December 1985, Quinn scored a goal, earning him the nickname "Mighty Quinn." Despite a strong start, his form remained inconsistent throughout the season.

By the 1986-87 season, Quinn had established himself as a regular in the Arsenal lineup, contributing to the team's success in the 1987 League Cup final. However, the arrival of Alan Smith in 1987 pushed Quinn to the fringes of the first team. Over his five-year stint at Arsenal, Quinn scored 20 goals in 94 matches.

#### Manchester City F.C.

In March 1990, Quinn joined Manchester City F.C. for £800,000. During his first full season, he netted 22 goals, and over six years, he scored 78 goals in 245 appearances. Despite his prolific scoring, Quinn's career at Manchester City was marred by a cruciate ligament injury in 1993-94.

One of Quinn's most memorable performances came on April 20, 1991, when he scored early and saved a penalty kick as City defeated Derby County 2-1, relegating Derby in the process. This match was particularly noteworthy as City's goalkeeper Tony Coton was sent off before halftime, leaving Quinn to take over in goal.

#### Sunderland A.F.C.

Quinn concluded his playing career with Sunderland A.F.C. in 1996, though he missed six months of his first season due to a knee injury. His partnership with Kevin Phillips proved highly effective, helping Sunderland achieve promotion to the Premier League. Quinn holds the distinction of being the first player to score at Sunderland's Stadium of Light, against Manchester City in 1997. He became a local legend at Sunderland, winning both the Sunderland and North East Sportswriters' Player of the Year awards in 1999 after scoring 21 goals in Sunderland's record-breaking Division One title-winning season.

Quinn's most notable international moment occurred in the 1990 World Cup when he scored the equalizer against the Netherlands, enabling Ireland to advance to the second round. In the 2002 World Cup, his header set up Robbie Keane's late equalizer against Germany, marking the only goal Germany conceded before the final.

## Post-Football Career

After retiring from professional football, Quinn has remained active in sports management. He currently serves as the chairman of Sunderland AFC and is heavily involved in the management side of horse racing. Quinn's contributions to various charitable causes have been widely recognized, including the Beacon Fellowship Prize awarded to him in 2003.

## Cultural Impact

Niall Quinn has left an indelible mark on the sporting world, particularly in football. His nickname "Saint Niall" reflects the respect and admiration he garnered from fans and teammates alike. Additionally, Quinn has inspired a song titled "Niall Quinn's Disco Pants," which originated from a night out during a pre-season tour in Penola, Italy, in 1992. The song humorously captures a memorable incident involving Quinn and his Manchester City teammate Steve McMahon.

### Overview of Piyapong Pue-on

Piyapong Pue-on (ปิยะพงษ์ ผิวอ่อน) is a renowned Thai football player who was born on November 14, 1959, in Prachuap Khiri Khan, Thailand. Nicknamed "Tuk," Piyapong is widely recognized as the national football hero of Thailand due to his exceptional skills and numerous achievements both domestically and internationally. He played as a striker and holds the record for being the top scorer for the Thai National Team [Data: Football player infobox (1)].

### Club Career

Piyapong's club career spanned from 1979 to 1997, during which he played for several notable teams:

- **1979-1984**: Royal Thai Air Force FC (Thailand)
- **1984-1986**: Lucky Goldstar Hwangso (South Korea)
- **1986-1989**: Pahang FA (Malaysia)
- **1989-1997**: Royal Thai Air Force FC (Thailand)

During his time with Lucky Goldstar Hwangso in South Korea, Piyapong played a pivotal role in helping the team win the 1985 K-League Championship, scoring 12 goals and providing 6 assists. His performance was particularly noteworthy under the guidance of coach Park Se-Hak, whom he still refers to as "Father" [Data: Football player infobox (1)].

### International Career

Piyapong represented the Thai National Team from 1981 to 1997, amassing a total of 129 caps and scoring 103 goals. Some of his notable international appearances include:

- **June 20, 1981**: Scored 1 goal against Indonesia in the President's Cup held in Seoul, South Korea.
- **November 11, 1981**: Scored 1 goal against Pakistan in the 1981 King's Cup held in Bangkok, Thailand.
- **December 9, 1981**: Scored 2 goals against Malaysia in the 1981 Southeast Asian Games held in Manila, Philippines.
- **April 10, 1983**: Scored 2 goals against Nepal in the Affa Cup.
- **May 29, 1983**: Scored 1 goal against Indonesia in the 1983 Southeast Asian Games held in Singapore.
- **July 5, 1983**: Scored 4 goals against Singapore in a friendly match held in Bangkok, Thailand.
- **November 10, 1983**: Scored 1 goal against South Korea and another against China in the 1984 Summer Olympics qualification matches held in Bangkok, Thailand.
- **December 8, 1985**: Scored 1 goal against Malaysia in the 1985 Southeast Asian Games held in Bangkok, Thailand.
- **September 29, 1986**: Scored 3 goals against Pakistan in the 1986 Asian Games held in Seoul, South Korea.

These performances highlight Piyapong's significant contributions to Thai football and his status as a national hero [Data: International goals (1-35, +more)].

### Post-Retirement Career

After retiring from playing, Piyapong transitioned into coaching. He has been actively involved in coaching since 1997, including roles with the Royal Thai Air Force FC and the Thailand U-18 team. Currently, he serves as the head coach for Nakhon Pathom FC and continues to coach the Thailand U-18 team [Data: Football player infobox (1)].

### Personal Life

Piyapong is married and has a son born in 1985, who works as a model and movie actor. Additionally, Piyapong has appeared in the 2004 film "Kerd Ma Lui" (also known as "Born to Fight" in European titles), further cementing his legacy in Thai culture and sports [Data: Football player infobox (1)].

In summary, Piyapong Pue-on's career is marked by outstanding achievements both as a player and a coach, making him a revered figure in Thai football history.

He had earlier gained first-team experience with 3-month loan spells at [[East Fife F.C.|East Fife]] and then [[Airdrieonians F.C.|Airdrieonians]]. McManus went on to become a first-team regular for Hibs, enjoying his best season in [[2002-03 in Scottish football|2002-03]], when he scored 11 goals finishing top goalscorer at the club. === Dundee === In August 2004, new manager [[Tony Mowbray]] decided McManus would not feature in Hibs first team plans due to his high appearance fee and he was loaned to [[Boston United F.C.|Boston United]]. McManus failed to settle in quiet [[Lincolnshire]] however, and returned north to sign for [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]] in January 2005. The ''Dark Blues'' were struggling in the league though, and despite McManus' goal in a relegation-decider against [[Livingston F.C.|Livingston]], Dundee fell short and were demoted to the [[Scottish Football League First Division|Scottish First Division]]. After the game McManus was photographed lying on the pitch in floods of tears. Financial difficulties at Dundee, resultant from relegation and an earlier spell in administration required them to remove the highest-earners from their wage bill and along with [[Lee Wilkie]], McManus negotiated a release settlement in the summer of 2006. === Falkirk and Dunfermline === He signed for Falkirk in August,{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/f/falkirk/5313068.stm|publisher=BBC Sport website|title=McManus wins contract with Bairns|date=8 September 2006}} however, after playing a largely peripheral role in the first half of the [[2006-07 in Scottish football|2006-07]] season, he was released by the Bairns.{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/f/falkirk/6318517.stm|publisher=BBC Sport website|title=McManus allowed to leave Falkirk|date=31 January 2007}} Four weeks later, McManus signed a short term contract with Dunfermline for the remainder of the current season.{{cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/d/dunfermline_athletic/6382311.stm|title=Dunfermline sign striker McManus|accessdate=1 January 2008}} He instantly became a huge hit with the Dunfermline fans, scoring two goals in six games. In June, he signed a new two-year deal at [[East End Park]] despite interest from at least three other SPL clubs.{{cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/d/dunfermline_athletic/6764895.stm|title=McManus agrees new deal at Pars|accessdate=1 January 2008}} He appeared as a substitute in the [[UEFA Cup]] against BK Hacken FC of Sweden on 30 August 2007 and scored the winning goal on 6 October 2007 against [[Queen of the South F.C.]] === Colorado === In March 2008, McManus was approached by [[Major League Soccer|MLS]] side [[Colorado Rapids]] and offered a trial while the club were playing a number of friendlies in England. McManus played 45 minutes against [[Ipswich Town F.C.|Ipswich Town]]{{citeweb|url=http://www.coloradorapids.com/News/NewsDetails.aspx?NID=pmHDwnmC3FE=#|title= Rapids Record 3-2 Victory over Ipswich in England |accessdate=8 March 2008}} in a pre-season game for the American side and was widely expected to sign for the side.{{cite news|url=http://www.dafc.premiumtv.co.uk/page/News/dugout/0,,10288~1259886,00.html|title=Jim McIntyre on Friday|date=8 March|accessdate=2008|publisher=DAFC.co.uk}}{{cite news|url=http://www.thecourier.co.uk/output/2008/03/08/sportstory11039314t0.asp|title=Three more signings as McIntyre builds his side|date=8 March|accessdate=2008|publisher=The Courier}} After over a week of extensive medicals, McManus eventually signed for the MLS outfit on 28 March 2008.{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/d/dunfermline_athletic/7319957.stm|title=McManus makes a rapid Pars exit|date=28 March|accessdate=2008|publisher=BBC.co.uk}} McManus made his [[Colorado Rapids]] debut on 12 April 2008, coming on as a half-time substitute in the game against [[New England Revolution]]. He scored his first Rapids goal in a 2-1 loss to [[Chicago Fire S.C.|Chicago Fire]] on 26 April 2008. McManus won the Week 9 Sierra Mist Goal of the Week honour for his 40 yard strike against [[C.D. Chivas USA]] on 24 May 2008.{{cite web|url=http://www.coloradorapids.com/News/NewsDetails.aspx?NID=zemT4cZNOAU=|title=McManus Wins MLS Goal of the Week Honors|accessdate=30 May 2008}} Despite being hugely popular with the Rapids fans due to his work-rate and spectacular goals, he was released by the club after refusing to accept a cut in wages. The Rapids had always planned on McManus being with the club for the 2009 campaign as they even printed his image on some of the tickets sent out to season ticket holders. === Derry City === McManus signed for [[FAI League of Ireland|League of Ireland]] club {{fc|Derry City}} on 26 March 2009.http://www.derrycityfc.net/cityweb/Latest/new-signing-announced.html McManus was signed for a second time by [[Stephen Kenny (football)|Stephen Kenny]], who was previously his manager at {{fc|Dunfermline Athletic}}. McManus scored his first competitive goal for Derry City on 16 July 2009, in their [[Europa League]] Second Qualifying Round first leg match away to Latvian side [[Skonto FC]] in a 1-1 draw. He left Derry City and returned to Scotland as a free agent due to an illegal contract scandal whereby Derry City were found to be paying salaries more than the 65% of turnover stipulated by the League rules. McManus began his professional career with Hibernian F.C., where he made his debut in 1999. He gained valuable first-team experience through loan spells at East Fife F.C. and Airdrieonians F.C. The club, formed on 24 February 1910, has been awarded 15 national championship titles (despite winning the Swedish football league 18 times) and 14 national cup titles, making them one of the most successful clubs in Sweden. For this, MFF were awarded the [[Svenska Dagbladet Gold Medal]], as of 2009 the only club to have been so. Malmö FF are currently playing in the highest Swedish league, [[Allsvenskan]], where they have played the majority of the seasons during their existence. However, the following year, 2000, Malmö FF regained their place in Allsvenskan - during this season, [[Zlatan Ibrahimović]] rose to fame and became an important player in their campaign to return to the top league. [http://www2.ifkmalmo.com/?id=xry5rlb056i0zz7rk6819a822cb190wi&pick=716] Malmö FF have in many ways reflected the multi-cultural nature of Malmö. In 1998, midfielder/striker [[Yksel Osmanovski]] became the first Muslim player for Sweden, when Sweden lost 1-0 to [[United States men's national soccer team|USA]]. ==History== {{Unreferenced section|date=April 2009}} Malmö FF, is a Swedish sports club located in [[Malmö]]. It used to have a ladies section, known as ''Malmö FF Dam'' but, in 2007 the ladies section left the organisation and became [[LDB FC Malmö]]. Established on 24 February 1910, it is one of the dominating football clubs in Sweden since modern time. The darkest spot in the history of Malmö FF was its relegation from [[Allsvenskan]] in 1999, for the second time. The root cause of the first relegation in 1933 was Malmö FF’s arch rival [[IFK Malmö]], which had reported that the club was paying its players. Since this was strictly against the sports ethics in the 1930-ies, the [[Swedish Football Association]] decided to relegate Malmö FF from Allsvenskan. A number of Malmö FF’s fans are still indignant about this action taken by [[IFK Malmö]]. In the top area of the shield is a white horizontal field over the three vertical fields. The abbreviation of the club name "MFF" is spelled out with sky blue letters in this field. Another example of a group with similar goals is Rex Scania. Many of the supporter groups work together to create [[Tifo|tifos]] for special occasions such as home and away games against the clubs main rivals Helsingborgs IF and IFK Göteborg. # Overview of Malmö FF

Malmö FF, or Malmö Fotbollförening, is a renowned Swedish professional football club based in Malmö. Founded on February 24, 1910, the club has a rich history and is one of the most successful in Swedish football. Known by their nicknames "Di blåe" (The Blue Ones) and "Himmelsblått" (Sky Blues), Malmö FF has achieved significant milestones, including 15 national championship titles and 14 national cup titles. They are also the only Swedish club to have reached the final of the European Champions Cup, losing to Nottingham Forest in 1979. This achievement earned them the Svenska Dagbladet Gold Medal, a prestigious honor in Swedish sports.

## Historical Achievements

Malmö FF has been a dominant force in Swedish football, particularly during the 1970s when they won five Swedish championships and four Swedish cup titles. Their most recent championship came in 2004, marking their 15th title. Despite winning the Swedish football league 18 times, they have officially been awarded 15 national championship titles due to some historical discrepancies. The club's success is well-documented, and they continue to compete in the highest Swedish league, Allsvenskan.

### Recent History

In 1999, Malmö FF faced a significant setback when they were relegated from Allsvenskan for the first time in 63 seasons. This relegation was due to a report filed by their arch-rivals, IFK Malmö, who accused Malmö FF of paying their players, which was against the rules at the time. However, the club bounced back quickly, regaining their place in Allsvenskan the following year in 2000. During this period, Zlatan Ibrahimović, a young talent, rose to prominence and played a crucial role in their return to the top league. '''Hull City Association Football Club''' is an English [[association football|football]] club based in [[Kingston upon Hull]], [[East Riding of Yorkshire]], founded in 1904. In [[2007-08 in English football|2007–08]] they achieved promotion to the top flight of English football for the first time in their history, by winning the [[Football League Championship|Championship]] [[Football League play-offs|play-off]] final at [[Wembley Stadium]]. They finished the [[2008-09 in English football|2008–09]] season 17th in the [[Premier League]] table, successfully avoiding relegation by one point. The previous highest position Hull City had finished in the English Football League was third in the old [[Football League Second Division|second division]] in [[1909–10 in English football|1909–10]], which they matched in [[2007-08 in English football|2007–08]] when they gained promotion. Their greatest achievement in cup competitions came in [[1930 in association football|1930]], when the team reached the semi-finals of the [[FA Cup]].

Hull play their home games at the [[KC Stadium]]. They previously played at [[Boothferry Park]], but moved to their current home in [[2002 in association football|2002]], with Boothferry Park set for demolition. They traditionally play in black and amber, often with a striped shirt design, hence their nickname of ''The Tigers''. The club's mascot is Roary the Tiger.

== History ==
Hull City Association Football Club was founded in June 1904. For some years previously, attempts had been made to found a football club, but this proved difficult because the city was then dominated by [[rugby league]] teams such as [[Hull F.C.|Hull FC]] and [[Hull Kingston Rovers|Hull KR]].<ref name="1904-1915: The Formative Years">{{cite web

| title = Hull City
| url = http://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Hull_City/Hull_City.htm
| work = Historical Kits| accessdate =2009-09-04}}</ref>  These early matches were played at [[The Boulevard (stadium)|The Boulevard]], the home of rugby league club Hull FC.<ref name="History Of The Tigers">{{cite web
| title = History Of The Tigers
| url = http://www.hullcityafc.premiumtv.co.uk/page/History/0,,10338,00.html
| publisher = Hull City AFC
| accessdate = 2007-06-15}}</ref> On 1 September 1904, Hull's debut match took place against [[Notts County F.C.|Notts County]]; with 6,000 in attendance at The Boulevard, Hull held County to a 2–2 draw.

Hull's first competitive football match was in the FA Cup, but they were eliminated, after a replay, in the preliminary round against [[Stockton F.C.|Stockton]], the score was 7–4 on aggregate.  After disputes with landlords at The Boulevard, Hull City moved to Anlaby Road Cricket Ground.<ref name="1904-1915: The Formative Years"/> After having played 44 friendly fixtures the previous season, Hull City were finally admitted into the [[Football League Second Division]] for the [[1905–06 in English football|1905–06 season]].<ref name="HULL CITY fchd">{{cite web
| title = HULL CITY
| url = http://www.fchd.info/HULLC.HTM
| publisher = Football Club History Database
| accessdate = 2007-06-15}}</ref>  Other teams competing in the league that season included the likes of [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] and [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]], as well as [[Yorkshire]] rivals [[Leeds City F.C.|Leeds City]], [[Bradford City A.F.C.|Bradford City]] and [[Barnsley F.C.|Barnsley]]. Hull faced Barnsley in their first game, a fixture which Hull won 4–1.<ref name="English Division 2 (old)">{{cite web
| title = English Division 2 (old)
| url = http://www.soccerbase.com/results3.sd?gameid=57680
| publisher = Soccerbase
| accessdate = 2007-07-20}}</ref> Eventually, Hull would finish the season in fifth place.<ref name="HULL CITY fchd"/>

The following season a new ground was built for Hull City across the road from the cricket ground. Still under the managership of [[Ambrose Langley]], Hull continued to finish consistently in the top half of the table. They came close to promotion in the [[1909–10 in English football|1909–10]] season, recording what would be their highest finish until they matched it in 2008.  Hull finished third, level on points with second placed [[Oldham Athletic A.F.C.|Oldham Athletic]], missing promotion on goal average by 0.29 of a goal.<ref name="HULL CITY fchd"/>  Hull regularly finished in the top half of the table prior to the [[World War I|First World War]], but after the war the team finished in the bottom half in seven seasons out of eleven, culminating in [[Promotion and relegation|relegation]] to the [[Football League Third Division North|Third Division North]] in 1930.<ref name="HULL CITY fchd"/>

=== Mid-20th century ===
[[File:Hull City30s.JPG|thumb|Hull City squad of 1936]]
Hull's greatest achievement in cup competitions was in 1930, when they reached the FA Cup semi-finals.<ref name="1919-1939: Inter War Promise Not Fulfilled">{{cite web

| url = http://www.hullcity-mad.co.uk/news/loadfeat.asp?cid=ED91&id=30225

They then knocked out [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]], to meet [[Newcastle United F.C.|Newcastle United]] in the quarter finals. The first leg at [[St James' Park]] finished as a 1–1 draw, but in the replay Hull beat Newcastle 1–0. The semi-final match against [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] took place at [[Elland Road]] in [[Leeds]], the game ended 2–2, and was taken to a replay. Arsenal knocked Hull out at [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]]'s home ground, the game ending 1–0.<ref name="HULL CITY fchd"/>

'''Fernando José Torres Sanz''' (born 20 March 1984) is a Spanish [[association football|footballer]] who plays for [[Premier League]] club [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] and the [[Spain national football team|Spanish national team]] as a [[forward (association football)|striker]]. 

Torres started his career with [[Atlético Madrid]], progressing through their youth ranks. He made his professional debut in 2001 and finished his career with the club having scored 75 goals in 174 [[La Liga]] appearances, earning the nickname ''El Niño'' ("The Kid"). Prior to his La Liga debut, Torres played two seasons in the [[Segunda División]], making 40 appearances and scoring seven goals. He joined Liverpool in 2007, after signing for a club record transfer [[fee]]. He marked his first season at [[Anfield]] by being Liverpool's first player, since [[Robbie Fowler]] in [[1995–96 in English football|1995–96]], to score more than 20 league goals in a season.

He is also a [[Spain national football team|Spanish international]] and made his debut for the country against [[Portugal national football team|Portugal]] in 2003. He has since participated in three major tournaments, [[UEFA Euro 2004]], [[2006 FIFA World Cup]] and [[UEFA Euro 2008]]. He did not score a goal at Euro 2004, but he scored three at World Cup 2006. Torres scored the winning goal for Spain in their 1–0 win over [[Germany national football team|Germany]] in the [[UEFA Euro 2008 Final]].

==Early career==
Born in [[Madrid]], Torres became interested in [[association football|football]] as a child and joined his first team, Parque 84, at the age of five.<ref name="Bio childhood">{{cite web|url=http://www.fernando9torres.com/index.php?s=biografia |title=Bio|publisher = Fernando Torres|accessdate=2008-11-09}}</ref> His father José worked during Torres' childhood, and his mother Flori daily traveled with him to training sessions.<ref name="Fernando Torres talks to Martin Samuel: Liverpool's Spain superstar on Kaka, feeling at home and the battle to stop Manchester United's title chase">{{cite news|first=Martin|last=Samuel|url=http://www.dailymail.co.uk/sport/football/article-1119803/FERNANDO-TORRES-TALKS-TO-MARTIN-SAMUEL-Liverpools-Spain-superstar-Kaka-feeling-home-battle-stop-Manchester-Uniteds-title-chase.html |title=Fernando Torres talks to Martin Samuel: Liverpool's Spain superstar on Kaka, feeling at home and the battle to stop Manchester United's title chase|publisher = ''Daily Mail''|date=2009-01-19|accessdate=2009-02-08}}</ref> His [[grandparent|grandfather]] was not a passionate football fan, but took pride in being an [[Atlético Madrid]] supporter, and Torres inherited the love for the club.<ref name="Bio childhood"/>

Torres started playing football as a [[Goalkeeper (association football)|goalkeeper]], the position his brother played in.<ref>{{cite news |title=Torres asegura que habría sido "un gran portero" |publisher=''Marca'' |language=Spanish|date=2008-04-17 |url=http://www.marca.com/edicion/marca/futbol/internacional/es/desarrollo/1113428.html |accessdate=2008-08-16}}</ref> When he was seven years old, however, he started playing regularly as a [[forward (association football)|striker]] in an indoor league for the neighborhood club, Mario’s Holland,<ref name="Bio childhood"/> using the characters from the [[anime]] [[Captain Tsubasa]] as inspiration.<ref name="Fernando Torres">{{cite web|url=http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v2HKRgIYiNI YouTube |title=Fernando Torres |publisher = YouTube |accessdate=2009-04-10}}</ref> Three years later, aged 10, he progressed to an 11-side team, Rayo 13.<ref name="Bio atletico">{{cite web|url=http://www.fernando9torres.com/index.php?s=biografia&ss=atmadrid |title=Bio|publisher = Fernando Torres|accessdate=2008-11-17}}</ref> He scored 55 goals in a season and was one of three Rayo 13 players to earn a trial with Atlético Madrid.<ref name="Bio atletico"/> He impressed the scouts and joined the club in 1995.<ref name="Bio atletico"/>

==Club career==
===Atlético Madrid===
After progressing through the ranks, Torres won his first important youth title in 1998. [[Atlético Madrid]] sent an under-15 team to compete in the Nike Cup, in Spain and Europe, to play against youth teams from other clubs. Atlético won the tournament.<ref name="Bio atletico"/><ref name=sidlowe>{{cite news|url=http://blogs.guardian.co.uk/sport/2007/07/04/will_torres_be_kops_new_god_or.html |author=Lowe, Sid|title=Will Torres be Kop's new God or just another Fernando? |publisher=''The Guardian''|date=2007-07-04|accessdate=2007-07-04}}</ref> He was later voted the best player in Europe for the age group.<ref name=sidlowe/> In 1999, Torres signed his first professional contract with Atlético Madrid.<ref name="Bio atletico"/> He spent his first year playing in the youth team and moved onto the participating in the Honor Division when he was 16.<ref name="Bio first team">{{cite web|url=http://www.fernando9torres.com/index.php?s=biografia&ss=primerequipo |title=Bio|publisher = Fernando Torres|accessdate=2008-11-17}}</ref> The [[Segunda División 2000–01|2000–01]] season had started badly, as Torres suffered from a cracked shinbone which kept him out until December.<ref name="Bio first team"/> Torres trained with the first team to get prepared

His grandfather was an Atlético Madrid supporter, and this influenced Torres' love for the club. Initially, he played as a goalkeeper, inspired by his older brother. However, at the age of seven, he transitioned to playing as a forward, inspired by the anime series Captain Tsubasa. By the age of ten, he was playing for Rayo 13, where he scored 55 goals in a season, leading to a trial with Atlético Madrid. He joined the club in 1995 and quickly rose through the ranks. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1); Bio childhood (2)]

## Club Career
### Atlético Madrid
At Atlético Madrid, Torres won his first significant youth title in 1998 when the club's under-15 team won the Nike Cup in Spain and Europe. He was later recognized as the best player in Europe for his age group. In 1999, he signed his first professional contract with Atlético Madrid. Despite suffering from a cracked shinbone early in the 2000–01 season, he eventually made his way into the first team. Over the course of six years, he scored 82 goals in 214 appearances for Atlético Madrid. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1); Bio atletico (3); Bio first team (4)]

### Liverpool F.C.
In 2007, Torres transferred to Liverpool F.C., joining the Premier League club for a then-record transfer fee. At Liverpool, he continued to showcase his goal-scoring abilities, scoring 48 goals in 67 appearances. His first season at Anfield was particularly notable, as he became the first Liverpool player since Robbie Fowler in 1995–96 to score more than 20 league goals in a season. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1); Bio first team (4)]

## International Career
Torres has been a key player for the Spanish national team since his debut in 2003. He has participated in three major tournaments: UEFA Euro 2004, the 2006 FIFA World Cup, and UEFA Euro 2008. Although he did not score in Euro 2004, he scored three goals in the 2006 World Cup. Most notably, he scored the winning goal in the UEFA Euro 2008 final, helping Spain secure its first European Championship title. Throughout his international career, he has earned 71 caps and scored 23 goals for Spain. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2 (1); Bio first team (4)]

Torres' journey from a young football enthusiast in Madrid to a world-class striker is a testament to his talent and dedication. His contributions to both Atlético Madrid and Liverpool, as well as his pivotal role in Spain's international success, have cemented his legacy in the sport.
