'''Loïc Rémy''' (born January 2, 1987 in [[Rillieux-la-Pape]]) is a [[France|French]] [[Association football|football]] player of [[Martinique|Martiniquais]] descent, who currently plays French club [[OGC Nice]] in the country's highest football division, [[Ligue 1]]. Rémy primarily plays in the [[Striker|lead striker]] role, but also operates in the [[Midfielder#Winger|winger]] and [[attacking midfield]] positions. He is a former [[France national under-21 football team|France under-21 international]] and currently plays for the [[France national football team|senior team]] having earned his first cap on [[2 June]] 2009 against [[Nigeria national football team|Nigeria]].<ref>http://www.espoirsdufootball.com/4797-equipe-de-france-premiere-selection-pour-loic-remy.html</ref>

==Career==
===Early career===
Rémy was born on [[2 January]] 1987 in a [[Red Cross]] hospital in [[Rillieux-la-Pape]], a [[Communes of France|commune]] in the city of [[Lyon]].<ref>[http://www.leprogres.fr/fr/permalien/article/991627/Remy-un-lionceau-qui-rugit.html Rémy, un lionceau qui rugit]</ref> He began his career, as a youth, playing for local outfit ASPTT Lyon, who were coached by [[René Jacquet]], the brother of [[Coach (sport)|manager]] [[Aimé Jacquet]]. After being spotted by [[Olympique Lyonnais]] scouts, he joined the [[Olympique Lyonnais Reserves and Academy|club's youth academy]]. While training at the [[Centre Tola Vologe]], Rémy trained alongside the likes of [[Karim Benzema]], [[Anthony Mounier]], and [[Hatem Ben Arfa]]. After spending several years in the academy, on [[11 October]] 2006, Rémy signed his first professional contract agreeing to a three-year deal. Three days later, on [[14 October]], he made his professional debut in a [[Derby du Rhône]] match against [[AS Saint-Étienne|Saint-Étienne]] appearing as a substitute, in the 73<sup>rd</sup> minute, for [[Sylvain Wiltord]].<ref>[http://www.lfp.fr/ligue1/feuilleMatch.asp?saison=2006/2007&code_evt=D1&code_jr_tr=J09&num_ordre=4 Lyon v. Saint-Etienne Match Report]</ref> He earned his first start the following month, on [[11 November]], playing 82 minutes in a 1–0 victory over [[CS Sedan Ardennes|Sedan]].<ref>[http://www.lfp.fr/ligue1/feuilleMatch.asp?saison=2006/2007&code_evt=D1&code_jr_tr=J14&num_ordre=9 Sedan v. Lyon Match Report]</ref>

===Loan to Lens===
The [[Ligue 1 2007–08|2007–08 season]] saw Rémy premenantly promoted to the senior team after being assigned the number 12 shirt. Despite being on the first team, he regularly played with the club's [[Championnat de France amateur]] team. Rémy only made six league appearances during the fall season with Lyon. In order to increased the player's playing time, on [[31 January]] 2008, Lyon announced that Rémy would be sent on loan to fellow Ligue 1 club [[RC Lens]]. The deal also included a purchased option, which was estimated to be within the [[€]]8—10 million range.<ref>[http://www.sport24.com/football/transferts/fil-info/loic-remy-prete-a-lens-114352/ Loïc Rémy prêté à Lens]</ref> Rémy was assigned the number 9 shirt and made his debut on [[9 February]] 2008 scoring his first professional goal in the club's 4–1 away victory over [[SM Caen|Caen]].<ref>[http://www.lfp.fr/ligue1/feuilleMatch.asp?saison=2007/2008&code_evt=D1&code_jr_tr=J24&num_ordre=2 Caen v. Lens Match Report]</ref> Two weeks later, he scored a goal in the club's impressive 5–4 victory over [[Le Mans Union Club 72|Le Mans]] in the [[Coupe de la Ligue]] semi-finals.<ref>[http://www.lfp.fr/coupeLigue/feuilleMatch.asp?saison=2007/2008&code_evt=D1&code_jr_tr=T98&num_ordre=1 Le Mans v. Lens Match Report]</ref> Rémy played 96 of the 120 minutes played. On [[15 March]], in front a 40,000+ Lens supporters, he scored the would be game-winning goal against [[Olympique de Marseille|Marseille]], though Marseille would equalize through [[Djibril Cissé]] in the waning minutes of the match. In the [[Coupe de la Ligue Final 2008|2008 Coupe de la Ligue final]] against [[Paris Saint-Germain F.C.|Paris Saint-Germain]], Rémy started the match, but played only 12 minutes before being substituted out due to injury. Lens lost the match 0–1.

Following the successful loan spell, in which Rémy made 12 total appearances and scored four goals, it was announced that he would be returning to Lyon for the [[Ligue 1 2008–09|2008–09 season]].

===Move to Nice===
Despite having two years left on his contract at Lyon, it was announced on [[5 June]] 2008 that Rémy would be joining [[OGC Nice|Nice]] with the player agreeing to a four-year deal and the transfer fee being approximately €8 million making Rémy the biggest transfer in Nice's history.<ref>[http://www.football365.fr/france/infos-clubs/nice/article_242762_Nice-Arrivee-de-Remy.shtml Nice : Arrivée de Rémy]</ref> Upon his arrival, Rémy was assigned the number 7 shirt and made his debut in the club's opening match of the season, a 0–1 loss to [[Le Havre AC|Le Havre]].<ref>[http://www.lfp.fr/ligue1/feuilleMatch.asp?saison=2008/2009&code_evt=D1&code_jr_tr=J01&num_ordre=3 Le Havre v. These goals included a strike against his former club Lyon and a brace against [[US Boulogne|Boulogne]] in the [[Coupe de la Ligue]]. Rémy was a [[France national youth football team|France youth international]] having earned caps with the [[France national under-19 football team|under-19 team]] and  [[France national under-21 football team|under-21 squad]]. Loïc Rémy, born on January 2, 1987, in Rillieux-la-Pape, France, is a professional football player known for his versatility in attacking roles such as striker, winger, and attacking midfielder. He has Martiniquais descent and currently plays for OGC Nice in Ligue 1, wearing the number 7 jersey. Rémy began his youth career with ASPTT Lyon, coached by René Jacquet, before being scouted by Olympique Lyonnais and joining their youth academy. His early professional career started with Lyon, where he made his debut on October 14, 2006, in a Derby du Rhône match against AS Saint-Étienne. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2]

### Loan to RC Lens

In the 2007–08 season, despite being part of the senior team at Lyon, Rémy often played with the club’s Championnat de France amateur team. Due to limited playing time, Lyon loaned him to RC Lens on January 31, 2008. At Lens, Rémy quickly made an impact, scoring his first professional goal on February 9, 2008, in a 4–1 win over SM Caen. He continued to impress, scoring in the Coupe de la Ligue semi-final against Le Mans and contributing to Lens's success in the competition. Although he suffered an injury in the Coupe de la Ligue final, his overall performance during the loan period was notable, leading to his return to Lyon for the 2008–09 season. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2]

### Move to Nice

On June 5, 2008, Rémy transferred from Lyon to OGC Nice for a reported €8 million, making him the biggest transfer in Nice's history. He immediately became a key player for Nice, scoring six goals in his first six matches, including a brace against US Boulogne in the Coupe de la Ligue. Despite a brief scoring drought during the winter months, Rémy returned to form in March 2009, scoring in three consecutive matches. By the end of the season, he had made 36 appearances and scored 13 goals, leading the club in goals. His performances caught the attention of Arsenal, who expressed interest in signing him. [Data: Infobox Football biography 2]

### International Career

Rémy has represented France at various youth levels, including the under-19 and under-21 teams. He notably participated in the 2007 Toulon Tournament with the under-21 squad, scoring against Ivory Coast and Japan. In total, he made nine appearances and scored three goals for the under-21 team. His performances led to his call-up to the senior national team in March 2008, replacing the injured Thierry Henry for friendly matches. '''Landon Donovan''' (born March 4, 1982, in [[Ontario, California]]) is an American [[Association football|soccer]] player who currently plays for [[Los Angeles Galaxy]] in [[Major League Soccer]]. He plays usually as a withdrawn [[forward (association football)|forward]], and can also be used as an [[midfielder (association football)|attacking midfielder]] on either wing.

A member of the inaugural class of the U.S. Soccer residency program in Bradenton, Florida, Donovan was declared player of the tournament for his role in the [[United States U-17 men's national soccer team|national U-17 team]] that finished fourth in the [[1999 FIFA U-17 World Championship]], before signing for [[Bayer 04 Leverkusen|Bayer Leverkusen]]. After six years with the club, including a loan spell at [[San Jose Earthquakes]], Donovan moved to [[Los Angeles Galaxy]] in 2005, though he returned to the [[Fußball-Bundesliga|Bundesliga]] for a six-month spell at the start of 2009 on [[loan (association football)|loan]] to [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]].

For the [[United States men's national soccer team|United States national team]], Donovan currently is the all-time leader in scoring and assists, and has the most [[cap (sport)|cap]]s of all active players.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.ussoccer.com/articles/viewArticle.jsp_14745621.html | title=U.S. Men's National Team Prepares to Kick Off 2009 Confederations Cup Against World Champion Italy | work=[[United States Soccer Federation]] | location=[[Chicago]] | accessdate=2009-06-25}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=FIFA makes Donovan's record official | url=http://soccernet.espn.go.com/print?id=512376&type=story&cc=null | work=[[ESPN]] | location=[[New York City|New York]] | date=29 February 2008 |accessdate=2008-10-29}}</ref> He is the only six-time winner of the [[Honda Player of the Year]] award.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://soccernet.espn.go.com/news/story?id=687455&sec=us&cc=5901 | title=Donovan wins sixth Honda Award | date=20 October 2009 | work=[[ESPN]] | publisher=[[Associated Press]] | location=[[Los Angeles]] | accessdate=2009-10-20}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
The son of Timothy Donovan (a former semi-pro [[ice hockey]] player) and Donna Kenney-Cash, Donovan grew up in [[Redlands, California]]. Encouraged by his older brother, Donovan was five years old when he started playing soccer. He attended [[Redlands East Valley High School]], where he was a standout gymnast and soccer player. 

Donovan was a member of the inaugural class of the [[United States Soccer Federation|U.S. Soccer]] residency program in [[Bradenton, Florida]] with many international teammates including [[Oguchi Onyewu]], [[DaMarcus Beasley]], and [[Bobby Convey]]. The U-17 team that was formed from that class competed at the [[1999 FIFA U-17 World Championship|1999 U-17 World Championship]], finishing in fourth-place with Donovan receiving the Golden Ball as the tournament's outstanding player. Shortly after the tournament, Donovan signed a professional contract with German club [[Bayer Leverkusen]], becoming the youngest American to sign with a foreign club.

==Club career==
===San Jose Earthquakes===
Unhappy with his situation in Germany, he was loaned to the [[San Jose Earthquakes]] of [[Major League Soccer]] for the 2001 season. In MLS, Donovan had immediate success, leading the Earthquakes to MLS Cup championships in 2001 and 2003 and becoming one of the most recognizable faces of soccer in America.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://web.mlsnet.com/news/mls_events_news.jsp?ymd=20051110&content_id=47956&vkey=mlscup2005&fext=.jsp | title=Los Angeles Galaxy mini bios | publisher=[[Major League Soccer]] | date=10 November 2005 | accessdate=2007-06-25}}</ref> In four years in the league, he scored 32 goals and 29 assists in league play, and 10 goals and six assists in the playoffs. Donovan was named [[U.S. Soccer Athlete of the Year]] in 2003.<ref name="athleteoftheyear">{{cite web | url=http://national.soccerhall.org/history/ChevroletWinners.htm | title=U.S. Soccer Athlete of the Year | publisher=[[National Soccer Hall of Fame]] | accessdate=2007-06-26}}</ref>

===Bayer Leverkusen===
On June 3, 2004, Bayer Leverkusen announced that Donovan would return to the club in 2005, and Landon followed suit, announcing his return to Germany on November 23, 2004. He then became the first man to be named U.S. Soccer Athlete of the Year two years in a row,<ref name="athleteoftheyear"/> taking the award for that year. After playing seven games with Bayer Leverkusen, only two of which were starts, Landon stated his intentions to return to MLS. Despite a late offer from English club [[Portsmouth F.C.|Portsmouth]], Bayer Leverkusen officials respected his wishes. However, because San Jose GM [[Alexi Lalas]] had traded away Donovan's rights, the [[Los Angeles Galaxy]], his hometown team, were able to trade leading scorer [[Carlos Ruíz (football)|Carlos Ruiz]] to [[FC Dallas]] to get on top of the [[allocation (MLS)|MLS allocation order]] one week before the season started.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.usatoday.com/sports/soccer/mls/2005-03-30-dallas-ruiz_x.htm | title=Galaxy trade Ruiz to Dallas, Donovan returning to L.A.? | work=[[USA Today]] | publisher=[[Associated Press]] | date=30 March 2005 | location=[[Carson, California|Carson]], [[California]] | accessdate=2007-06-26}}</ref>

===Los Angeles Galaxy===
In his first season with the Galaxy, Donovan scored twelve league goals and ten assists and added four goals and an assist in the playoffs as the Galaxy won the MLS Cup (his third MLS championship to date). He was named to the [[MLS All-Time Best XI]] after the season.<ref>{{cite news | first=Jonathan | last=Nierman | url=http://web.mlsnet.com/news/mls_events_news.jsp?ymd=20051111&content_id=47999&vkey=mlscup2005&fext=.jsp | title=MLS All-Time Best XI t

With a strong leadership team and a passionate fan base, Histon continues to strive for further success in the English football league system.

The '''Faroe Islands 1. deild''', the second division of [[association football|football]] in the [[Faroe Islands]], was founded in 1942. It is organised by the [[Faroe Islands Football Association]]. The league has been known as '''1. deild''' since 2005, because the top division was renamed ''Formuladeildin'' for sponsorship reasons.

It currently has 10 participating clubs. At the end of each season, two teams are relegated and two promoted from what is now the Second Division, pending the fact that the winning team in any given division doesn't already have a senior team in the division it is being promoted to. In such cases the team that finished second will be promoted in its stead. If a team is relegated to a division where one of its teams are already playing, the second best team will move one division down, thereby saving another team from relegation.

==History==
Although the league was founded in 1942, clubs did not compete in European competition until 1993. From 1942 to 1975 it was called ''Meðaldeildin'' (The Middle Division) and from 1976 to 2004 it was called ''2. deild'' (Second Division). The third tier has since adopted this name.

'''Oliver Joseph St John Gogarty''' ([[August 17]], [[1878]] - [[September 22]], [[1957]]) was an [[Ireland|Irish]] [[poet]], [[author]], [[otolaryngologist]], [[athlete]], [[politician]], and well-known [[wit|conversationalist]], who served as the inspiration for [[Buck Mulligan]] in [[James Joyce]]'s novel ''[[Ulysses (novel)|Ulysses]]''. 

==Life==
===Early life===
Gogarty was born [[August 17]], [[1878]] in [[Parnell Square|Rutland Square]], [[Dublin]], the eldest child of Henry Gogarty, a well-to-do [[Dublin]] [[physician]], and Margaret Gogarty (née Oliver), the daughter of a [[Galway]] mill owner.  Three siblings (Henry, Mary, and Richard) were born later.  Gogarty's father, himself the son of a [[physician|medical doctor]], had been educated at [[Trinity College, Dublin|Trinity College]] and owned two fashionable homes in [[Dublin]], which set the Gogartys apart from other [[Irish Catholic]] families at that time and allowed them access to the same social circles as the [[Protestant Ascendancy]].<ref>{{cite book |title= Oliver St. John Gogarty: A Poet and His Times |last= O'Connor |first= Ulick |year= 1963 |publisher= Jonathan Cape |location= London |pages= 12-13}}</ref>

In [[1887]] Gogarty's father died of a [[Appendicitis|burst appendix]], and Gogarty was sent to [[Mungret College]], a [[boarding school]] near [[Limerick]].  He was unhappy in his new school, and the following year he transferred to [[Stonyhurst College]] in [[Lancashire]], [[England]], which he liked little better, later referring to it as "a religious jail".<ref>{{cite book |title= It Isn't This Time of Year At All! |last= Gogarty |first= Oliver |year= 1954 |publisher= Doubleday & Company, Inc. |location= New York |page= 41}}</ref>

Gogarty returned to [[Ireland]] in [[1896]] and boarded at [[Clongowes Wood College]] while studying for [[examinations]] with the [[Royal University of Ireland]].  He was a talented [[athlete]]; in [[England]] he had briefly played for the [[Preston North End FC]] Reserve, and while at [[Clongowes Wood College|Clongowes]] he played for the [[Bohemian FC]].  He also played on [[Clongowes Wood College|Clongowes's]] [[football]] and [[cricket]] elevens.  His extracurricular interests, which also included [[cycling]] and [[alcohol|drinking]], prevented him from being an attentive student, and in [[1898]] he switched to the medical school at [[Trinity College, Dublin|Trinity College]], having [[failure|failed]] eight of his ten [[examinations]] at the [[Royal University of Ireland|Royal]].<ref>O'Connor, pp. 14-16</ref>

===University days===
As one of [[Dublin]]'s "[[medical student|medicos]]", Gogarty was known to be fond of public [[pranks]]<ref>O'Connor, pp. 22-23</ref> and midnight carousing in "the Kips", [[Dublin]]'s red-light district.<ref>O'Connor, pp. 54-55</ref> He had a talent for [[light poetry|humorous]] and [[ribaldry|bawdy verse]], which quickly made the rounds through the city, and sometimes composed [[mnemonic]] lyrics to aid his [[medical school|medical studies]].  He also enjoyed a highly successful [[cycling]] career before being [[banned]] from the tracks in [[1901]] for [[bad language]], and between [[1898]] and [[1901]] he rescued at least four people from [[drowning]].<ref>O'Connor, pp. 24-25, 39</ref>  He became interested in [[Irish nationalism]] after meeting [[Arthur Griffith]] in [[1899]], and contributed [[propaganda]] pieces to ''[[United Irishman|The United Irishman]]'' over subsequent years.<ref>O'Connor, pp. 92-93</ref>

[[File:OSJGogarty1897.jpg|thumb|left|Gogarty in 1897]]

A serious interest in [[poetry]] and [[literature]] also began to manifest itself during his years at [[Trinity College, Dublin|Trinity]].  His [[wit|witty conversation]] made him a favorite with the [[university don|dons]], particularly [[John Pentland Mahaffy]] (formerly the tutor of [[Oscar Wilde]]) and [[Robert Yelverton Tyrrell]], and between [[1901]] and [[1903]] he won three successive Vice-Chancellor's prizes for [[poetry|verse]].  In [[1900]] he made the acquaintance of [[W.B. Yeats]] (of whom his mother highly approved) and of [[George Moore (novelist)|George Moore]] (of whom she did not) and began to frequent [[Celtic revival|Dublin literary circles]].<ref>O'Connor, pp. 29-30</ref>  He also formed close friendships with other up-and-coming young [[poets]], such as [[Seamus O'Sullivan]] and [[James Joyce]].  In [[1904]] he spent two [[academic term|terms]] at [[Oxford]] in order to compete for the [[Newdigate Prize]], but lost to [[George Bell (bishop)|G.K.A. Bell]], the future [[Bishop of Chichester]], who became a friend and frequent correspondent over the next few years.<ref>O'Connor, pp71-75</ref>

[[File:James Joyce Martello Tower.jpg|thumb|right|The Tower in Sandycove]]

Upon returning to [[Dublin]] in the summer of [[1904]], Gogarty made arrangements to [[rent]] the famous [[James Joyce Tower|Martello Tower in Sandycove]].  The primary goal of this scheme, as described by Gogarty in a letter to [[George Bell (bishop)|G.K.A. Bell]], was to "house the Bard" (i.e. [[James Joyce]]), who was without money and required "a year in which to finish his novel."<ref>{{cite book |title= Many Lines to Thee |last= Carens |first= James |year= 1972 |publisher= Dolmen Press |location= Dublin |page= 16}}</ref> The two friends quarreled in [[August]], however, and [[James Joyce|Joyce]] either failed to move in or left shortly after doing so.  [[James Joyce|Joyce]] briefly took up residence in the [[James Joyce Tower|Tower]] the following month, together with Gogarty and his [[Oxford]] friend Samuel Chenevix Trench (a setup which later provided inspiration for the opening chapter of ''[[Ulysses (novel)|Ulysses]])'' but left again suddenly after only six days.<ref>{{cite book |title= James Joyce |last= Ellmann |first= Richard |year= 1982 |publisher= Oxford University Press |location= Oxford |pages= 175}}</ref> Forty years later in [[United States|America]], Gogarty would attribute [[james Joyce|Joyce]]'s abrupt departure to his and S.C. Trench's midnight antics with a loaded [[revolver]].<ref>{{cite book |title= Mourning Became Mrs. Spendlove |last= Gogarty |first= Oliver |year= 1948 |publisher= Creative Age Press |location= New York |pages= 56-57}}</ref>.  [[James Joyce|Joyce]] and Gogarty corresponded intermittently during the early years of Joyce's continental exile and occasionally planned meetings, but contemporaneous letters from Joyce to his brother reveal deep distrust of Gogarty's motives,<ref>Ellmann, p. 842</ref> and their friendship was never fully renewed.  Gogarty made use of the [[James Joyce Tower|Martello Tower]] during the following year as a writing retreat and party venue, and officially held the lease until [[1925]].

In [[1904]] and [[1905]] Gogarty published several short poems in the [[London]] publication ''The Venture'' and in John Eglinton's journal ''Dana''.<ref>{{cite book |title= Surpassing Wit |last= Carens |first= James |year= 1979 |publisher= Columbia University
